rules.text: In Algomancy, each player's goal is to eliminate all of their opponents. A player is eliminated by bringing their life total to 0.
The game is played as a series of global turns. Every player goes through each turn's phases together.
examples: One player finishing planning does not start the battle, and one player finishing deployment does not end the turn: both players move on together, into the same turn 2.

rules.text: A game combines a game mode (such as live draft or constructed) with a player setup (such as 1v1, free-for-all or teams). Any game mode can be played with any player setup.
The digital client this document describes plays two-player games only: 1v1 live draft and 1v1 constructed.

Printed text beats the general rules and the engine's defaults. Where a card's printed text says something different from a general rule or a default, the card is followed, unless the designer has stated a different intent for that card (rule 101.2).
Where the designer has stated that his intent for a card differs from its printed wording, the card works as the designer intended.
examples: Crevice Lurker prints "Abilities cost [one] more to activate or trigger during battle". By Caleb's stated intent it also taxes the {Resonant} attribute's trigger.

rules.text: A designer answer in the rules Q&A (RAQ) takes precedence over this project's own rulings. Where the two disagree, this document states the designer's answer.
When a card's text can be read two ways and neither reading is absurd, take the reading that lets more things happen.

An effect that cannot do everything it says does as much as it can. A part of an effect that cannot happen does not stop the other parts from happening. This does not make half of an action happen: a fight or an exchange that has lost one of its two units does not happen at all (704).
examples: Recall: "Each player recalls a unit and loses 2 life." A player with no unit to recall still loses 2 life.

Amphivore carries two grafts, Flame Juggle and Ralph, and its ability runs three times. The first pass gives Amphivore to the opponent and makes three 1/1s; later passes cannot give it again, so their "If you do" makes nothing, but Flame Juggle still happens all three times.

rules.text: A part of an effect that begins "If you do" happens only if the action before it was done. Parts that are not joined this way are independent.
examples: Shoreline Specter: "After combat, you may recall target ally. If you do, each opponent loses 2 life." If its controller declines the recall, no opponent loses life.

rules.text: Paying a cost is not done "as much as you can". A cost that cannot be paid in full is not paid at all, and the effect it pays for does not happen.
examples: Lost Guardian with Darkblast grafted must pay [Discard a card] twice. With one card in hand nothing is discarded and nothing happens.

rules.text: Every effect is specific to the region it happens in. It never affects anything in another region, and it treats the players and cards in other regions as if they do not exist. A card that says "all" or "each" means all or each in this region.
examples: Cosmic Reversal, cast in one region, leaves a spell unit in another region alone.

rules.text: Regions limit what effects can reach and count. In the digital client they do not limit what players may see: a player may read what happens in a region they are not in.
Each player has their own region and their own life total.
"Each opponent" means each opponent in the region where the effect happens.
examples: Bloated Manablub dies in a region where its opponent is present: that opponent loses 3 life and its controller loses none.

rules.text: If no opponent is in that region, an "each opponent" effect affects nobody. This is normal during deployment, when each player is alone in their own region.
examples: Bloated Manablub's "Each opponent loses 3 life" resolved in a region holding no opponent takes no life from anyone.

rules.text: "Each player" means each player in the region where the effect happens.
examples: Recall ("Each player recalls a unit and loses 2 life") cast in a battle makes both players present in that battle region lose 2 life.

rules.text: A card's owner is the player whose card it is. A card's owner never changes, whoever controls it and whatever zone it goes to.
examples: A unit whose control has been taken is recalled: the player it was stolen from is still the card's owner.
The same recalled unit goes to the hand of the player who controls it, not its owner's hand.

rules.text: A token is owned by the player who created it.
examples: Accelerated Germination makes two tokens owned by its caster; an Arcane Echo copy of an opposing token is owned by the copier; a token taken with Download stays owned by its creator.

rules.text: A card's controller is the player who controls it. The controller and the owner of a card can be different players.
examples: Uglk: each player puts a unit from their own bin into play under the opponent's control. The opponent controls the unit; the card is still owned by the player whose bin it came from.

rules.text: Putting a card into play out of another player's zone makes you its controller, not its owner.
examples: Wake the Dead raising a unit out of the opponent's bin: the caster controls it, and the opponent still owns it.

rules.text: "You" on a card means the controller of the effect. An instruction that names no player (such as "Gain rot") is done by the controller of the effect.
examples: Primordial Coalescence (“Create three Wraiths and gain 2 Rot.”) gives its controller the Wraiths and the rot. Thought Extraction aimed at the opponent makes the opponent discard, and its “You gain 1 rot” still goes to its controller.

rules.text: On a mod, "you" means the controller of the unit the mod is on. A mod applied to another player's unit is controlled by that unit's controller, with its ability.
examples: Pathogenic Enclave augmented onto an enemy unit: when that unit despawns, its controller's tokens are deleted, not yours.

rules.text: "The deck" means the deck of the effect's controller: the shared deck in live draft, and that player's own deck in constructed.
examples: In constructed, Foretell glimpses the top card of its controller's own deck and leaves the opponent's deck alone. In live draft it glimpses the top card of the shared deck.

rules.text: When an effect needs a cost paid before it can happen, the player who would control the effect pays it. If that player does not pay, the effect does not happen.
examples: With an opponent's Crevice Lurker in the battle, a triggered ability asks its own controller whether to pay [one]; paying puts it on the stack.

rules.text: An ally is a unit under your control in the region where the effect is happening.
A unit is its own ally. Only the word "another" leaves the source out.
examples: Shoreline Specter's "recall target ally" may target the Specter itself.
Riftwalker's "another target ally in my formation" offers its column-mate and not itself.

rules.text: Ally and enemy follow control, not ownership. A unit you have taken control of is your ally and its owner's enemy for as long as you control it.
examples: A Good Whale whose control was taken is offered to its new controller as an ally target, and not to its owner.

rules.text: An enemy is a unit not under your control in the region where the effect is happening.
examples: The same stolen Good Whale is offered to its owner as an enemy target, and not to the player who now controls it.

rules.text: To set up a live draft game, follow these steps in order.
Choose the elements the deck is built from. A game of 2 or 3 players uses 3 elements.
Shuffle all the cards of the chosen elements together, with the hybrid cards for each pair of chosen elements, to form the shared deck.
Randomly choose one player to have the initiative.
Each player's life total starts at 30.
Give each player two prismites. They start dormant.

Deal each player 16 cards from the shared deck: 4 for their starting hand, 10 for their pack, and 2 for the draw of their first turn. The 4 and the 2 together are the player's opening hand of 6 cards.
In live draft, the first turn's draw is dealt with the opening hand, so players do not draw in the draw step of the first turn.
In constructed there is no shared deck and there are no packs. Each player plays from their own deck.

In constructed, the first turn has a draw phase like every later turn: each player draws 4 cards, then puts 2 cards from their hand on the bottom of their deck. Print gives the draw phase; no source says the first turn takes it, which is the client's convention.
In constructed, each player's opening hand is 4 cards. No source gives the constructed opening hand; it is the client's convention.
A player whose life total reaches 0 is eliminated.
examples: Haunting Memories sets a player's life total to twice the number of cards in all bins. With every bin empty that is 0, and that player loses.
A player at 3 life takes combat damage from an unblocked attacker and the game is over.

rules.text: A life total reaching 0 ends the game at once, even in the middle of resolving an effect or paying a cost. Nothing waits for the effect to finish. A life cost that would by itself bring its payer to 0 cannot be paid at all (111).
A player wins when all of their opponents have been eliminated. In a two-player game, when one player is eliminated the other player wins.
In a team game, a team wins when the entire opposing team has been eliminated.
In a game of more than two players, the game continues after a player is eliminated. The regions on either side of the eliminated player's region become neighbours.
When a player is eliminated, their pack is recycled: put on the bottom of the deck.
A player may concede. Conceding ends the game in the same way as that player being eliminated: the player who conceded loses.
examples: A player concedes during deployment: the game is over and the other player has won.

rules.text: A player may concede at any time, with no priority and in any phase, even while a decision is waiting on them.
examples: A player who must choose a target for their own spell may concede instead; nothing else can be done until they choose.

rules.text: Running out of cards does not end the game. A player who has to draw from an empty deck draws as many as there are and does not lose.
examples: A player with an empty deck and an empty recycle pile is told to draw 3: nothing is drawn, and nobody has won.

rules.text: The printed Manual names five elements: Fire, Water, Earth, Wood and Metal. The card pool this document describes has seven: those five, plus Light and Dark.
A hybrid card belongs to two elements. A live-draft deck is built from the cards of the selected elements together with the hybrid cards for each pair of them.
Affinity is a card's elemental requirement. A card shows it as element pips, and a player must meet it to play the card.
examples: With three Shards and no water, a player cannot play Curio Drifter [b]; with one water resource they can.

rules.text: The 2023 Rulebook calls the affinity requirement the threshold.

A player's affinity for an element is the number of resources of that element the player has, other than dormant ones (see the dormant rule below). A requirement of N pips of one element is met when the player's affinity for that element is at least N.
examples: With two wood resources, a player meets a [g][g] requirement however many times they play such cards.

rules.text: Expended resources count toward affinity. Whether a resource has been expended this turn does not matter.
examples: All-Consuming Blaze counts two open fire resources and one expended fire resource: 3 damage.
Sylvan Sprouting makes a 1/1 for each wood resource, expended ones included.

rules.text: Meeting an affinity requirement uses nothing up. The same resources meet the affinity requirement of every card a player plays; only the mana cost is paid.
examples: Two wood resources and many Shards pay for many [g][g] cards in one turn: the Shards pay the mana, the two wood meet every requirement.

rules.text: A dormant resource gives no affinity until it is activated.
examples: A dormant fire resource adds nothing to All-Consuming Blaze; two open and one expended fire resource deal 3.

rules.text: Prismites and Shards give no affinity. A Prismite is not wild: it meets no element's requirement.
examples: With six fire resources and two active Prismites, a player still cannot meet Dreadwave Devourer's [b][b]; two water resources meet it.

rules.text: Card text can use a player's affinity as a number. "Your [r]" means the player's fire affinity: the number of fire resources they have, not counting dormant ones (see the dormant rule under 105's affinity count).
examples: A player with two open fire resources and one expended fire resource casts All-Consuming Blaze: their [r] is 3, so it deals 3 damage. A dormant fire resource would not add to it.

rules.text: Some effects let a player play a card ignoring affinity. Such a play does not check the card's affinity requirement. Ignoring affinity does not waive the mana cost: the cost is still paid unless the effect also makes the play free.
examples: A glimpsed card can be played without its pips, but a player who cannot pay its mana cannot play it.
Tides of the Cosmos plays a fire unit for a player whose only resources are water.

rules.text: Applying a modification needs its affinity just as playing the card does. An augment from hand, a Virus applied in battle and a graft from hand or bin each require the card's affinity, and each pays its cost.

Each game has a set of elements. In a live draft it is the selected elements; in constructed it is all seven. An element resource a player creates, by recycling or by exchanging a Prismite, must be of one of the game's elements.
examples: In a fire-water-earth draft, wood and metal resources are refused and never offered.

rules.text: In constructed, a player may create a resource of any of the seven elements, including an element their deck has no cards of.
Resources are the source of mana: a player needs them to play cards. Resources are permanents, and they stay in play.
examples: Two open water resources are two mana and pay for Curio Drifter; a turn later every resource is still in play.

rules.text: There are three kinds of resource: element resources, Prismites and Shards. Each element resource is of one element.
An element resource counts one toward its controller's affinity for its element, except while it is dormant (see 105).
A resource is either dormant (face down) or active (face up). Every resource enters play dormant. Activating a resource turns it face up.
examples: A Shard created by Swirling Shardform enters dormant.

rules.text: Each player starts the game with two dormant Prismites.
A dormant resource cannot be expended for mana. It must be activated first.
examples: Three dormant fire resources give no open mana and cannot pay Ignis Sprite.

rules.text: A player may activate at most two resources per turn. Activating a Shard counts toward that limit.
examples: With a Shard and a Prismite activated, a third activation that turn is refused.

rules.text: Resources are created and activated in the resource step of the planning phase.
A resource can be expended (turned sideways) once per turn for 1 mana, to pay the mana cost of a card or an ability. Expended resources refresh at the beginning of each turn.
Mana has no element. Every resource, of whatever kind, pays generic mana.
examples: Shards pay the mana for [g][g] cards; the two wood resources only meet the affinity.

rules.text: To pay a mana cost, a player expends that many un-expended resources.
examples: Rampart Guardian costs 2: of three open earth, two become expended and one stays open.

rules.text: In the resource step a player may create a resource by recycling a card from hand. The resource enters dormant. There is no limit to how many resources a player creates this way.
examples: Four cards recycled in one resource step make four fire resources, all dormant.

rules.text: Recycling may create a Prismite or a Shard instead of an element resource.
A Prismite made by recycling is the same as a starting Prismite: it enters dormant, takes an activation, gives no affinity, and once active may be exchanged.
When a player activates an element resource, if they then have at least three affinity of that element, they create a Shard. The Shard enters dormant.
examples: Activating a third fire resource creates a dormant Shard.
With fewer than three fire, activating a fire resource creates nothing.

rules.text: The resource being activated counts toward the three.
examples: Two active fire resources plus the one being activated make three: the Shard is created.

rules.text: The bonus is paid on every such activation, not once per game.
examples: A fourth fire resource activated later creates another Shard.

rules.text: The bonus applies to every element, including those whose resource face is not among the printed cards.
Activating a Prismite or a Shard never creates a Shard, however many the player has.
A Prismite is a resource with no element. It gives no affinity, and like any resource it can be expended for 1 mana.

A player may exchange an active Prismite for another resource only in the resource step of the planning phase, never in the haste step (which resources: the element-only rule below). The new resource takes the Prismite's place and keeps its current state, so an exchange never adds mana: an expended Prismite becomes an expended resource.
examples: An expended active Prismite exchanged into fire becomes an expended fire resource; once the player has finished the resource step, a further exchange is refused.

rules.text: A dormant Prismite cannot be exchanged.

The exchange activates the new resource. If that gives the player three affinity of its element, the affinity bonus creates a Shard. The exchange does not use one of the player's two activations for the turn.
examples: A Prismite exchanged into a third copy of an element creates a Shard.
A Prismite exchanged into a second copy creates nothing: the bar is three.

rules.text: A Prismite may be exchanged for any non-Prismite resource: an element resource of one of the game's elements, or a Shard. It cannot be exchanged for another Prismite.
A Shard is a resource of its own kind. It enters dormant, pays one generic mana once activated, gives no affinity, and cannot be exchanged.
An effect that creates a Shard creates a Shard, never a Prismite.
examples: Swirling Shardform creates two dormant Shards, not Prismites.
Hooba-Lan's attack creates a dormant Shard for its controller.

rules.text: X stands for a number that the card defines. An X in a mana cost is chosen by the player who plays the card. A token's X is set by the card that created it. Other cards define X with a "where X is …" clause.
examples: Wildfire asks its caster for X; Self-Assembly with three metal makes a Robot 3.

rules.text: An X spell's mana cost is X alone: the player chooses X, and pays X. Its pips are not part of its cost.
X is chosen and paid when the spell is cast, before it goes on the stack. Only values the player can pay are offered. Responses see the X already chosen.
examples: Wildfire: its caster chooses X from the values they can pay and pays it as the spell is cast, so the spell is on the stack with that X.

rules.text: X may be 0 unless the card says otherwise. Choosing X = 0 is legal even when it makes the effect do nothing.
examples: No Hand Killer can be activated with an empty hand at X = 0, and its [once] is spent.
Torrential Reclamation for X = 0 recalls nothing, but each player still sacrifices a unit.

rules.text: An X spell (a card whose mana cost is X) that prints "X can't be zero" must be cast with X of at least 1. A player who cannot pay at least 1 cannot cast it.
examples: Frosted Denial cannot be cast with no open mana.

rules.text: An effect that refers to a spell's cost reads its printed cost, not what was actually paid after cost modifiers. For an X spell, that is the X it was cast for.
examples: Squish taxed up to 4 by Stasis Sentry and Tranquility is still a 2 to Arcane Concentrator and Channeled Amalgam.

rules.text: An X card that is not being cast has a cost of 0. This holds for an X card in a hand, a bin, the deck or the cache, and for a unit in play.
examples: Living Vault caches a card from hand by paying its cost: an X card in hand costs 0, so it can be cached for [0].

rules.text: When an effect lets a player play an X spell for free, the spell is played with X = 0. An X that is a bracketed additional cost is not the mana cost: it is still chosen and paid.
examples: A fulfilled prophecy releases an X spell for X = 0: no X is asked and no mana is paid.
Tides of the Cosmos counts an X spell as cost 0 and plays it at X = 0.

rules.text: An X spell that prints "X can't be zero" therefore cannot be played for free. An effect that plays cards for free cannot play it.
examples: Tides of the Cosmos cannot pick Frosted Denial; an X card that may be zero is still a pick.

rules.text: Stasis Sentry gives spells with a base cost of [three] or less a base cost of [three] during battle. On an X spell it raises the X instead of the price: X must be at least 3, and the spell costs exactly X.
examples: Under a Stasis Sentry the X menu starts at 3, and X = 3 deals 3.
Under a Stasis Sentry, X = 3 costs [3] and X = 5 costs [5].

rules.text: A copy of a spell uses the original's X. The X is not chosen or paid again.
examples: Maelstrom Charger copies Volatile Toxicity: the copy uses the original's X, and no second unit is sacrificed for it.

rules.text: A token's X is set by the card that created it. "Create a Crystal 3" creates a Crystal whose X is 3.
examples: A Poison created with X = 5 reads "Put 5 -1/-1 counters on target unit."

rules.text: A Robot's X is the number of +1/+1 counters on it. It spawns with X counters, and if the number of counters changes, so does its X.
A number an effect counts, such as a "where X is …" clause or an amount "equal to" or "for each" something, is counted when the effect resolves, not when it was played or triggered.
examples: Flamebreath Initiate removed with its trigger on the stack has no adjacent allies, so X = 0 and it still makes a Fireball 1.

rules.text: An X that a paid cost defines is read as the cost is paid. Volatile Toxicity's X is the sacrificed unit's defense as it was when the unit was sacrificed.
When a card asks a player to choose or predict a number, there is no limit the card does not print. A player may name any number in the card's range.
examples: Prediction Prophet: a player predicts a life total nine higher than their current one. They gain 9 life during the battle, the prediction is matched at the start of deployment, and they get the 5/5.

rules.text: This document writes the game's symbols in brackets, as the card data does. The element pips are [r] Fire, [b] Water, [e] Earth, [g] Wood, [m] Metal, [l] Light and [d] Dark.
[x] is X generic mana. A number in brackets, as a digit or a word ([1], [three]), is that much generic mana. A number followed by pips ([3b]) is that much mana together with that affinity.
A card is a physical Algomancy card: one with an Algomancy card back.
Units, spells and spell units are cards. Card text that refers to a "card" being played includes a unit being played.
examples: Void Mandible ("When a nontoken card is played during battle, sacrifice me. If you do, negate that effect.") answers a {Battle} unit being played.

rules.text: Every card has a name, and most cards have abilities. The other parts a card can have are described in section 200.
A token is a unit or a spell that an effect creates directly into play. A unit token functions as a unit, and a spell token is a spell.
examples: Mycelial Mentor reads "When you create a token, target ally gains +3/+3." Its controller creates a Poison, a spell token, and the Mentor triggers just as it would for a 1/1 unit.

rules.text: For card text, a token is not a card: text that refers to a "card" does not include a token, even though a unit token is a unit and a spell token is a spell. The printed rules call tokens "temporary cards" to describe them to players; that does not make a token a card.
examples: A player casts a Fireball token in battle. That is playing a spell, so abilities that watch for a spell being played see it; it is not playing a card, so abilities that watch for a card being played do not.

rules.text: A spell token is a token wherever it is: in play, and also on the stack after it has been cast.
examples: Download ("Gain control of target token") can take a Fireball token that has already been cast and is on the stack.

rules.text: A unit that an effect creates is a unit token, including an X/X unit whose X the creating card sets.
examples: Spawntender creates an 8/8 unit. That unit is a token, so Download ("Gain control of target token") can take it.

rules.text: A token is created in the region its source is in when the effect that creates it resolves, not in its controller's home region.
examples: Life Plant attacking in the enemy region creates its 1/1 units in that region.

rules.text: A token is never trashed, because only a card can be trashed. A unit token can still die.
examples: A unit token dying in battle does not add to the number of cards trashed in that battle.

rules.text: A card in play that transforms is the same unit with its other face up. It does not leave play or enter play, and it keeps its counters and damage.
examples: Scholar of the Void transforms into Beyond, Codex Incarnate: same unit, and its counters and damage survive.

rules.text: A back face is not a token, and a transformed card is still a card.
examples: A transformed Scholar of the Void that died can be returned from the bin as a Scholar.

rules.text: A card can only transform into a back face it has. A unit that gains a transform ability from a mod transforms only if that unit's own card has that back face.
examples: Scholar of the Void augmented onto another unit cannot transform its host.

rules.text: A copy of a spell is a new effect on the stack. It was not played.
examples: Earthbound Replicator copies a spell that targets it. The copy is not played, so it does not set off the Replicator again: one copy, and no more.

rules.text: A copy of a spell is not a token.
examples: Download cannot take a spell copy made by Earthbound Replicator.

rules.text: A token that an effect creates as a copy of a card is a token.
examples: The copy Echo of Despair makes of itself is a token.

rules.text: A nontoken unit that becomes a copy of a token is still a nontoken unit.
examples: Borrower of Forms copying a Robot token is a nontoken unit, which Download cannot take.

rules.text: Two copies of the same card are two different objects. Card text that says "another" or "other" compares objects, never card names.
examples: A host wearing two Rotbeast augments: each Rotbeast's "my other Augments" includes the other Rotbeast.

rules.text: An object stays the same object while it stays where it is. A unit that leaves play and comes back is a new object.
examples: Engorged Caudex recalled and played again draws again from its once-per-turn graft in the same turn.

rules.text: An ability is text on a card that describes the card's effects. Most cards have abilities.
An activated ability is written with a colon. Everything before the colon is a cost that must be paid to activate the ability; what follows the colon is its effect.
examples: Living Forge reads "[three]: Create a Robot 2." With two resources its ability cannot be activated; paying three makes a Robot.

rules.text: A player may activate an activated ability any time they have priority, in battle or in deployment, as many times as they can pay its cost, unless the ability limits itself (see [once]).
examples: With six resources, Living Forge makes two Robots in one deployment, and makes another in battle when its controller holds priority and pays again.

rules.text: An activated ability that is used from the hand can be used during battle even if its card has no {Battle} icon.
examples: Dropslime's discard-me ability can be used in battle.

rules.text: A triggered ability happens when something else takes place. "When" and "Whenever" mark a triggered ability; one can also happen at a stated time, such as "After combat" or "At the end of turn".
examples: Skittering Blight gains its controller a rot when it spawns; Harbinger of Immolation makes a Fireball at the end of the turn; an attacking Wisp sacrifices itself after combat.

rules.text: A trigger condition is checked once, when the event happens. If it was false then, nothing that happens later makes the ability trigger; once the ability has triggered, it resolves even if the condition stops being true.
examples: A spell played at another unit and then retargeted onto Earthbound Replicator makes no copy: "a spell targeting me" is judged as the spell is played.

rules.text: An amount a triggered ability uses is measured when the ability resolves, so responses can change it.
examples: Astral Tidewraith attacks: its trigger deals each player damage equal to the cards in their hand, counted as the trigger resolves, not when it triggered.

rules.text: A triggered ability checks its condition again when it resolves only if its text says so, as "if I am still in formation" does.
examples: Hooba-Nan says "if I am still in formation", so that is checked again on resolution: if Hooba-Nan dies with its attack trigger on the stack, no 1/1s are made.

rules.text: An ability that triggers when an ally becomes the target of a spell triggers once for each targeted ally.
examples: An enemy spell targeting two allies puts Earnest Defender's ability on the stack twice.

rules.text: A static ability makes a continuous change to the game for as long as its card is in play.
examples: While Glowhaven Elder is in play, your other units are +1/+1; when it leaves play, they lose the bonus.

rules.text: A replacement effect, written "If … instead", changes an event as it happens. The replacement itself does not use the stack.
examples: With Flux Resonator in play, Living Forge's Robot 2 arrives with three counters, and no extra item goes on the stack for the replacement.

rules.text: If the substitute a replacement effect names includes a target, the event is still replaced at once, and the substitute is put on the stack as a triggered ability so that its target can be chosen.
examples: Beyond, Codex Incarnate's rot replacement removes the rot damage at once, then asks its controller for the target unit that gets the -1/-1 counters.

rules.text: An option a card offers as a spell is played, such as Maelstrom Charger's, is neither a triggered nor an activated ability. It does not go on the stack, it cannot be responded to, and effects on triggered or activated abilities do not apply to it.
examples: Crevice Lurker's tax on triggered abilities does not reach Maelstrom Charger's option.

rules.text: Text after a card's [Augment] or graft symbol is active when the card is played normally, not only when the card is a mod.
examples: A Wraith token in play uses its own [Augment] text: at the start of deployment its controller puts a -1/-1 counter on an ally.

rules.text: An effect can give units an ability. The ability goes to the units the effect names as it resolves; a unit that arrives afterwards does not gain it.
examples: Reforge the Dead's grant lasts until regroup and reaches only the units already there.

rules.text: A granted ability is an ability the unit has. An effect that removes a unit's abilities removes the granted abilities the unit has when the removal applies; an ability granted to the unit afterwards is not removed.
examples: A unit that loses all abilities also loses an ability Reforge the Dead gave it earlier; if Reforge the Dead resolves after the removal, the unit has the new ability.

rules.text: An ability marked [once], and a bounded graft ([Switch1]), can be activated or triggered only once per turn.
examples: Unstable Apparition ([once]: when you play a nontoken spell, create a Fireball X) makes a Fireball for the first spell its controller plays this turn, nothing for the second, and a Fireball again next turn.

rules.text: The use is spent when the ability is activated or put on the stack, whether or not it then resolves. A fizzle, a negation, or a run that finds nothing to do does not give it back. Only a declined or impossible optional choice leaves the use unspent (rule 109.9b), even when that choice comes as the ability resolves.
A player who declines an optional ("you may") bounded ability, or who could not be offered it at all, has not spent the use. The ability can trigger again later in the turn.
examples: Hexbane Shiitake declined on one spell is offered again on the next spell that turn.

rules.text: Activating a [once] ability with X = 0 is legal, and it spends the use.
examples: No Hand Killer can be activated with an empty hand, and the activation spends its [once].

rules.text: A change of controller does not give back a spent use: the limit stays with the unit.
Moving a mod onto another unit (Reconfigure) does not give back its spent use.
examples: A Graxxlid augment already activated this turn and moved by Reconfigure cannot be activated again that turn.

rules.text: A unit that leaves play and is played again is a new object, and its abilities have their uses again, even in the same turn.
examples: Engorged Caudex recalled and played again draws from its [Switch1] graft a second time that turn.

rules.text: Turning a card over does not give back a spent use: a transformed card is the same unit.
If the cause of a graft composite is bounded, the whole composite can trigger only once per turn, unbounded grafts included.
If the cause is unbounded, the composite can trigger any number of times, but each bounded graft in it is included only the first time in a turn.
examples: Omniwield Evoker activated twice in a turn creates the Robot from its bounded graft only the first time.

rules.text: An effect that repeats a graft composite (Amphivore, Lost Guardian) repeats its bounded grafts too.
examples: Amphivore triples a bounded "Create three" graft.

rules.text: Each mod has its own use. Two copies of the same bounded graft on one host each have one use.

A bounded ability that works while its card is in a bin, such as Rotling's "When I leave your bin", is limited once per turn for each player and card name: copies of one card in one player's bin share one use.
examples: Rotling's [Switch1] works once per turn from the bin and is available again the next turn.
Two Rotling leaving one bin in the same turn share one [Switch1] use: the second copy is not offered it.

rules.text: A bounded "When I am trashed" ability is limited for each trashed card, not for each player and card name: two copies of one card trashed in the same turn each trigger.
examples: Two Maw of Despair discarded in the same turn each trigger their [Switch1] Glimpse 2.

rules.text: A target is something a card or ability chooses, with the word "target", to receive its actions. The targets are selected as the card is played.
examples: Fight ("Target ally and another target unit fight") takes both units as targets as it is played.

rules.text: Targets are chosen as the effect is put on the stack: when a card is played, when an ability is activated, and when a triggered ability is put on the stack. Every target of the effect is chosen then.
examples: Plodding Pebble carries a grafted Leaping Lillik ("Delete target unit"). A Fireball damages the Pebble: as the trigger goes on the stack, the delete's target is chosen. With no enemy in the region, it must be one of your own units.

rules.text: Each "target" in an effect's text is a separate target. An effect that says "target" twice chooses two targets.
examples: Squish chooses two targets as it is played: an ally and another unit.

rules.text: "Up to N target" lets the player choose any number of targets from none to N.
examples: Twin Flame ("up to two target units") can be played with no targets.

rules.text: The number of targets an effect has is the number chosen as it was put on the stack. A target that is later lost still counts.
examples: Twin Flame declared with two targets, one of them later removed, is still not "a single target" for Envoy of Lightning.

rules.text: A choice that an effect's text does not make with the word "target" is not a target. Nothing is declared for it as the effect goes on the stack, and an effect that answers targeting cannot answer it.
examples: Meteor Shower's rockfall chooses rather than targets, so Boon of Protection has nothing to negate.

rules.text: Such a choice cannot be redirected by an effect that changes targets, and it does not trigger "when I become targeted".
examples: The Wraith's "an ally" never fires a "becomes targeted" ability.

rules.text: Dividing or distributing an amount among a targeted player's units is not targeting those units. The division is made as the effect resolves.
examples: Channel Through targets X allies and an opponent as it is played, and divides its damage among that opponent's units only as it resolves.

rules.text: The Wraith's "an ally" is not a target, but the ally is chosen as the trigger is put on the stack. If that ally has left play when the trigger resolves, the trigger fizzles.
examples: Three Wraith triggers may all choose the same 1/1; one -1/-1 counter lands and the other two fizzle.

rules.text: Only a legal target can be chosen. Whether a target is legal depends on the kind of thing the text names (a unit, an ally, a player, an effect, a card in a bin) and on any restriction written on the target itself.
examples: Minor Kraken ("target unit with 5 or less defense") cannot target a unit with 6 defense.

rules.text: A clause that describes the target ("with 5 or less defense", "that targets an allied effect", "in your bin") limits which targets are legal. An "if" clause attached to the action ("delete target unit if it has a -1/-1 counter on it") does not limit the choice; it is checked as the effect resolves.
examples: Boon of Protection is not offered against an effect that targets nothing allied.

rules.text: An effect on the stack can be a target. A unit in play is not an effect, so it cannot fill a target that asks for an effect.
examples: Enigmatic Warder cannot become the target of a negate that wants a spell effect.

rules.text: "Target player" can be any player present in the region where the effect resolves, the effect's controller included. "Target opponent" is any such player other than the effect's controller. In battle both players are present.
examples: Soul Siphon played in battle offers its own controller as well as the opponent as "target player".

rules.text: "Target formation" targets one player's whole side of a battle in that region: every unit arrayed there, not a column.
examples: Galactic Germination counts three units across two columns of the targeted formation.

rules.text: A formation stays a legal target while its battle lasts, even if every unit leaves it.
examples: Galactic Germination aimed at a formation that has emptied creates nothing, and does not fizzle.

rules.text: An ally is a unit under your control in the region the effect is happening in. An enemy is a unit not under your control in that region.
A unit is its own ally. An effect that targets "an ally" or "target ally" can choose its own source unless the text says "another".
examples: Shoreline Specter's "recall target ally" may target the Specter itself.

rules.text: Ally and enemy follow control, not ownership. A unit you have taken control of is your ally and its owner's enemy, in that region, for as long as you control it.
examples: An opponent ambushes with Orblish Horroth to recall target ally. Before it resolves, you take control of that unit; it is no longer their ally, and the ambush recalls nothing.

rules.text: Ally is measured from the effect's controller, never from the player making the choice.
examples: With the opponent's Fight on the stack, an enemy unit cannot fill its ally target, while another of the Fight controller's units can.

rules.text: "Another" excludes whatever the sentence's other noun is. It excludes the source only when that other noun is the source ("I fight another target unit"); in "from target unit onto another target unit" it excludes only the first target.
An effect can target a unit only in the region where the effect is happening.

An effect on the stack can be targeted only by an effect in its own region, since each region has its own stack (rule 601.2a). A card in a player's bin can be targeted only by an effect that resolves in a region where that player is present.
A player's cache, and a player as a target, can be targeted only by an effect that resolves in a region where that player is present.
examples: In deployment Prismatic Observer reaches only its controller's cache; in battle it reaches both.

rules.text: Where an effect asks for two or more targets together, one object cannot be two of them, as with Twin Flame's "up to two target units". This holds when targets are changed as well as when they are chosen.
examples: Divine Intervention cannot make Twin Flame target one unit twice.

rules.text: Different effects may target the same object.
examples: An opponent's Luminous Arc is aimed at one of your Good Whales; you answer with Organic Exchange targeting both your Good Whales. The Luminous Arc still resolves.

rules.text: A card or ability that needs targets can be played only if every target it requires can be chosen at the same time, each one legal and different from the others. A card that targets nothing has no such requirement.
examples: Fight cannot be played unless its region holds an ally and another unit.
Rebalance, which targets nothing, can be played with no unit of its controller's.

rules.text: A target that was legal when it was chosen but is not legal when the effect begins to resolve is lost, as if it had left play.
examples: A unit that grows past 5 defense before Minor Kraken resolves is not recalled.

rules.text: An effect that changes another effect's targets must choose each new target as that target was first chosen: legal for that target's own kind and restriction, and not an object already chosen for another target of the same part of the effect.
examples: Enigmatic Warder cannot take Throw off a Cliff, which needs a unit with 4 or more defense.
Enigmatic Warder cannot move itself into a target already held by the same effect's other target.

rules.text: A target that is kept when targets are changed is not a change, and it is not judged again then.
examples: Divine Intervention can keep one target of an effect while changing another.

rules.text: Changing an effect's targets before it resolves can save it from fizzling.
examples: A spell whose target is about to become illegal is given a legal new target by Enigmatic Warder before it resolves, and then it does not fizzle.

rules.text: Applying an augment, a graft or a Virus to a unit targets that unit.
examples: Grafting onto Mohruung targets it, so its "when I become targeted" ability makes a Crystal.

rules.text: A Virus being applied is an effect on the stack that targets its host. It can be redirected, and an effect that answers "target effect targeting me" or an effect targeting an ally can answer it.
examples: Graxxlid ("Negate target effect targeting me") can negate a Virus being applied to it.
Boon of Protection can negate a Virus being applied to an allied unit.

rules.text: An ability that triggers "when I become targeted" triggers whenever its unit is targeted, by a spell, an ability, an augment, a graft or a Virus. When the effect that targeted is put on the stack, the trigger goes on the stack above it and so resolves first. When a graft targets the unit, the unit triggers first, before the graft is applied.
examples: Mohruung targeted by an augment makes a Crystal 2.
Grafting onto Mohruung makes a Crystal 2.
A spell aimed at Mohruung waits on the stack under Mohruung's trigger, so the Crystal 2 is made before the spell resolves.

rules.text: A unit that "must be targeted if able" (Gatekeeper of Souls) must be one of the targets of an effect whose targets are selected during battle, when it can legally be one. Once it is among the targets, the effect's other targets may be anything legal.
examples: Twin Flame aims at Gatekeeper of Souls first, then at any other unit.

rules.text: With two such units in the region, each must be targeted if able: a two-target effect must target both.
examples: With two Gatekeepers in the region, a two-target spell targets both.

rules.text: "If able" means "if it is a legal target for this effect". An effect whose targets cannot be units, such as one that targets a formation, is not compelled.
examples: Gatekeeper of Souls does not compel Galactic Germination, which targets a formation.

rules.text: The compulsion applies only to choosing targets. It never makes a target already chosen illegal.
examples: A Gatekeeper of Souls that arrives after an effect's targets were chosen does not make those targets illegal.

rules.text: A cost is something a player must pay to do something: to play a card, to apply a mod, or to activate an ability. A card's mana cost, the additional costs in its brackets, and everything before the colon of an activated ability are costs.
A mana cost is paid by expending resources: each resource can be expended once per turn for 1 mana, to pay the mana cost of a card or of an ability.
examples: with two open resources, paying [one] for Auric Ascendant's ability and then playing Shard Sprite expends both; a second 1-cost card is not playable that turn, and both resources are open again next turn.

rules.text: Meeting a card's affinity requirement is not paying a cost. Nothing is spent to meet it, and resources that are already expended still count toward it.
examples: a player with two Wood resources, both already expended, still meets a requirement of two Wood pips.

rules.text: Besides mana, a cost may require a player to pay life, gain debt, discard cards, sacrifice units, erase cards from their bin, remove counters, recall an ally or erase a mod. A cost of any kind is paid in full before the thing it pays for is put on the stack.
examples: Slag Spewer's "[one], Erase one of my mods:" erases the mod as the ability is activated, before anyone can respond.

rules.text: A cost that sacrifices units can be paid only with units the player controls in the region where the cost is paid. They cannot sacrifice a unit they do not control, or a unit of theirs that is in another region.
examples: when Volatile Toxicity is played in battle, its sacrifice menu offers the unit in the battle region and not the unit the player left at home.

rules.text: A cost that removes counters from the player's allies, or recalls an ally, likewise uses only the player's own units in the region where the cost is paid.
examples: Auric Ascendant’s "Recall another ally" cost offers the ally fighting beside it, never the ally at home and never itself.

rules.text: What was paid is fixed at the moment it is paid. An effect that reads a paid cost (such as "the defense of the sacrificed unit") reads it as it was when it was paid.
examples: Volatile Toxicity is cast by sacrificing a Good Whale (7/5). Its X is fixed at 5 as the cost is paid, and it makes a Poison 5 and a Fireball 5.

rules.text: A copy of a spell does not pay the original's additional cost again. It uses what the original paid, including the original's X.
examples: Maelstrom Charger copies a Volatile Toxicity; the copy makes its Poison and Fireball from the one sacrifice the original paid for.

rules.text: A cost that cannot be paid in full cannot be paid at all. A card whose cost cannot be paid cannot be played, and an ability whose cost cannot be paid cannot be activated; nothing is paid, and the play or activation is not offered.
examples: Auric Ascendant ("[one], Recall another ally:") is not offered while it has no other ally, so its [one] is never paid.

rules.text: A cost made of several parts is paid all or nothing. If any part cannot be paid, no part is paid, including the mana.
examples: Instrument of Reassignment ("[x], Sacrifice another nontoken unit:") with no other nontoken unit pays neither the mana nor anything else.

rules.text: A player may pay N life only while they have more than N life. A life cost that would bring them to 0 cannot be paid.
examples: at exactly 9 life, Glararr's "Pay 9 life:" cannot be activated.

rules.text: An activated ability's whole cost is paid when the ability is activated, before it is put on the stack. A fixed cost is paid after the ability's targets are chosen. A variable cost (one whose amount is X) is paid first, and what is paid sets X, before any target is chosen. No player may respond between the payment and the ability going on the stack, and negating the ability does not refund it.
examples: Infernal Cultivator's "Sacrifice X units:" kills the units as the ability is activated, so a negation cannot give them back.

rules.text: When an activated ability's cost sacrifices its own source, the source is in the bin while the ability waits on the stack.
examples: Throwing Boulder ("Sacrifice me: I deal 3 damage to any target.") is in the bin as soon as the ability is on the stack.

rules.text: A printed condition on activating an ability ("Activate this ability only if …") is checked before any cost is paid. If it is not met, the ability cannot be activated. It is not checked again when the ability resolves.
examples: Throwing Boulder with no adjacent ally is not offered its ability.

rules.text: When a triggered ability's effect says "sacrifice me. If you do, …", the sacrifice is part of the effect, not a cost: the ability goes on the stack with its source still in play, players may respond, and the source is sacrificed as the ability resolves. The sacrifice is not optional. If the source is no longer in play when the ability resolves, it cannot be sacrificed, and the "If you do" part does nothing.
examples: Eldritch Dreamtender's column deals combat damage to an opponent. Its ability goes on the stack with Dreamtender still in play; Dreamtender is sacrificed when the ability resolves, and only then is the opponent's hand looked at and a card discarded.
Dreamtender is destroyed in response to its ability. When the ability resolves, nothing is sacrificed, so no hand is looked at and nothing is discarded.

rules.text: A sacrifice the text makes optional ("you may sacrifice me. If you do, …") is the player's choice. A player who declines it gets nothing from the "If you do" part.

A payment that an effect's text asks for while it resolves ("you may pay [one] to …", "unless its controller pays [x]") is not a cost of putting it on the stack. The ability goes on the stack without it, and the player decides whether to pay when it resolves.
examples: Xenopod Progenitor's trigger goes on the stack with no payment asked; its [1] is asked as it resolves.

rules.text: Some cards in play change what it costs to play cards or to activate or trigger abilities. Such a cost modifier works only while its source is in play, only in its source's region, and, unless it says otherwise, for every player in that region, its controller included.
examples: an opponent's Crevice Lurker in the battle region taxes your abilities, not only its controller's.
Tranquility applied as an augment still taxes spells from its host.

rules.text: Cost modifiers add up. Two modifiers that each add [one] add [two].
examples: two Crevice Lurkers make an activated [1] cost [3] in battle.

rules.text: A cost reduced below zero is zero.

A cost modifier applies to what its text names. One that names "spells" applies to every spell played, spell units and spell tokens included. One that names "cards" applies to every card played, units included, and not to spell tokens, which are not cards. Neither applies to applying a mod, which is not playing a card.
examples: Tranquility ("Spells cost [one] more") taxes a Fireball token cast in battle.
Arbiter of Armistice ("Cards played during battle gain [Pay 2 life]") takes no life for a spell token.

rules.text: A cost modifier may give cards an additional cost ("Cards played during battle gain [Pay 2 life]"). The player who plays the card pays it, with the card's other costs, before the card is put on the stack. If it requires a sacrifice, that player chooses the unit from their own units. A card whose imposed cost cannot be paid cannot be played.
examples: under an opponent's Vengeance, the player choosing the sacrifice is offered only their own units.
under Arbiter of Armistice, a player who cannot pay the 2 life cannot play the card.

rules.text: A card played as an Ambush is a card played. During battle, an imposed cost on "cards played" applies to it.

A modifier that makes abilities cost more "to activate or trigger" applies to activated abilities and to triggered abilities, graft triggers and the triggers of attributes such as Alluring and Resonant included. It does not apply to static abilities, to playing or applying cards, or to an option that is neither activated nor triggered.
examples: Crevice Lurker taxes a graft trigger.
Crevice Lurker taxes Resonant's extra damage, by the designer's stated intent.
applying an augment during battle is not taxed.

rules.text: When a triggered ability would be put on the stack while such a tax applies, the player who would control it chooses whether to pay the tax. If they pay, the ability is put on the stack. If they decline, or cannot pay, it does not trigger.
examples: with a Crevice Lurker in the battle, you decline to pay the tax on your own Origon's trigger, so Origon does not negate your first spell of the battle.

rules.text: A triggered ability that does not trigger because its tax was declined or could not be paid does not use up a "[once]" or other once-per-turn limit.

A modifier that gives spells a minimum base cost ("Spells with base cost [three] or less have a base cost of [three]") raises the cost of a spell whose printed cost is a number. For a spell whose cost is X, it instead makes the smallest X that may be chosen equal to that minimum, and the spell costs exactly the X chosen.
examples: under Stasis Sentry in battle, Wildfire's X menu starts at 3, and X = 3 deals 3.

rules.text: A spell token's printed cost is 0, so such a modifier makes a spell token cost its minimum.
examples: under Stasis Sentry, casting a Fireball token in battle costs [3].

rules.text: A cost reduction a player has already paid for belongs to that player. It stays when its source leaves play, it applies in whatever region the player plays their next card, and it ends when its text says it ends: "the next card you play this phase" lasts until that card is played or the phase ends.
examples: sacrificing Deferral Drone in response does not take away the discount already paid for.
the discount ends when the phase ends, even within the same turn.

rules.text: When an effect refers to a card's cost, it means the card's printed cost. Cost modifiers do not change it. The cost of an X spell that is being or has just been cast is the X paid; an X card that is not being cast has a cost of 0.
examples: Squish, paid at [4] under Stasis Sentry and Tranquility, is read as a 2-cost spell by Arcane Concentrator.

rules.text: Some cards print another way to play or use them, with its own cost: a Prophecy or Ambush banner, or a "Discard me" line. Such a cost is paid like any other cost: its mana is spent and its affinity requirement must be met.

Discarding a card through its "Discard me" line is not playing it. A player may do it whenever they hold priority in battle, and during their own deployment, unless the line itself is marked with a timing.
examples: Dropslime's discard-me line is offered in battle.

rules.text: A card played for free (released by a fulfilled prophecy, or played by an effect such as Tides of the Cosmos) pays no mana cost and ignores its affinity requirement. Its additional bracketed costs are still paid.
examples: Tides of the Cosmos plays a fire unit for a player with only water resources.
Volatile Toxicity played by Tides still sacrifices a unit.

rules.text: An X spell played for free is played with X = 0. A card that says "X can't be zero" therefore cannot be played for free.
examples: Tides of the Cosmos cannot play Frosted Denial.

rules.text: When an effect is repeated by a multiplier ("trigger two copies of this graft ability"), a cost the repeated effect carries is paid once for each copy. The whole multiplied cost is paid all or nothing: if it cannot all be paid, none of it is paid and that effect does not happen.
examples: under Lost Guardian, a "[Discard a card]:" graft pays twice and resolves twice.
with one card in hand, the doubled [Discard a card] is not paid at all.

rules.text: A cost a graft adds ("{graft} [cost]: effect") must be paid; it cannot be declined. If it cannot be paid, none of the composite ability goes on the stack: not the graft's effect, the host's own effect, or any other graft with it. The exception is a played spell that carries a {Modular} graft part: there an unpayable grafted cost skips only that part, and the spell is not withheld.
Each player begins the game with 30 life. A player whose life is reduced to 0 is eliminated.
A life total changes only by being gained or lost. Damage dealt to a player makes that player lose that much life, and paying life is losing it.
examples: Throwing Boulder's 3 damage to a player is a loss of 3 life, and the [Pay 2 life] that Arbiter of Armistice adds to a card played during battle is a loss of 2 life.

rules.text: An effect that makes players gain or lose life reaches only the players in its region. "Each opponent loses 1 life" means each opponent in the current region.
examples: Bloated Manablub dying in battle makes each opponent in that region lose 3 life.

rules.text: The life a player has lost in a battle is the sum of all their life losses in that battle. Life gained in the battle does not reduce it.
examples: a player loses 10, gains 8 and loses 3 in one battle; Soul Siphon makes a 13/13.

rules.text: Effects that multiply life gained or lost multiply together: with n effects that each double it, the amount is multiplied by 2 to the power n. The multiplied amount is gained or lost at once, before it is checked whether the player has reached 0 life.
examples: three Arbiters of Vitality multiply a life loss by 8.

rules.text: If a player's life total "can't change", that player neither gains nor loses life while the effect lasts.
examples: Suspend stops the target's life total moving in either direction for the battle.

rules.text: Damage is dealt by a source to a unit or a player. Damage dealt to a unit is marked on it, and a unit whose total marked damage is greater than or equal to its defense dies. Damage dealt to a player makes them lose that much life.
examples: an attacker with 2 power blocked by a 0/2 kills it, and an unblocked 1-power attacker makes the defending player lose 1 life.

rules.text: Damage marked on units is removed during the regroup phase.
examples: a blocker that took 2 damage in the battle has no damage marked on it after regroup.

rules.text: All the damage dealt to a unit is dealt, including any beyond what destroys it, and counts as damage dealt.
examples: Arc Lightning deals 6 to a Vulnerable 3/8 with nowhere for its Electric damage to jump: all 12 are dealt to that unit, not just the 8 that destroy it.

rules.text: The source of damage is the thing that deals it. When a spell makes a unit deal damage (Squish, Fight, Battle), the unit is the source: its own attributes apply, and the spell's attributes do not.
examples: a Powerful ally squishing deals double its defense.
a Powerful Squish does not double.

rules.text: Damage a unit deals because a spell told it to is that unit's damage, not damage from a spell effect.
examples: Squish damage does not trigger Ember of Life ("When one of your spell effects deals damage").

rules.text: Combat damage is the damage columns deal to each other and to players in the combat damage step. All other damage is noncombat damage, including damage dealt by an ability that combat damage causes, such as Resonant's extra damage.
examples: Resonant's extra damage is not combat damage, so Oorblak does not take it in place of the player.

rules.text: All the damage one resolution of one effect deals is dealt at once. A recipient that the effect damages more than once is dealt the total once, and units destroyed by that damage are destroyed together, after all of it is dealt.
examples: Channel Through deals damage to a unit twice; Restitution triggers once, for the total.

rules.text: Each copy of an effect is a separate source and deals its damage separately.
examples: Meteor Shower's three Rockfalls are three separate dealings of damage.

rules.text: When a source would deal noncombat damage, its amount is worked out in this order: first, modifiers that add to it (such as Conduit of Pain's "plus 1") apply; then Powerful doubles the result; then a Vulnerable recipient is dealt double what reaches it.
examples: a Powerful Bellowing Boulder beside Conduit of Pain deals (1+1)x2 = 4 to each unit.

rules.text: Damage dealt in the form of -1/-1 counters (by a Poisonous source) is still damage dealt: it triggers abilities that trigger on a unit being dealt damage.
examples: Awoken Tomb hit by a Poisonous source makes its X/X.

rules.text: Damage that is prevented is not dealt. It triggers nothing that triggers on damage being dealt, places no -1/-1 counters, and does not destroy a unit, even from a Deadly source.
examples: a Deadly source cannot kill through Phytochemical Protection.

rules.text: Damage that an effect replaces with something else (for example, damage dealt "as" rot) was still dealt. Abilities that care whether damage was dealt see it, even though the recipient took something else instead.
examples: a column whose face damage Blightsea Polyp turns into rot still pays out Vroot's "that much".

rules.text: Rot is a counter a player has. At the start of each deployment phase, each player is dealt damage equal to their rot, in initiative order.
examples: a player with 3 rot is dealt 3 damage as deployment begins.

rules.text: Rot never decreases on its own. It deals its damage again every deployment until an effect removes it.
The source of rot damage is the damaged player's own rot, which is a source that player controls.
Rot damage is dealt as the deployment phase begins, before abilities that trigger "at the start of deployment". No player can respond to it.

Rot damage can be replaced. A replacement that names no target replaces it on the spot. One that names a target ("put that many -1/-1 counters on target unit instead") puts a triggered ability on the stack to choose the target, and the damage is replaced whether or not that ability finds a target.
examples: Skittering Blight takes your rot damage as +1/+1 counters.
Beyond, Codex Incarnate asks its controller for a target, and the rot damage never lands.

rules.text: An effect that says "gain rot" without naming a player gives the rot to the effect's controller.
examples: Primordial Coalescence gives its caster 2 rot.

rules.text: Debt is a counter a player has. At the end of each of their resource steps, a player pays 1 mana for each debt they have, and each mana paid removes one debt.

Paying debt is not a choice and takes no action. It is the last thing in the resource step, so no resource can be expended after it in that step, and the mana spent on debt cannot be used for anything else that turn.
If a player cannot pay all their debt, they pay what they can. The rest stays and is charged again at their next resource step. There is no other penalty.
Gaining debt can be a cost. Debt gained to pay a cost is gained when the cost is paid, and is kept even if the spell or ability is negated.
examples: Hyper Beam negated by Dematerialize deals no damage, and the debt its caster gained to play it stays.

rules.text: Rot and debt are counters on players. An effect that removes counters from players removes them. An effect that changes the number of counters "put on" a player does not change how many are removed.
examples: Burn the Blight removes rot and debt from players.
with Proliferating Slime in play, 2 rot put on its controller's opponent arrives as 3, but removing 2 rot from that player removes exactly 2.

rules.text: Effects that apply to the same layer apply in timestamp order. Where they conflict, the later effect takes precedence over the earlier one.
examples: Monke resolves in battle, so other units lose all attributes. Afterwards a player augments Chitin Shredder, a Virus, onto their unit: that unit has Powerful, because the virus is later than Monke.

rules.text: An effect's timestamp is when it began to apply. A static ability's effect has the timestamp of the card that carries it, a mod's has the time it was applied, and an effect from a resolved spell or ability has the time it resolved. What a card prints is older than any effect.
examples: an attribute granted to a unit while Suppression Field is still on the stack is lost when the spell resolves; one granted after it resolves is kept.

rules.text: An effect that removes attributes or abilities removes those the object has when the effect applies. An attribute or ability the object gains afterwards is not removed.
examples: a Powerful virus attached after Suppression Field resolved makes the suppressed unit Powerful.
a Powerful virus attached after Transmogrifant is in play works.

rules.text: A continuous effect that removes attributes or abilities removes the printed ones of a unit that enters play after it began, because what a card prints is older than the effect. When that effect ends, the units get them back.
examples: a unit entering play under Transmogrifant has no attributes, and gets them back when Transmogrifant leaves.

rules.text: What a removal effect took stays taken until that effect ends (for a removal that lasts until regroup, at regroup). The unit does not get it back by leaving the column the effect applies to. This does not stop the unit gaining an attribute or ability from a later source (rule 113.3).
When two effects set a unit's base stats, the later one applies.
examples: an opponent's Aberrant Statweaver ("Your units are base 3/3") makes their Wisp base 3/3. You cast Body Swap on your 1/1 and that Wisp: until regroup your unit is base 3/3 and the Wisp base 1/1, though the Statweaver is still in play.

rules.text: An Algomancy card can show these parts: a name, a mana cost, an affinity requirement, a timing icon, stats (power and defense), a type line of types and attributes, abilities, and a set symbol. Every card has a name; the other parts appear only on the cards that need them. Some cards also print an alternative-cost banner (203) or an augment symbol (208).

The physical printed card is the source of truth for what a card says. Where the transcription a client reads differs from the printed card, the printed card governs and the transcription is corrected; the difference is not a ruling on the card.
Every card has a name.
"Other" and "another" compare objects, never names. Two cards with the same name are two different things, and each is "another" to the other.
examples: A unit wearing two Rotbeast augments: each Rotbeast's trigger moves the other one.

rules.text: Where a card speaks of a "unique" token, a token is identified by its name and its X together: a Robot 2 and a Robot 5 are two unique tokens.
examples: Automaton of Abundance: when its controller creates a Robot 3, a Robot 2 and a Robot 1 together, those are three unique tokens, so three extra Robots are made.

rules.text: A card with a back face exists as its front face in every zone other than play. A transformed card that leaves play turns back over, and is binned under its front name. A back face is not a token.
examples: A transformed Scholar of the Void killed in play goes to the bin as Scholar of the Void.

rules.text: A copy takes the name of the card it copies while it is a copy, but the physical card keeps its own name: when it leaves play it is binned, erased or returned to hand as itself.
examples: A Borrower of Forms that copied a Good Whale and dies puts Borrower of Forms in the bin.
Recalled, it returns to the hand as Borrower of Forms.

rules.text: The cost orb shows the card's mana cost: the number of resources a player must expend to play it.
examples: Good Whale (cost orb 6) cannot be played with five resources; played with seven, it expends six and leaves one open.

rules.text: The pips with the cost are the card's affinity requirement. To play the card, its controller must have at least that many resources of each pip's element among their resources. The requirement is met, not paid: expended resources count toward it.
examples: Two wood resources and any number of shards can pay for many [gg] cards in one turn.

rules.text: The pips are not part of a card's cost. Where a card or rule refers to a card's cost, it means the mana number alone.
examples: Resurrect ("cost 2 or less") can return Chitin Shredder, whose cost orb is 2 with two earth pips: its cost is 2, not 4.

rules.text: An effect that reads a card's cost reads its printed cost. Effects that make a card cost more or less to play do not change the cost other effects read.
examples: Squish paid at 4 under Stasis Sentry and Tranquility is still a 2-cost spell to Arcane Concentrator and Channeled Amalgam.
Tides of the Cosmos' "total cost 8 or less" is not shrunk by Tranquility.

rules.text: A cost orb may show X. While a card with X in its cost is being cast, X is the amount chosen and paid, and that amount is the card's cost.
examples: With Unstable Apparition in play ("create a Fireball X, where X is the spell's cost"), its controller casts Wildfire for X = 0. Wildfire's cost is 0, so no Fireball is made.

rules.text: A card with X in its cost has a cost of 0 wherever no X has been paid for it: in the deck, the hand, the cache, the bin, or as a unit in play. An X spell played by an effect that plays cards for free is played with X = 0.
examples: Tides of the Cosmos counts an X spell as cost 0 against its budget of 8, and plays it at X = 0.
Living Vault caches a card from hand by paying its cost: an X card in hand costs 0, so it can be cached for [0].

rules.text: A copy has the cost of the card it copies.
examples: A Borrower of Forms that copied a Robot costs 0, so Lumengrove Lurker can recall it.

rules.text: Some cards print a banner that offers another way to play the card, for a cost of its own: Ambush and Prophecy are printed this way. A banner shows its own mana cost and affinity pips, and a Prophecy banner also shows a condition.
A banner's cost is paid like any other cost, in place of the card's cost orb: its own mana is spent and its own affinity pips are required.
examples: Lurking Slimebeast ambushes for 3 mana with one water pip.

rules.text: A banner's cost is not the card's cost. Anything that reads the card's cost reads its cost orb, even when the card is played through its banner.
examples: Lurking Slimebeast played through its Ambush banner (3 mana) still has a cost of 4, its cost orb.

rules.text: Prophesying pays a Prophecy banner's cost and puts the card into the cache with the banner's condition attached. Once the condition has been fulfilled, the card may be played from the cache for free and ignoring affinity, at its printed timing (see 803).
examples: A fulfilled prophecy whose card needs earth affinity its controller lacks is released from the cache with nothing paid.

rules.text: A timing icon printed in a banner governs only the play the banner offers, not the card.
A [Battle] icon on an Ambush banner lets the card be played as an Ambush during battle even though the card itself has no Battle timing.
examples: Good Whale, a deployment unit, ambushes into the attacking column for [4bb] during battle.

rules.text: A [Haste] icon at the end of a Prophecy condition lets the card be prophesied during the haste step as well as during deployment. It does not change when the card may be played once the prophecy is fulfilled: that is always its printed timing.
examples: Divine Intervention ("Your life is 5 or less [Haste]") may be prophesied in the haste step.

rules.text: The type line describes what the card is. It holds the card's attributes, its subtypes and its card type, and on some cards the augment symbol (208).

The type line of a card that can be played ends with its card type: Unit, Spell, or Spell Unit (a spell that is also a unit). A token's type line says so: Token Unit for a unit token, Spell Token for a spell token. A resource card's type line ends with Resource.
A Spell Unit is both a spell and a unit: an effect that asks for a unit or for a spell accepts it.
examples: A spell unit played from hand through Hooba-Pon's ability counts as playing a spell.

rules.text: The words of the type line other than its markers and its card type are subtypes, such as Whale, Squid or Jellyfish. A marker may stand among them.
An attribute printed on the type line is part of the card's rules. It is an attribute, not an ability.

Attributes are printed in bold yellow (gold) or purple. Yellow attributes are combat attributes, which are shared by the units in the same column of a formation (see 603 and 802). Purple attributes, such as Burst and Unstable, are non-combat attributes and are not shared in formation.
examples: Aberrant Statweaver attacking behind Chitin Shredder is Powerful through the column, but Chitin Shredder does not become Unstable: when it dies it is binned, while the Statweaver is erased.

rules.text: Attributes apply in the order they are printed, top to bottom.
examples: A Lonely Forager (3/1) given Tough and then Balanced is 3/3; given Balanced first and then Tough, it is 3/6.

rules.text: A timing icon is not an attribute. A card whose only marking is its timing icon has no attributes.
The text box holds the card's abilities, which describe its effects. Most cards have abilities; some have none.
Reminder text, in italics, restates what an attribute or keyword does. An [Augment] mentioned inside reminder text is not an augment symbol (see 208.4a).
examples: Reconfigure mentions [Augment] in its reminder text, but it cannot be applied as an augment.

rules.text: Text in square brackets in a text box is either an additional cost or a choice between modes. A bracketed cost must be paid, and a bracketed mode chosen, to play the card.
examples: Darkblast's [Discard a card] is a cost: with no other card in hand it cannot be cast.
Retribution Thing's "[lost or gained]" is a mode: X is one of the two, never the sum.

rules.text: The owner of the effect pays a bracketed cost and chooses a bracketed mode, as the card or ability is put on the stack — never on resolution.
examples: Void Memory's caster declares "unit" or "spell" at cast; each opponent then discards one of that type if able.

rules.text: A payment written in prose rather than in brackets, such as "unless its controller pays", is not the owner's: the player it names decides it, when the effect resolves.
Only bracketed prose is a cost or a mode. Symbols the transcription writes in brackets, such as [Augment], [Switch1], [once] or a cost like [2] or [4bb], are not bracketed text.
A bracketed additional cost is still paid when an effect lets the card be played for free.
examples: A card played by Tides of the Cosmos still pays its bracketed cost, and a unit played by the same Tides is not yet in play to pay it.

rules.text: On a graft card the graft symbol divides an ability into a cause, before the symbol, and an effect, after it. When the card is grafted onto another, only the text after its graft symbol is added.
examples: Omniwield Evoker reads "[three]: [Switch] Put a +1/+1 counter on me." Grafted onto another unit, it adds only the +1/+1 counter to the host's ability; the [three] before the symbol is not added, so nothing is paid for it.

rules.text: A unit's stats are two numbers, printed power/defense. Power is how much damage the unit deals in combat. Defense is how much damage it can take before it dies.
examples: An unblocked Rune Channeler (4/3) deals 4 damage; a Good Whale (7/5) survives 4 damage and dies to a fifth.

rules.text: Stats mark a card as a unit. Spell units also have stats, and enter play as units with them when they resolve.
examples: Lonely Forager, a Spell Unit, resolves into play as a 3/1 unit; Resurrect, a plain spell, goes to the bin.

rules.text: A unit's printed stats are the numbers shown on the card. Any difference from the printed stats is a stat change.
examples: A unit whose base stats an effect has set differently has a stat change, so it is not a "unit with no stat changes" for Leave None Pure.
A 0/4 Tough unit with a +1/+1 counter is a 1/10: the counter (layer 3) applies before Tough doubles defense (layer 4).

rules.text: An effect that makes a unit "base N/N" replaces its base stats; it does not add to them. Counters and other stat changes still apply on top. When two such effects apply, the later one wins.
examples: An opponent's Aberrant Statweaver makes their Wisp base 3/3. Body Swap on your 1/1 and that Wisp makes yours base 3/3 and the Wisp base 1/1 until regroup.
Unmake reads base power, and counters do not count toward it.

rules.text: A stat change that an effect gives ("gains +1/+1") is temporary: it lasts only as long as the effect says, such as until regroup, or as long as a static ability applies. A +1/+1 or -1/-1 counter is a permanent change. A stat change is a counter only if the effect says it places counters.
examples: A Good Whale with a +1/+1 counter hit by Jelly ("gains -2/-2 until regroup") is 6/4 in battle and 8/6 after regroup.

rules.text: When a unit has both a +1/+1 counter and a -1/-1 counter, the two cancel and both are removed.
examples: A -1/-1 counter put on a unit with +1/+1 counters removes one of them, and leaves no -1/-1 counter.

rules.text: Every counter is a counter, whatever its sign: a card that speaks of "a counter" counts +1/+1 and -1/-1 counters alike, unless it prints a sign.
examples: Flux Resonator adds one more to -1/-1 counters too.

rules.text: A unit with negative power deals 0 damage.
examples: A -3/1 unit attacking beside a 1/1 in an unblocked column: the column deals 1 damage.

rules.text: A timing icon in the top right corner of a card changes when, and how, the card can be played. The icons printed there are Haste, Battle and Virus (207.3–207.5).
examples: Surly Stalker, a Battle unit, cannot be played in deployment but can be in battle; Ignis Sprite, with no icon, can be played in deployment.

rules.text: A card with no timing icon can be played only during deployment.
examples: A unit with no timing icon cannot be played in battle, except when Tides of the Cosmos lets it ignore timing.

rules.text: A card with the Haste icon can be played during the haste step as well as during deployment.
A card with the Battle icon can be played only while its player is in battle with another player. It cannot be played during deployment.
