Gaining Haste does not let a Battle card be played outside battle. A Battle card that an effect lets be played as if it had Haste can still be played only in battle.
examples: Dispatch Courier's grant does not let a {Battle} unit be played in the haste step.

rules.text: A card with the Virus icon can also be applied as an augment from hand during battle, as well as being played and augmented normally during deployment (see 723).
examples: In battle a Virus can be augmented from hand; a card without the Virus icon cannot, unless Rook allows it.

rules.text: A timing icon other than Virus does not change when a card can be applied as a mod. A Battle card cannot be applied as a mod during battle, and a Haste card cannot be applied in the haste step.
examples: Molten Upheaval has Haste, but it can be grafted onto Bellowing Boulder only during deployment: not in the haste step, and not in battle.

rules.text: An effect may let a card be played ignoring its timing, as Tides of the Cosmos does ("You may play them now"). A card played that way may be played whatever its timing icon, or lack of one.
examples: Tides of the Cosmos plays a deployment unit and a deployment spell unit in battle.

rules.text: An effect that only lets a card be played from somewhere else, such as the bin or the cache, does not waive its timing. Cards that waive timing say so.

A timing icon printed on one line of a card, rather than on the card, governs only that line. A "Discard me" line with no icon of its own is usable in battle as well as in deployment; one printed with a Battle icon is usable only in battle.
examples: Nothyr's battle-marked discard-me line is refused outside battle.

rules.text: The augment symbol marks what a card can give to another card when it is applied as an augment. It appears either at the start of a line in the text box, or at the start of the type line, before the card's attributes.
An augment symbol in the text box gives all the text in the paragraph after it to the card the augment is applied to.
examples: Vengeance applied as an augment gives its host "Cards your opponents play during battle gain [Sacrifice a unit]", with the host's controller as "you".

rules.text: An augment symbol on the type line gives the type line's attributes to the card the augment is applied to. An augment gives text, never stats.
examples: Bubb's type-line augment donates {Unaware} and no stats.

rules.text: A card that prints the augment symbol can be applied as an augment, from hand, bin or cache (see 721), whether or not its augment text does anything a client can carry out.
examples: A Pile of Rubbish can be applied as an augment from hand, from the bin, or from the cache while a glimpse lets it be played.

rules.text: An [Augment] mentioned inside reminder text is not an augment symbol, and does not make the card an augment.
examples: Reconfigure mentions [Augment] in its reminder text, but it cannot be applied as an augment.

rules.text: A copy does not have the augment symbol printed on the card it copies.
examples: A Borrower of Forms that copied Bubb cannot be the first target of Reconfigure, though a real [Augment] unit in play can be.

rules.text: The set symbol shows which expansion a card belongs to. Its colour shows the card's complexity: gold means complex.
Complexity is used to choose which cards are in a game. The Quick Start suggests that inexperienced players remove the gold-symbol cards from their decks.
Apart from resource cards (106), there are three card types: unit, spell and spell unit. There are two kinds of token: unit tokens and spell tokens.

A card's type line names its type. A unit's type line ends "Unit", a spell's ends "Spell", and a spell unit's ends "Spell Unit". A token's type line also contains the word "Token": "Robot Token Unit" is a unit token, and "Spell Token" a spell token.
Units, unit tokens and spell units have stats: power and defense. Spells and spell tokens have no stats.
examples: A Good Whale is 7/5 and a Robot token with two counters is 2/2. A Crystal ("Put X +1/+1 counters on target unit") can target the Whale, but not the Fireball token beside it: a spell token is not a unit and has no stats.

rules.text: Every unit, spell and spell unit is a card, including a unit that is in play. A token is not a card (see 304).
examples: Void Mandible, which watches for a nontoken card being played during battle, sees a {Battle} unit being played.

rules.text: When printed text names a type, the noun it uses decides what it reaches.
examples: Tranquility ("Spells cost one more") taxes a Crystal token, but Arbiter of Armistice ("Cards played during battle") charges it no life.

rules.text: "Spell" includes spell units and spell tokens.
examples: Emberflame Enlightener gives "your spells" {Powerful}, and that includes your spell tokens.

rules.text: "Unit" includes unit tokens and spell units, but not spell tokens.
examples: The World Shepherd watches for a unit token being created; a spell token being created does not trigger it.
Automaton of Abundance copies unit tokens; a spell token in the same batch is not a unit and is not copied.

rules.text: "Token" with no other qualifier includes both unit tokens and spell tokens.
examples: Mycelial Mentor triggers when its controller creates a Fireball, a spell token.

rules.text: "Card" never includes a token. A spell token being cast is a spell being played, but not a card being played.
examples: Arbiter of Armistice makes cards played during battle cost 2 life more; casting a spell token costs no life.

rules.text: "Nontoken" excludes every token.
examples: Void Mandible says "nontoken card"; a spell token being cast does not trigger it.

rules.text: A unit is a permanent: once it enters play, it stays in play until something removes it.
examples: A Good Whale stays in play through two turns and their regroups until it is destroyed.

rules.text: Units are what players use to build armies, and to attack and defend.
A unit's power is how much damage it deals in combat.
examples: An unblocked The Foretold (power 3) deals 3 damage to the defending player.

rules.text: A unit's defense is how much damage it can sustain in battle before it dies.
examples: A Good Whale (defense 5) survives a Fireball 2 with 2 damage on it, then dies to a Fireball 3.

rules.text: A unit that has been dealt a total amount of damage greater than or equal to its defense during battle dies.
examples: A 3/3 dealt exactly 3 dies; dealt 2 it lives.

rules.text: When a unit dies or is deleted, it is put into the bin.
A unit does not have to wait before it can attack or block: as long as a unit is in play, it can attack and block.
examples: A unit that spawned during the attack step may still be declared as a blocker.

rules.text: A unit that enters play during battle is placed outside of formation: it is in the region, but it is not attacking or blocking. It enters a formation only if the effect that put it into play says so.
examples: A 2/2 that Tidelurker creates mid-attack stays in the enemy region, in no column, and cannot block the counterattack.
A spell unit that Hooba-Pon plays spawns into an open position in Hooba-Pon's formation, because Hooba-Pon says so.

rules.text: A unit whose text says it spawns with counters enters play already carrying them. This is a fact about the unit as it arrives, not an ability: it does not use the stack, and nothing can respond to it.
examples: Aethercap Siphoner (printed 4/4, spawns with three -1/-1 counters) is already a 1/1 when an ability that watches allies spawn looks at it.
Nothing goes on the stack for Powerforge Synergist's or Aethercap Siphoner's spawn counters.

rules.text: No player puts those counters on the unit, so an ability that triggers when a player puts counters on a unit does not trigger. An effect that changes how many counters would be put on a unit does change them.
examples: Aethercap Siphoner arriving with its counters does not count as "you put counters on an ally".
With an allied Flux Resonator, Powerforge Synergist enters with three +1/+1 counters instead of two.

rules.text: A unit that an effect "puts into play" was not played. A unit that an effect lets a player "play" was played, wherever it came from.
examples: Bloomcaster creates a 1/1 when its controller plays a unit, but not when a unit is put into play.
The units Wake the Dead plays out of a bin are played: Bloomcaster and Stalwart Sentinel both see them.

rules.text: A spell provides a one-time effect.
examples: Manufacture creates three Robots once and goes to the bin; it never enters play.

rules.text: When a spell resolves, it goes directly to the bin.
A spell token is a spell.
examples: Emberflame Enlightener's "your spells" includes its controller's spell tokens.

rules.text: A spell unit is both a spell and a unit. Like a spell it has a one-time effect; like a unit it has stats.
examples: A played Jelly is a played spell, gives the target -2/-2, and then its body is a 2/1 unit in play.

rules.text: A spell unit that has been played goes on the stack. It is not in play while it is on the stack.
examples: A Jelly that has been played sits on the stack beneath Bloomcaster's trigger; negated there, it never enters play.

rules.text: When a spell unit resolves, its spell effect happens first. Then the unit enters play, instead of the card going to the bin.
examples: Spawntender creates its 8/8, and then its own 2/2 body enters play.

rules.text: If a spell unit is prevented from resolving (it is negated, or every one of its targets has become invalid), the unit does not enter play and the card goes to the bin.
examples: A spell unit played through Hooba-Pon and negated never enters play.

rules.text: Playing a spell unit is playing a spell, and while it is on the stack it is a spell: anything that refers to a spell, or to an allied spell, applies to it.
examples: A spell unit played through Hooba-Pon counts as playing a spell.
Origon negates a spell unit when it is the first spell a player plays in the battle.
If Molten Riftbreaker despawns while an allied spell unit is on the stack, its "negate all allied spells" negates that spell unit.

rules.text: A spell unit is also a unit card. An effect that lets a player play a unit lets them play a spell unit, and it is played as a spell.
examples: Hooba-Pon offers a spell unit from the hand; its spell part happens and its body takes the open position.
Insidious Invitation's "play a unit from hand" lets each player play a spell unit.

rules.text: A spell unit played during battle enters play in the region where it resolved, outside of formation, unless its own text or the effect that played it places it in a formation.
examples: Played through Hooba-Pon, a spell unit spawns into Hooba-Pon's formation.

rules.text: A spell unit that enters play without being played (for example, one put into play from a bin) does not produce its spell effect.
examples: Exhume puts a Jelly from the bin into play: its -2/-2 does not happen, and Bloomcaster does not trigger, because the Jelly was not played.

rules.text: A spell unit that an effect lets a player play from somewhere other than the hand is still played: its spell effect happens, and the unit enters play only if the spell resolves.
examples: A Jelly that Wake the Dead plays from a bin has its spell part happen, and its body enters play only if that spell resolves.

rules.text: If a spell unit's own text says that another player gains control of it, it enters play under that player's control. There is no moment when its caster controls it. Its owner does not change.
examples: Hush Mush negates an opponent's effect and enters play already under that opponent's control; its caster never controls it.
The caster's Flourishing Flora, which watches allies spawn, does not see Hush Mush arrive.

rules.text: If a spell unit's own text says it becomes a copy of something, it enters play already as that copy. Becoming the copy is not a triggered ability.
examples: Borrower of Forms has the copied unit's name, stats and attributes from the instant it enters play.

rules.text: While a spell unit is a copy of a unit, it is not a spell unit.
examples: Cosmic Reversal returns spell units in play to their controllers' hands; a Borrower of Forms copying a unit stays in play.

rules.text: Tokens are created by effects, directly into play.
examples: Manufacture creates three Robot tokens straight into play, through no hand, stack or bin.

rules.text: A token is not a card.
A token is either a unit token or a spell token.
A unit that an effect creates is a unit token, whether or not the effect calls it a token.
examples: Spawntender creates an 8/8 unit without calling it a token; it is still a token, so Download ("Gain control of target token") can take it.

rules.text: A copy of a unit that an effect creates is a token, even when the unit copied is not.
examples: The copy Echo of Despair creates of itself is a token.

rules.text: A copy of a spell made on the stack, such as one made by Earthbound Replicator or Maelstrom Charger, is not a token.
examples: Download cannot take a spell copy that Earthbound Replicator made.

rules.text: A nontoken unit that becomes a copy of a token does not become a token.
examples: A Borrower of Forms that copies a Robot token is a nontoken unit.
With that Borrower in play beside a real token, Download can take the token but not the Borrower.

rules.text: The back face of a card that transforms is not a token. The transformed card is still a card, and in every zone other than play it is its front face.
examples: A transformed Scholar of the Void that dies goes to the bin as Scholar of the Void.

rules.text: A token enters play in the region where the source that created it is when the effect resolves.
examples: Life Plant, attacking in the enemy region, creates its 1/1s there and not at home.

rules.text: A unit token created during battle in an enemy region stays in that region, outside of formation. It cannot block a counterattack, and it returns to its controller's home region at regroup.
examples: Tidelurker's 2/2, created mid-attack, stays in the enemy region and cannot block the counterattack.

rules.text: A unit token is a unit. It works exactly as a unit card does, except as these rules say otherwise.
examples: A Robot token with two counters attacks unblocked and deals 2 damage.

rules.text: Unit tokens stay in play through regroup.
examples: A unit token survives regroup while a spell token beside it is erased.

rules.text: A token that leaves play goes to the zone it was sent to: a unit token that dies enters the bin, and a recalled token, unit or spell, enters its controller's hand. It really is there, so abilities that watch that zone see it. It is then erased from the game, before anything that triggered on its arrival resolves.
examples: A unit token that dies enters the bin, is not trashed, and is then erased.
Rider of the Tides, which watches cards entering a hand during battle, sees a recalled unit token.
A Fireball recalled off the stack enters its controller's hand, Rider of the Tides sees it, and it is erased.

rules.text: A token that enters a bin is not trashed.
examples: A unit token dying in battle does not add to the count of cards trashed in that battle.

rules.text: A unit token that dies still dies: abilities that trigger when a unit dies see it, unless they say "nontoken".
A spell token is a spell that is in play. Its controller may cast it from play; casting it works the same way as casting a spell from the hand.
A spell token can be cast only in the region it is in.
Casting a spell token is playing a spell. It is played from play, so it is played from somewhere other than the hand.
examples: Casting a Fireball token triggers Stalwart Sentinel.
Tranquility ("Spells cost [one] more to play during battle") makes a spell token cost [1].

rules.text: A spell token is never in a hand. An effect that counts the cards in a hand does not count spell tokens.
examples: Dreadspawn Horror does not count spell tokens as cards in hand.

rules.text: A spell token that has been cast is still a token while it is on the stack.
examples: Download can take a Fireball that has already been cast and is on the stack.

rules.text: A token has a mana cost, which is often 0. Effects that change the cost of playing spells apply when a spell token is cast.
examples: Tranquility makes a spell token cost [1] in battle.

rules.text: Many tokens have an X value, set by the effect that created them: "Create a Crystal 3" creates a Crystal whose X is 3. A token's X is its size, not a cost.
A spell token with Burst is cast together with every other spell token of the same name that its controller has in that region. They are still separate spells.
A spell token is not a unit and has no stats. An ability that refers to a unit token does not apply to a spell token.
examples: The World Shepherd watches for unit tokens being created; a spell token being created does not trigger it.

rules.text: A spell token cannot move to another region on its own. Its controller may bring it into the enemy region with an attack, but only together with at least one attacking unit, and the move cannot be undone.
examples: A Fireball rides into the enemy region with an attacking The Foretold and stays there after the Foretold dies; with no attacking unit it stays home.

rules.text: A counterattack may bring spell tokens the same way: spell tokens that stand in the region the counterattacking units leave from may go with them.
A spell token created in an enemy region during combat can be cast there at once.
examples: A Fireball created for the attacker in the enemy region during combat is castable there at once.

rules.text: During regroup, every spell token still in play is erased, including unused spell tokens in their controller's own region.
examples: With Harbinger of Immolation in play, its controller's spell tokens stay through regroup.

rules.text: When an effect refers to each unique token (Automaton of Abundance), two tokens are the same unique token only if they have both the same name and the same X.
examples: With Automaton of Abundance in play, Manufacture creates a Robot 3, a Robot 2 and a Robot 1: three unique tokens, so one extra of each is made.
Three Robot 2s are one unique token.

rules.text: Creating a token is not playing it. A unit token that an effect created was not played.
examples: Manufacture creates Robot tokens. That is not playing them, so Bloomcaster and Stalwart Sentinel do not trigger.

rules.text: A modification (mod) is a card that is applied to another card instead of being played. A modified card is treated as a single card with all of the text its mods add, except that a spell or a spell token that is modified gains only the mod's attributes (721). The two kinds of modification are augment and graft.
examples: Curio Drifter augmented onto a Good Whale is not played and gives the Whale Evasive; Biotoxicity is grafted; a Fireball augmented with Bloomcaster does not create 1/1s.

rules.text: Applying a mod is not playing a card, so an ability that triggers on playing a unit or a spell does not trigger on it.
examples: A Virus applied from hand during battle is not a card being played, so Void Mandible ("When a nontoken card is played during battle…") does not trigger.

rules.text: Modifying is done during the deployment phase. A Virus can also be applied from the hand during battle.
A card's augment and graft text works when the card is played normally, not only when it is applied as a mod.
A spell or spell unit with a graft symbol resolves normally when it is played, and can later be applied as a graft from the bin.
examples: Spawntender, a spell unit with a graft icon, resolves normally when played: it creates its 8/8 and its own body spawns.
A dead Leaping Lillik in the bin can be applied as a graft.

rules.text: During deployment, a spell token in play may be augmented, with any augment and not only a Virus. The spell token gains only the mod's attributes, not its text.
examples: A Fireball augmented with a mod granting {Powerful} deals double damage when cast.
Carapace Devourer, an augment that is not a Virus, may augment a spell token during deployment.

rules.text: The zones of the game are the deck, the hand, the cache, play, the bin, the stack, the erased pile, the recycle pile and the pack.
Play and the stack are the active zones. The hand, the deck, the bin, the cache and the erased pile are inactive zones.
examples: A printed Unstable card is erased leaving play or the stack, and only binned leaving the hand, the deck or the cache.

rules.text: Whether a zone is active matters to {Unstable}: an {Unstable} card is erased in place of entering a bin only when it leaves an active zone. A card leaving an inactive zone for a bin is binned normally, {Unstable} or not.
examples: Aberrant Statweaver (printed {Unstable}) discarded from a hand goes to the bin and stays there: the hand is inactive.
The same card negated off the stack is erased: the stack is active.

rules.text: Each player has their own hand, cache, bin and erased pile.
A card that leaves play for a bin, a hand, a cache or an erased pile goes to that zone of the player who controlled it when it left play, not to its owner's.
examples: A unit stolen with a control-changing effect is recalled. It goes to the hand of the player who stole it.
A stolen unit dies. It goes to its controller's bin, and its controller trashes it.

rules.text: A card's owner never changes. Changing zones, changing controller and being put into play out of another player's zone all leave the card owned by the same player.
examples: Wake the Dead puts a unit from the opponent's bin into play under the caster's control; the opponent still owns it.
A stolen unit that is recalled is still owned by the player it was stolen from.

rules.text: If the effect that moves a card names where it goes, the card goes there instead.
examples: Pull Under: "Delete target unit. If you do, put it and all of its mods into your bin." The deleted unit and its mods go to the bin of Pull Under's caster, whoever controlled the unit.

rules.text: In constructed, a card's owner is the player who brought it to the game.
An ability that works while its card is in a bin or a cache ("if I am in your bin") works only while the card is in that zone. It never works while the card is in play.
examples: Cinder Scuttler ("When you deal combat damage to an opponent, if I am in your bin, recall me.") dies in the same combat damage sub-step in which another attacker hits the opponent. It was not in the bin when the damage was dealt, so it is not recalled.

rules.text: Copies of one card in the same bin or cache share one such ability: it triggers once for that zone, not once per copy.
examples: Two Cinder Scuttlers in a bin: one combat hit on the opponent recalls one of them, not both.

rules.text: "Your bin" in such an ability means the bin the card is in: the player whose bin it is controls the ability, whoever once played the card.
examples: Rotling ("When I leave your bin, … You may pay [1] to draw a card") leaves the opponent's bin. The opponent, whose bin it left, is the one offered the draw.

rules.text: The deck is the face-down pile that cards are drawn from and that packs are dealt from.
The cards in the deck are hidden: no player may look at them or at their order. A card put on the bottom of the deck is not revealed unless the effect says so.
In live draft, all players draw from one shared deck.
In constructed, there is no shared deck: each player has their own deck.
"The deck" in card text means the deck of the effect's controller: the shared deck in live draft, that player's own deck in constructed.
examples: In constructed a Glimpse 1 reveals the top of the deck of the effect controller, not of the opponent.

rules.text: A player who must draw from an empty deck when the recycle pile is also empty draws as many cards as there are. Running out of cards does not make a player lose.
examples: With deck and recycle pile both empty, a draw of two draws nothing and the game goes on.

rules.text: Each player has a hand. Drawn cards go to the hand, and cards in the hand are played from there.
A hand is hidden from the other players.
An effect that lets a player "look at" a hand shows it to that player only. An effect that makes a player "reveal" their hand shows it to every player.
examples: Thought Extraction aimed at its caster's own hand shows that hand to nobody else.

rules.text: A spell token is never in a hand. An effect that counts or refers to the cards in a hand does not count a spell token.
examples: Dreadspawn Horror does not count spell tokens as cards in hand.
Astral Tidewraith's damage, equal to the number of cards in each player's hand, does not count spell tokens either.

rules.text: A card enters a hand whenever an effect puts it there: a draw, a recall, or a move out of a bin, the stack, a cache or another hand. Several cards that enter one hand in a single move enter it together, as one event ("one or more cards enter a hand").
examples: Collect Remains puts a card from a bin into its caster's hand during battle; Rider of the Tides sees a card enter a hand, though it was neither drawn nor recalled.
Two cards that move from a bin to a hand in one move enter it together: an ability watching for cards entering a hand triggers once, not twice.

rules.text: Discarding a card moves it from its hand to the bin. Discarding is not playing the card: nothing goes on the stack.
Card text that restricts playing a card "from your hand" restricts only the hand. The card may still be played from any other zone an effect allows.
examples: Calming Force ("I can't be played from your hand.") cannot be cast from the hand, but a copy in the cache under a live permission can be played.

rules.text: The cache is a zone of its own, beside the hand, the bin and the deck. Effects put cards into it ("cache"), out of the hand, the bin, the deck or play.
The cache is public. Every player can see every cached card, and any prophecy attached to it.
Being in the cache does not by itself let a player do anything with a card.
A cached card can be used only while a permission on it is live: a prophecy on it that has been fulfilled, or a glimpse that cached it this turn.
While a permission is live, the cached card can be used in every way the same card could be used from the hand: in every play mode, in every window, and as a mod.
examples: A glimpsed Virus in the cache is augmented onto an enemy unit during battle.

rules.text: A card used under a fulfilled prophecy costs nothing and ignores affinity. A card used under a glimpse costs its mana but ignores affinity. This holds for every way of using it, mods included.
A cached card keeps its printed timing. A permission says that the card may be used, not when.
The cache is not the hand. A cached card cannot be discarded, and card text that names the hand does not reach the cache.
When a glimpse permission ends, the card stays in the cache, with no permission.
A cached card can be targeted. A player's cache can be targeted only by an effect that resolves in a region where that player is present.
examples: In deployment, Prismatic Observer can recall only a card from its own player's cache.
In battle, with both players present, it can reach the opponent's cache.

rules.text: When a unit in play is cached, only the card goes to the cache. Its mods go to the bin.
A card in the cache under a live glimpse permission may be prophesied where it stands. It does not move and is not cached a second time, and the glimpse permission is used up.
Play is the zone of the units, resources and tokens on the table. A unit stays in play until something removes it.
A token is created directly into play, in the region where it was created.
examples: Galactic Germination cast by the attacker creates its unit tokens straight into play in the battle region.

rules.text: A spell unit enters play as it resolves, in place of going to the bin.
examples: Jelly resolves into play as a unit and does not go to the bin.

rules.text: The bin is a player's discard pile.

A card goes to the bin when: a unit dies or is deleted; a unit is sacrificed; a spell resolves; a card is discarded; or a card that was being played is negated or fails to resolve, unless a rule sends it elsewhere.
A spell unit that is prevented from resolving (for example because its targets became invalid) does not spawn. It goes to the bin.
examples: A negated Jelly, a spell unit played through Hooba-Pon, does not enter play.

rules.text: An ambushing unit whose ambush fails to resolve goes to the bin.

A unit that dies goes to the bin of the player who controlled it when it died, unless the effect that kills it names another bin or the unit is {Unstable} (see rule 405.5). If it is a card, the player whose bin it enters trashes it; a token is never trashed.
examples: Pull Under deletes an enemy unit and puts it into its caster's bin; the caster trashes it.
A token that Pull Under deletes enters the caster's bin but is not trashed.

rules.text: A card that enters a bin from any zone except the stack is trashed. A card that comes from the stack is not, and a token is never trashed. A nontoken mod erased together with its {Unstable} host is not trashed either. See 801.
A spell played for free while another effect resolves (for example by Tides of the Cosmos) and then put into the bin counts as coming from the stack, so it is not trashed.
examples: Tides of the Cosmos plays an ordinary spell for free; it goes to the bin and is not trashed.

rules.text: An {Unstable} card that would enter a bin from an active zone is erased instead: it goes to the erased pile, not the bin. See 803.
examples: A unit carrying a mod is {Unstable}. When it dies, it ends on the erased pile and is not left in the bin.

rules.text: Copies of one card in a bin cannot be told apart. A card in a bin is identified only by its name and by which copy of that name it is.
"Another" said by a card in a bin excludes that one copy, not every card with its name.
examples: Blightwalker is trashed while another Blightwalker is already in the bin; the older copy is "another" and can be chosen.

rules.text: An effect that refers back to a card that just entered a bin ("that card", "it") means that copy. If that copy has left the bin, the effect finds nothing. It never takes a different copy of the same name.
examples: An {Unstable} unit dies and is erased instead of staying in the bin. Biomass Devourer's "erase it" then finds nothing, and does not erase an older copy of the same card already in that bin.

rules.text: A card leaves a bin whenever an effect takes it out, for any reason: recalled, played, cached, erased, recycled, prophesied, or applied as a mod. A "when I leave your bin" ability triggers on every such departure.
examples: Writhing Host leaves the bin when it is erased to pay for a haste play.

rules.text: An augment or graft may be applied from the bin as well as from the hand, during deployment, if its cost is paid and its affinity met.
A {Virus} card in a bin can be applied only as an ordinary mod during deployment. It cannot be used as a mod during battle.
examples: Bumblecrab, a {Virus}, sits in a player's bin. In deployment it can augment out of the bin; in battle it is offered only from the hand.

rules.text: A card can be played from a bin only when an effect or the card's own text allows it. The card keeps its printed timing unless the permission says it may be played "now".
examples: Abyssal Evocation lets its caster play spells from the bin in this battle; only {Battle} spells there can be played.

rules.text: A card played from a bin is {Unstable} only if the permission says so. A card played from a bin under its own text does not become {Unstable}.
examples: A spell played from the bin under Abyssal Evocation gains {Unstable}, so it is erased rather than going back to the bin.

rules.text: The stack is the zone where cards being played, and abilities, wait to resolve. The last thing put on the stack resolves first. See 703.
A spell unit on the stack is not yet in play. It enters play only when it resolves.
examples: Mycelial Mentor, played with Bloomcaster out, is still on the stack while Bloomcaster's 1/1 is made, so the Mentor never sees the 1/1.

rules.text: A spell token that has been cast is on the stack, and is still a token there.
examples: Download can take a Fireball token already cast and on the stack.

rules.text: When a card on the stack resolves, is negated or fails to resolve, it goes to the bin unless it enters play or something sends it elsewhere: an {Unstable} card is erased (see rule 405.5), a card whose own text erases it goes to the erased pile (see rule 406.4a), and a recall puts it into a hand. A card that goes to the bin this way is not trashed, because it comes from the stack.
examples: A non-{Unstable} virus negated off the stack goes to the bin.

rules.text: A spell whose text says "Erase me" goes to the erased pile when it resolves, instead of the bin.
examples: Tides of the Cosmos plays Suspend for free; Suspend goes to the erased pile, never the bin.

rules.text: A self-erasing spell that is negated or fails to resolve goes to the bin. Its "Erase me" never happened.
Erasing a card takes it out of the game. An erased card goes to the erased pile.
examples: Celestial Purge takes a unit out of the game onto the erased pile: no bin and no death.

rules.text: The erased pile is public.
Nothing takes a card back out of the erased pile.
Erasing is not dying and not trashing: an erased card never enters a bin.
examples: A unit erased by Banishment does not die and is not trashed.

rules.text: A card that an effect erases goes to the erased pile, including a mod erased off a host that stays in play (for example to pay a cost).
A mod taken off its host and put into play as a card of its own (Reclaim the Fallen) does not leave the game and does not go to the erased pile.
examples: A Pile of Runes is augmented onto a unit. Reclaim the Fallen targets that unit: A Pile of Runes comes off it and stands in play as a unit of its own. It never goes to the erased pile.

rules.text: A token that ceases to exist after entering a zone is recorded on the erased pile.
A token mod is recorded on the erased pile once when its host leaves play, however the host leaves.
A transformed card is recorded on the erased pile as its front face.
examples: A transformed Scholar of the Void erased by Banishment is recorded as Scholar of the Void.

rules.text: To recycle a card is to put it on the bottom of the deck. A recycled card has not left the game.
examples: A card recycled for a resource is drawn again once the rest of the deck is gone, so it never left the game.

rules.text: A deck has a mark where it originally ended. A card put on the bottom of the deck goes past the mark, into the recycle pile, not onto the bottom of the cards still to be drawn.
Every card put on the bottom of the deck goes past the mark, whatever put it there: recycling for a resource, the constructed put-back, the cards a glimpse did not cache, and recycled packs alike.
When the deck runs out and more cards are needed, the recycle pile is shuffled and becomes the new deck, with a new mark and an empty recycle pile.
Every player can see how many cards are in the recycle pile. No player may look at them.
The order in which cards were recycled does not matter to the game.
Each deck has its own recycle pile. In live draft, all players share one pile; in constructed, each player has their own.
A card recycled out of a hand is not revealed unless the effect says so.
examples: Bripp recycles a card from a hand without naming it to the table.

rules.text: During the resource step, a player may recycle a card from their hand to create a resource. See 502.
In live draft, each player has a pack: a face-down pile of 10 cards dealt from the deck at the start of the game, which that player drafts from.
Constructed has no packs.
A pack may be looked at and used only during the draft step, and no player may look at another player's pack.
In the draft step, a player combines the non-token, non-resource cards in their hand with their pack, keeps any of them, and passes the pack on with exactly 10 cards in it. See 503.
After each cycle of N+1 turns, where N is the number of players, every pack is recycled and each player is dealt a new pack of 10 cards.
In team draft, packs are never refreshed.
When a player is eliminated, their pack is recycled.
A card that leaves play and comes back is a new object. It does not remember its earlier time in play.
examples: Engorged Caudex is recalled and played again; its once-per-turn grafted draw works again the same turn.

rules.text: An effect aimed at a card that has since changed zones does not affect it. An effect aimed at a card that is still in the same zone affects it only if the card is still a legal target for the slot it was chosen for; otherwise that target is lost as well. If every target is lost, the effect fails to resolve.
examples: An opponent's Luminous Arc is aimed at one of your units; you answer with Organic Exchange on two of your own units. They are still in play, so the Luminous Arc still resolves.
An opponent ambushes with Orblish Horroth to recall target ally; you take control of that unit in response. It is no longer their ally, so nothing is recalled.
Minor Kraken's target grows past 5 defense before it resolves, and is not recalled.

rules.text: Moving a mod from one unit to another is not a zone change: the mod never leaves play, and nothing despawns.
examples: Reconfigure moves Bubb and its Growing Plague onto a Robot; Growing Plague's "when I despawn" does not trigger.

rules.text: A unit despawns whenever it leaves play, by any route: dying, being recalled, being cached, being exchanged or being erased. A "when I despawn" ability triggers whichever way the unit leaves.
examples: A Pile of Runes ("[Augment] When I despawn, create a Crystal X") is augmented onto Rune Channeler. Rune Channeler is recalled to its owner's hand: that despawn ability triggers, and a Crystal is created.
Demon of the Depths ("Whenever one of your units despawns…") triggers when one of your units is erased.

rules.text: A unit exchanged out of play (Hooba-Mon, Necromorph) despawns and goes to the bin, where it is trashed, but it does not die.
examples: Necromorph's exchange triggers no death ability, but the unit despawns and is trashed.

rules.text: A transformed card exists as its front face in every zone except play. It turns back over as it leaves play, before anything sees it leave.
examples: A transformed Scholar of the Void that dies goes to the bin as Scholar of the Void.
It can then be returned from the bin as a Scholar.

rules.text: A unit that is copying another card (Borrower of Forms) leaves play as itself. If it dies it goes to the bin as Borrower of Forms; if it is recalled it goes to the hand as Borrower of Forms.
examples: A Borrower that became something else still goes to the bin as Borrower of Forms.
Recalled, it goes back to the hand as Borrower of Forms.

rules.text: When a modded unit is recalled or cached, its mods go to the bin and the unit goes on alone. A token mod ceases to exist instead (see rule 410.4c).
A mod that goes to a bin when its host leaves play goes to the bin of the host's controller.
examples: A virus on an opponent's unit goes to that opponent's bin when the unit leaves play.

rules.text: A modded card is {Unstable}. When it dies or is erased, it and all of its mods are erased.
A token mod has no card of its own. It never enters a bin; when its host leaves play it ceases to exist.
An exchange is not a death. But a modded unit is {Unstable}, so when it is exchanged out of play, it and all of its mods are erased, just as they would be if it died.
examples: Hooba-Mon exchanges itself while it carries a mod; it is erased, not left in a bin.
An unmodded Hooba-Mon exchanged the same way stays in the bin.

rules.text: A token that leaves play goes to the zone it was sent to (a hand, a bin, a cache) and really is there. It ceases to exist there the next time state-based actions are checked, which is before anything it caused to trigger can resolve.
A unit token that dies enters the bin and is then erased. It is not trashed.
A recalled token, unit or spell, enters its controller's hand and is then erased. It counts as a card entering a hand for anything that is watching.
examples: A Fireball token recalled off the stack enters its controller's hand, Rider of the Tides sees it, and it is erased.
Recalling a unit token triggers Rider of the Tides too.

rules.text: A token put into a cache enters the cache and is then erased.
Any spell tokens still in play are erased during regroup.
A card is played from the zone it came out of, even when another effect plays it as it resolves. A card played from the cache, a bin or the deck is not played from the hand.
examples: Tides of the Cosmos plays cards off the top of the deck; Proph and Stalwart Sentinel ("from anywhere other than your hand") both see it.

rules.text: A spell token is cast from where it stands in play, so it is played from somewhere other than the hand.
examples: Casting a Fireball token triggers Stalwart Sentinel.

rules.text: A token created by an effect was not played and came from no zone.
examples: A token created by an effect was not played, so neither Proph nor Stalwart Sentinel triggers.

rules.text: When a unit leaves play for a bin, it dies (or, if it was exchanged out of play, despawns) before anything is trashed. The unit and its mods leave play; then its death or despawn happens, and the abilities that trigger on it trigger; only then is any card trashed (see rule 801.2).
examples: A unit with no mods dies and goes to its controller's bin. Its death comes first, then it is trashed.
Hooba-Mon exchanges itself for a unit card in its controller's bin. It despawns, and only then is it trashed. It does not die.

rules.text: A turn has four phases, in this order: the planning phase, the battle phase, the regroup phase and the deployment phase.

Turns are global: all players share the same phases and sync up at the end of each step. In a 1v1 or team game, the printed rules take some steps in initiative order: the initiative player, or team, acts first, and the non-initiative player waits to see what they did before acting (see rule 501.4 and rule 507.3).

This client makes the turn fully global. In the resource step, the haste step and deployment, both players act at the same time, and neither sees what the other does until both are done (see rule D1.4). This is a digital convention: a paper game cannot hide one player's actions while the other acts.
In each turn one player has the initiative. In a 1v1 game the initiative player (IT) acts first and the non-initiative player (NIT) acts after them.
The initiative is not a token. The Initiative token of the physical game only marks which player has it.

The battle phase is the only phase of the turn in which players can interact, because it is the only time a player can enter another player's region. Outside it, every player is alone in their own region: in deployment a player can do what they like to their own units, but no opponent is there to interact with (see rule 601.4b).

When the deployment phase and its end-of-turn step are over, the turn is over. The initiative and any packs pass to the next player clockwise (see 508), and the next turn begins with its planning phase.
examples: After turn 1 ends, turn 2 opens with each player drawing 2 and the draft step open again.

rules.text: The planning phase is the first phase of the turn. In it, players prepare for the turn ahead by curating their hands and preparing their resources.
The planning phase has five steps, taken in this order.
Refresh: each player's expended resources refresh.
examples: A resource expended to pay debt in one turn is open again for mana in the next.

rules.text: The draw step: see 503.
The draft step: see 503. In constructed, this step is a draw of 2 and a recycle of 2.
examples: Turn 2 of constructed: the hand gains 4 (2 for the draw step, 2 for the draft step), then 2 cards are recycled, a net gain of 2.

rules.text: The resource step: see 502.
The haste step: see 504.
There is no player interaction in the planning phase. No player receives priority in it, and nothing a player does in it can be responded to.

In a 1v1 game, the refresh, the draw step and the draft step happen for both players simultaneously. The resource step and the haste step are taken first by the initiative player and then by the non-initiative player.
A step of the planning phase ends for all players together. No player begins the resource step until every player has finished the draft step.
The resource step is the step of the planning phase in which players create and activate resources.
In the resource step, a player may take these actions.
Create a resource by recycling a card from their hand. The resource enters play dormant. There is no limit to how many resources a player may create.
examples: Recycling a hand card for a fire resource puts a dormant fire resource into play and the card into the recycle pile.

rules.text: Activate dormant resources by turning them face up, up to two activations per turn.
Exchange an active Prismite for a resource of one of the game's elements. A dormant Prismite cannot be exchanged.
examples: Two starting Prismites are activated, then one is exchanged for a fire resource, which keeps its active state.

rules.text: The resource step ends when every player has created and activated all the resources they want.
examples: One player declaring done leaves the other free to keep activating; the haste step opens only when both are done.

rules.text: At the end of their resource step, a player with debt pays 1 mana for each debt, and each mana paid removes one debt. The payment is automatic: it is not a choice and needs no action.
examples: A player with 5 open fire and 3 debt ends the resource step with 0 debt and 2 open mana.

rules.text: Paying debt is the last thing in the resource step. After it the player can activate no more resources this turn, and the mana spent on debt is not available to play cards this turn.
examples: With 3 open mana and 2 debt, the player is left 1 mana: no resource action is offered and a [3] unit cannot be played in deployment.

rules.text: In the draw step, each player draws 2 cards.
examples: On turn 2 of a live draft each player's 6-card hand becomes 8.

rules.text: In a live draft, no player draws in the draw step of the first turn: each player's first draw was dealt with their opening hand (see 103).
Players draw in clockwise order, starting with the initiative player.
examples: In a live draft the initiative player takes the top 2 cards of the shared deck at the start of the turn, and the other player the next 2.

rules.text: In the draft step of a live draft, each player combines the cards in their hand with the cards in their pack, then chooses which cards of the combined pile to keep in hand. The rest go back into the pack.
examples: A player keeps three pack cards and puts three hand cards into the pack; the hand keeps its size.

rules.text: A player must leave exactly 10 cards in the pack, so they end the draft step with as many cards in hand as they began it with.
Within that limit the choice is free: a player may keep their whole hand and take nothing, exchange their whole hand for pack cards, or anything in between.
examples: A player who keeps their hand exactly passes the pack exactly as dealt.

rules.text: When a player has finished drafting, they pass their pack clockwise to the next player. The draft step is complete once every player has passed their pack.
An effect may make a player skip their draft step.
examples: With Worldbender in play in a live draft, its controller is never offered the pack and ends the step with 3 more cards: the 2 drawn in the draw step and Worldbender's 1.

rules.text: After every cycle of N+1 turns, where N is the number of players, every pack is recycled and each player is dealt a new pack of 10 cards. In 1v1 this happens after the third turn, right before the fourth draft.
So each player drafts a second time from the pack they were first dealt before the packs are refreshed.
examples: In 1v1, the pack a player is dealt on turn 1 comes back to them on turn 3 with what they left in it.

rules.text: In constructed there are no packs. In the draft step each player draws 2 more cards from their own deck and then recycles 2 cards from their hand. Since this comes straight after the draw step, the two are taken together: draw 4, then recycle 2.
examples: Worldbender skips the constructed draft step: its controller draws only the draw step's 2 plus Worldbender's 1, recycles nothing, and loses 3 life.

rules.text: The player chooses which 2 cards of their hand to recycle. Until they have, they can take no other planning action.
The draw of 4 and the recycle of 2 happen on the first turn of a constructed game too.

Drawing and drafting are actions like any other: a unit that a change in hand size leaves with 0 defense, or with damage equal to its defense, dies as soon as the action is over, except as the constructed sub-rule below says (see 713).
examples: A Dreadspawn Horror (-1/-1 for each card in hand) taken to 0 defense by the turn's draw dies at once, before any other action is taken.

rules.text: In the draft step the combined pile of hand and pack is never a hand: only the cards a player keeps count toward their hand size.
examples: A Dreadspawn Horror whose controller holds 1 card, draws 2 and keeps 3 through the draft ends the step a 4/2 and lives.

rules.text: In constructed, the draw of 4 and the recycle of 2 count as one step. A player's units are not checked for death until that player has recycled their 2 cards, so they are judged on the hand that remains.
examples: With 1 card in hand, a Dreadspawn Horror goes through draw 4 and put back 2 and ends a 4/2.
With 3 cards in hand it nets to 5 and dies once its controller has put 2 back.

rules.text: The haste step is the last step of the planning phase. It comes after the resource step.
In the haste step, players may play only haste cards.
examples: Molten Upheaval, a haste card, is refused in the resource step and accepted in the haste step.

rules.text: A card with battle timing cannot be played in the haste step, even when an effect gives it haste or lets it be played as if it had haste. This holds for units and spell units alike.
examples: Under Dispatch Courier, a battle unit in hand is still not playable in the haste step.

rules.text: A card played in the haste step resolves immediately. It does not use the stack, no player receives priority, and no player can respond to it.
examples: Tidal Menace played in the haste step is in play at once as a 7/2.

rules.text: The haste step ends when every player has played all the haste cards they want to play, which may be none.
The haste step happens every turn, whether or not any player has anything they could play in it.
examples: On turn 1, with only two dormant Prismites each, the step still opens for both players.

rules.text: No player is treated as finished with the haste step because they have nothing to play. Each player finishes the step themselves, and a player may stay in it holding nothing they could play.
The end of the haste step is an event. An ability that triggers "at the end of [Haste]" triggers then, before the battle phase begins, including in a turn in which nobody played anything in the step.
examples: Keeper of Tithes creates an X/X for its controller's expended resources as the step closes.

rules.text: An instruction a card carries out "during [Haste]" happens in the haste step. This client asks for it as the step ends.
examples: Prediction Prophet asks its controller for a number at the end of the haste step, and creates a 5/5 at the start of deployment if it matched.

rules.text: An effect may let a player play, in the haste step, a card that lacks haste, "as if it had [Haste]". The grant changes only when the card may be played.
examples: Dispatch Courier lets its controller play a deploy unit in the haste step.
Writhing Host in its owner's bin lets them play a deploy unit in the haste step, erasing the Host as the additional cost.

rules.text: A grant that says "Each turn" allows one such play per turn for each card that grants it: two Dispatch Couriers allow two plays.
examples: One Courier grants one play: a second unit in the same haste step is refused.

rules.text: Mods are applied in deployment, not in the haste step, even when the mod card has haste. The exceptions are a card that allows mods in the haste step (the sub-rule below) and a Virus applied in battle (see 723).
A card that says so can allow mods in the haste step: Slurpr lets its controller apply other mods, augments and grafts alike, during [Haste] as if it were deployment.
A card whose prophecy condition ends in [Haste] may be prophesied in the haste step as well as in deployment. Any other prophecy may be prophesied only in deployment.
examples: Divine Intervention's prophecy ("Your life is 5 or less [Haste]") may be prophesied in the haste step.

rules.text: The [Haste] marker does not move a fulfilled prophecy's release: the card is played from the cache only at its printed timing.
The battle phase is the only interactive phase of the game. In it players manage their units across the regions: they attack into other regions or keep units back to defend.
examples: Player A attacks with a Good Whale: the Whale moves into Player B's region, and Player A enters that region too.

rules.text: A player can interact with opponents and their units only during the battle phase.
examples: In deployment, an effect that targets a cached card can reach only its controller's own cache; once an attack brings both players into a region in battle, it can reach the opponent's cache too.

rules.text: An effect that applies "during battle" applies only in the battle phase. It does not apply in the haste step or in deployment.
examples: Crevice Lurker makes abilities cost [one] more "during battle". Outside battle the same activation costs its printed [1].
Counter Thief takes counters placed "during battle"; outside battle it does nothing.

rules.text: Battle is made of four steps: the attack step, the block step, the combat step and the after-combat step. They take place separately inside each region.
In a region that is not attacked, the combat step and the after-combat step are skipped.
examples: When both players decline to attack, neither round has a combat step, and the battle phase ends with no priority window at all.

rules.text: An attack step in which no attack is declared opens no priority window. If both battle rounds are declined, the battle phase has no priority window at all.
examples: The initiative player declines to attack, then the non-initiative player declines too: the game goes to regroup without either player getting priority, so a Fireball token held for the battle is erased unused.

rules.text: In 1v1 and team games the battle phase has two battle rounds. In round 1 the initiative team attacks into the non-initiative team's regions. In round 2 the non-initiative team's counterattackers attack into the initiative team's regions.
examples: The initiative player attacks in round 1; the units the non-initiative player sent at blocks attack in round 2.

rules.text: Round 1 runs in this order: (1) the initiative team declares its attacks, sending units into non-initiative regions; (2) a priority window; (3) the non-initiative team declares its blocking formations and may at the same time send units out to counterattack; (4) a priority window; (5) the combat step, in which all units in formation deal combat damage at the same time; (6) the after-combat step, the last priority window in that region.
examples: The initiative player attacks with a 2/2 Curio Drifter; the non-initiative player blocks nothing and sends a Rune Channeler to counterattack. The unblocked Drifter deals 2, and after the after-combat window round 2 begins.

rules.text: Units sent out to counterattack leave the region at once, and are treated as if they do not exist until round 1 is finished.
examples: A Rune Channeler sent to counterattack is absent for the rest of round 1, and arrives in the initiative player's region for round 2.

rules.text: Round 2 runs in this order: (1) the non-initiative team puts its counterattacking units into formation; (2) a priority window; (3) the initiative team declares its blocking formation; (4) a priority window; (5) the combat step; (6) the after-combat step, the last priority window in that region before regroup.
examples: The counterattacking Rune Channeler arrives in the initiative player's region, attacks, is not blocked and deals 4; after the after-combat window the game goes through regroup to deployment.

rules.text: Each team gets only one chance to attack in a battle phase. There is no counterattack in round 2.
examples: The non-initiative player sent a Rune Channeler at blocks and attacks with it in round 2; the initiative player may block it but cannot send a unit of their own out, and the battle phase ends after round 2.

rules.text: The non-initiative team may declare attacks in round 2 even if the initiative team declared none in round 1. It may then attack with any of its units, because it never had a block step in which to send counterattackers.
examples: The initiative player could attack and declines; the non-initiative player then attacks in round 2 with a unit that was never sent.
Only the non-initiative player has a unit; the initiative player declares no attack, and in round 2 that unit attacks from home.

rules.text: If round 1 had a battle, only the units sent out at the block step can attack in round 2. If none were sent, there is no round 2.
examples: The initiative player attacks, the non-initiative player blocks and sends nobody: the battle phase ends after round 1, and the unit that stayed home is untouched.
A Good Whale that stayed home while a Rune Channeler was sent out cannot be declared as a round-2 attacker.

rules.text: Battle is resolved one region at a time. Once players begin interacting in a region, every step of battle is completed in that region before those players can interact anywhere else.
examples: In 1v1, every step of round 1 finishes in the non-initiative player's region before round 2 starts in the initiative player's region.

rules.text: The regions resolve in clockwise order, starting with the region to the left of the initiative player, so the initiative player's region resolves last.
examples: In a four-player game the region to the initiative player's left resolves first and the initiative player's own region last.
In 1v1, round 1 is fought in the non-initiative home region and the initiative home region comes last, in round 2.

rules.text: In 1v1, round 1 is fought in the non-initiative player's region, and round 2, if there is one, in the initiative player's region.
While a region's battle is being resolved, units in any other region, including units that stayed home and counterattackers that were sent away, are treated as if they do not exist.
examples: Player A attacks with a Rune Channeler and leaves a Good Whale at home. Player B casts Luminous Arc: it can target the attacking Channeler, but not the Whale that stayed home.

rules.text: In free-for-all games there are no battle rounds: all players declare their attacks at the same time, using intent cards.
Anything counted "in this battle" is counted separately for each region, and the count starts again at the start of each battle phase. Things that happen outside the battle phase are not counted.
examples: During a battle a player discards a card, then their attacking unit dies in combat: two cards have been trashed in this battle. At the next battle phase the count starts again from zero.

rules.text: The life a player has lost in a battle is the total of every loss in that battle. Life gained in the battle does not reduce it.
examples: A player loses 10, gains 8, then loses 3: they have lost 13 life in this battle, and Soul Siphon makes a 13/13.

rules.text: Regroup is a global step that takes place once battle has ended in every region. It resets the game between battles.
No player gets priority or takes any game action during regroup.
examples: When the last player passes in the after-combat window, the game goes through regroup and straight into deployment; no one is given priority in between.

rules.text: Regroup comes before the deployment phase, not at the end of the turn. So a spell token made, or a temporary change applied, during deployment lasts until the regroup after the next battle.
examples: Overbloom played in deployment gives +7/+7 "until regroup"; the bonus lasts through the next battle and is gone after its regroup.

rules.text: Regroup does these things, in this order: (1) all players and units return to their own regions; (2) all damage on units is removed; (3) all temporary stat changes are removed; (4) all units leave formation. All spell tokens are also erased.
examples: After a battle the attacker is back home, both players are back in their own regions, its marked damage and its -2/-2 are gone, there is no formation, and the spell token is erased.

rules.text: Each unit that is not in its controller's home region returns there. This includes a unit that was created in another region.
examples: Life Plant's 1/1s, created in the enemy region during an attack, walk home at regroup.
The attacker and the counterattacker are both back in their home regions after regroup.

rules.text: Each player who entered another region during battle stops being present there, and is present only in their own region again.
All damage on units is removed.
examples: A Good Whale carrying 1 marked damage has none after regroup.

rules.text: All temporary stat changes are removed. An effect that lasts "until regroup" ends here.
examples: Overbloom's +7/+7 "until regroup" is gone after the next regroup.
Jelly's -2/-2 on an attacker is gone after regroup.

rules.text: All units leave formation.
All spell tokens in play are erased, including unused spell tokens in a player's own region.

A card can keep spell tokens through regroup. While Harbinger of Immolation's [Augment] text applies, its controller's spell tokens are not erased; they keep their X, and they still lose their temporary changes. Other players' spell tokens are still erased.
examples: With Harbinger of Immolation in play as a unit, your spell tokens stay through regroup.
With Harbinger of Immolation in play, your Fireball 7 token survives regroup still a Fireball 7, but any temporary changes on it are gone.

rules.text: A spell token erased at regroup takes its mods with it.
examples: A Fireball token augmented during deployment and not cast is erased at regroup, and its augment is erased with it.

rules.text: Unit tokens are not erased at regroup. They stay in play like other units.
examples: The 1/1 unit tokens Life Plant made in the enemy region are still in play after regroup, back in their home region.

rules.text: The deployment phase is the last phase of each turn. In it players build up their forces for the next battle by playing cards, activating abilities, and modifying cards with graft and augment.
examples: In deployment a player plays Ignis Sprite (its spawn trigger makes a Fireball) and then Flame Juggle.

rules.text: Any card can be played during deployment except a battle card, which can be played only in the battle phase.
examples: In deployment a player plays Flame Juggle and gets a Fireball token. Fireball is a battle card, so the token cannot be cast until the battle phase.

rules.text: During deployment each player is alone in their own region. A player cannot interact with other players or their units, and treats every other player as if they did not exist.
examples: Beyond's rot replacement says "target unit", and in deployment only its controller's own units are offered.

rules.text: An effect in deployment that refers to opponents finds none. "Each opponent loses 1 life" does not affect any other player.
examples: Thoughtripper trashed outside battle makes no opponent discard, because no opponent is present.

rules.text: Modifications are applied during deployment. A mod may be applied from the hand or the bin, and a glimpsed mod also from the cache.

Grafting is done during deployment, whatever the card's speed, even for a card with Haste, and never in battle. A graft can be applied in the haste step only where an effect lets mods be applied then as if it were deployment, such as Slurpr's.
examples: With a Slurpr in its controller's region, a graft lands during the haste step.

rules.text: During deployment a player may augment a spell token they have in play. Only the augment's attributes pass to the token.
examples: A Fireball 3 token augmented in deployment with Chitin Shredder gains {Powerful}, and when cast in battle it deals 6.

rules.text: In 1v1 and team games the printed rules have the initiative team deploy first. Its players deploy in any order they wish, and then the non-initiative team does the same.
examples: In a 2v2 game both initiative players finish deploying before either non-initiative player begins.

rules.text: In this client both players deploy at the same time. Neither sees what the other does in deployment until both are done, and either may finish first.
examples: The non-initiative player is offered plays at once, and can finish deploying while the initiative player is still acting.
During deployment Player A plays Ignis Sprite; nothing of it appears in Player B's game log while deployment is under way.

rules.text: The deployment phase begins in this order: (1) each player is dealt damage equal to their rot, in initiative order; (2) then abilities that trigger "at the start of deployment" trigger.
examples: A player controls Beyond, Codex Incarnate and has 2 rot. At the start of deployment the rot comes first: Beyond asks them to pick a unit (they pick their Good Whale), and only after that do 'at the start of deployment' abilities trigger.

rules.text: All abilities that trigger at the start of deployment are put on the stack before any of them resolves.
Deployment uses the stack. Each player's plays and triggered abilities in deployment go on that player's own deployment stack, and that stack normally resolves without anyone having to act.
A decision one player must answer during deployment does not make the other player wait: the other player may keep playing, and their own deployment stack keeps resolving.
examples: Player B is answering a choice; meanwhile Player A plays a card in deployment and it resolves.
Player B has three Wraiths, and their start-of-deployment triggers are asking B to choose. Meanwhile Player A can still act, and can even finish deploying; B's triggers then resolve normally.

rules.text: The end of turn is a special step after deployment finishes. In it, abilities that trigger "at the end of turn" resolve.
examples: Harbinger of Immolation creates a Fireball X at the end of turn.

rules.text: No player can play cards during the end-of-turn step, either after the end-of-turn triggers or in response to them.
examples: While a General Smof end-of-turn trigger is asking its question, neither player is offered a card, spell token, ability, graft or augment, and an Ignis Sprite play is refused.

rules.text: After deployment and the end of turn, the turn is over. The next turn begins with the planning phase.
examples: Once both players are done deploying and the end-of-turn trigger is answered, the turn number goes up by one and the phase is planning.

rules.text: When the turn is over, the initiative token is passed to the next player clockwise. In 1v1 and team games this means the initiative alternates between the teams every turn.
examples: The player without the initiative this turn has it once the turn ends, declares the first attack of the next battle, and the turn after that it passes back.

rules.text: Draft packs are passed in the draft step: each player passes their pack clockwise to the next player when they finish drafting, and the draft step is complete once all players have passed their pack. The end-of-turn passing of "any draft packs" with the initiative names this same pass; a pack is not passed a second time when the turn ends.
examples: After both players finish drafting, each holds the pack the other drafted from.

rules.text: The initiative token is not a token. An effect that refers to tokens never affects it.
examples: Download says "Gain control of target token"; it cannot be used to take the initiative token.

rules.text: Units are the basis of combat. They attack opponents, enter other players' regions and defend against units that enter their own. Combat takes place inside regions (rule 601), with the units that take part arranged in formations (rule 602) made up of columns (rule 603).
examples: Two units attack into the opponent's region. The defender blocks one of them; the other is unblocked and deals its damage to the defending player.

rules.text: All gameplay takes place inside regions. There is one region for each player, and each player starts in their own region.
Each region is isolated from every other region. Nothing in one region interacts with anything in another region, and each region treats the players and cards in other regions as if they don't exist.
examples: Towering Colossus prints “Enemies gain +2/+2.” An enemy unit standing in a different region from the Colossus does not get the bonus.

rules.text: Every effect is specific to the region it takes place in, and never affects anything in another region. Read every card as if it said “in this region”: “Delete target unit” means “Delete target unit in this region”, and “Each player sacrifices two units” means “Each player in this region sacrifices two units in this region”.
examples: Ghord's controller sacrifices a unit, and each opponent sacrifices a nontoken unit. Only the opponent's units in Ghord's region can be sacrificed this way.

rules.text: “All” means all in this region. An effect that affects or counts “all” of something affects or counts only the ones in its own region.
examples: Cosmic Reversal recalls all other spell units. A spell unit that its opponent left at home, outside the battle region, is not recalled.

rules.text: A static ability sees and affects only things in its own region. A triggered ability triggers only on events in its own region: a spell played in one region does not trigger an ability of a unit in another region.
examples: Flourishing Flora watches for another ally spawning. An ally that spawns in a different region does not trigger it.
Crevice Lurker makes abilities cost [one] more during battle. It taxes both players' abilities in its region, the opponent's as well as its controller's.

rules.text: A player cannot sacrifice a unit that is in a different region, even a unit they control, and cannot do so to pay a cost in their current region.
examples: A player's only units are at home, outside the battle region, when Cull says "Each player sacrifices a unit." They sacrifice nothing.

rules.text: Every unit and every spell token in play is in exactly one region at a time.
examples: A unit attacks and a Fireball token rides along with it. Both are now in the battle region and no longer in their home region.

rules.text: The stack, the bins, the hands and the caches are bound by the regional rule like everything else (rule 101.6). Each region has its own stack. No player owns it: it is shared by the players present in that region, and only they can put effects on it or respond to them. A player's bin, hand and cache are tied to that player: an effect can affect them only in a region where that player is present (rule 601.4c).
examples: During deployment, an effect that targets a cached card can reach only its controller's own cache. In battle, where both players are present, it can reach either cache.
Frosted Denial, cast while battle resolves in one region, cannot negate an effect that was played in another region.

rules.text: The regions are arranged in a circle. Each player's region has two neighbouring regions, one to the left and one to the right, except in a two-player game, where each region has one neighbouring region.
examples: In a two-player game there is only one region to attack into: the attackers go into the opponent's region, and the counterattack goes into the first attacker's region.

rules.text: When a player is eliminated, the regions on either side of theirs become neighbours, and the game continues.
In a team game, once a player's neighbouring opponents have been eliminated, that player may send attacks through allied regions into the nearest enemy region.

A player is always present in their own region. A player who attacks into another region becomes present in that region as well, and stays present there until regroup, even if every unit they sent into it is removed.
examples: A player attacks into the opponent's region. From then until regroup, both players are present there, so a unit that dies in that region dies in front of both of them.

rules.text: Attacking is the only way a player enters another player's region. A player who declares no attack does not enter the region they could have attacked.
Outside the battle phase, every player is alone in their own region. A player cannot interact with any other player, or with another player's units, outside the battle phase.
examples: During deployment, Prismatic Observer can recall a card from its controller's own cache only. The opponent's cache is out of reach, because the opponent is not in the Observer's region.

rules.text: While a player is present in a region, effects in that region can affect that player, and that player's hand, bin, cache and resources. While a player is not present, effects in that region cannot affect any of them.
examples: In battle, both players are present in the battle region, so Prismatic Observer may recall a card from either player's cache.

rules.text: “Each opponent” and “each player” mean each such player who is present in the effect's region. If no such player is present, that part of the effect does nothing.
examples: A player sacrifices Bloated Manablub during deployment. “Each opponent loses 3 life” reaches nobody, because no opponent is in that player's region.
Rebalance resolves in a region where no opponent is present. No unit changes hands.

rules.text: An ally is a unit under your control in the region where the effect is happening. An enemy is a unit in that region that is not under your control. A unit in another region is neither.
At regroup, every player and every unit returns to its own region: a unit returns to its controller's region (see rule 506).
examples: Life Plant's 1/1s, created in the enemy region during an attack, return to their controller's region at regroup.

rules.text: A unit or spell token created by an effect is created in the region where the effect's source is when the effect resolves. That need not be its controller's own region.
examples: Life Plant attacks into the opponent's region, and its controller loses life there. Its 1/1s are created in the opponent's region, not at home.
Tidelurker attacks and creates a 2/2 in the enemy region. That 2/2 cannot block the counterattack in its controller's own region.

rules.text: Battle is resolved one region at a time. Once players have begun interacting inside a region, every step of battle is completed in that region before those players can interact anywhere else.
examples: The non-initiative player sends a counterattacker at block time. Battle in the first region runs through to its end before the counterattack battle begins in the other region.

rules.text: While battle is being resolved in a region, units in any other region are treated as if they don't exist.
examples: A unit with an “After combat” ability stays at home while its controller attacks. When battle ends in the opponent's region, the ability does not trigger.

rules.text: Regions are resolved in clockwise order starting with the region to the left of the initiative player, so the initiative player's region resolves last. In a two-player game, battle is resolved first in the non-initiative player's region and then, if there was a counterattack, in the initiative player's region.
examples: The initiative player attacks into the non-initiative player's region. After that battle, the counterattack is fought in the initiative player's region.

rules.text: An “After combat” ability works for a unit that is present in the region where the battle happened, whether or not that unit is in a formation. It does not trigger in a region where no battle took place.
examples: A unit with an “After combat” ability is in the battle region but outside the formation. Its ability still triggers after combat.

rules.text: Regions limit what effects can reach and count. The printed statement that there is “zero information or interaction between regions” is read as a limit on effects: no effect carries information from one region into another. It does not hide anything from players: a player may see what happens in a region they are not present in.

When units attack or block, they are placed in a formation. The units a player attacks with make up that player's attacking formation; the units a player blocks with make up that player's defending formation.
examples: A player attacks with three units in two columns; those three units are the attacking formation. The two units the defender blocks with are the defending formation.

rules.text: A formation has a front row and a back row, and any number of columns. Each column of a formation holds at most two units: one in the front row and one in the back row.
examples: A player may attack five columns wide, but cannot put three units in one column.

rules.text: An attacking formation is set during the attack step. A defending formation is set during the block step.
examples: The defender cannot declare blockers during the attack step, and the attacker cannot change the attack once the block step has begun.

rules.text: A player's formation is that player's whole side of the battle in that region: every unit they have arrayed there, in every column. It is not a single column. An effect that targets a formation targets one player's whole side.
examples: Galactic Germination targets an attacking formation of three units in two columns. It creates three 1/1s.

rules.text: A formation remains a formation for as long as its battle lasts, even when every unit in it has been removed. An effect that counts the units in an empty formation counts zero.
examples: Galactic Germination targets a formation, and every unit in it dies before the spell resolves. It resolves and creates no units.

rules.text: Once a formation is set, its units are locked in their positions until regroup, when they all leave formation. A unit's position changes only as rules 602.3–602.5 describe, or when an effect moves it.
examples: Riftwalker's ability switches its position with another ally in its formation.

rules.text: A unit can be in a battle region without being in a formation. A unit outside the formation is neither attacking nor blocking.
