examples: A defending unit stands in the battle region but is not declared as a blocker. It blocks nothing, and the unblocked attacker deals its damage to the defending player.

rules.text: A unit that spawns during battle, whether created by an effect or played as a spell unit, is placed in its region outside the formation, unless the card says otherwise.
examples: Aberrant Populace attacks and creates two Wisps. The Wisps are in the battle region, outside the formation.

rules.text: A unit that comes under another player's control during a battle, after the formations are set, leaves its formation, unless the effect that changes its control itself gives it a position. It stays out of every formation for the rest of that battle, attacking and blocking for nobody, and joins its new controller's side at regroup.
examples: Download steals an enemy Robot token after blocks. The Robot leaves the formation and takes no further part in the battle.
At regroup, the stolen Robot joins its new controller's side.

After attacks, the defender casts Organic Exchange on an attacking Bubb and their own 1/1, which is in no formation. The two swap positions as the card says: the 1/1 takes Bubb's attack slot and deals the combat damage, and Bubb is in no formation.

rules.text: The front row of a column must be filled before a unit can be placed in its back row. So a column of a formation holds no unit, one unit in its front row, or two units. It never holds a unit in its back row alone.
examples: While building an attack, a player puts a unit in the back slot of an empty column. When the attack is declared, that unit stands in the front row.

rules.text: If a unit in the front row of a column leaves the formation, the unit behind it moves up into the front row. This happens whenever it occurs during the battle: before blocks, after blocks and during combat damage.
examples: Blocks have been declared. The front unit of an attacking column dies; the unit behind it moves to the front of that column.

rules.text: If the last unit in a column of an attacking formation leaves it before blocks are declared, the columns on either side close in to fill the gap, so the line has no empty column.
examples: A three-column attack loses the only unit of its middle column during the attack window. The right-hand column moves left, and the line is two columns wide.

rules.text: After blocks are declared, columns never move to fill a gap. A column emptied after blocks stays in the line as a hole for the rest of the battle, even if its blockers are removed too.
examples: After blocks, the only attacker in the middle column dies. The column stays where it is, empty, and the columns to its right do not move.
Later in the same battle the blockers of that column die too. The hole still does not close.

rules.text: Rules 602.4 and 602.5 apply however a unit leaves its formation: it may die, be recalled, cached or erased, or leave in any other way.
examples: Before blocks, the only unit of a middle column is recalled to its owner's hand. The line closes up just as it would after a death.

rules.text: A formation closes up immediately when a unit leaves it, as a state-based action. An ability that triggers on that unit leaving play sees the formation already closed up.
examples: Before blocks, the only unit of a middle column dies. By the time any ability that triggers on the death looks at the formation, the gap has already closed.

rules.text: A defending formation may have empty columns, and they are never closed up.
examples: The defender blocks the first and third attacking columns and leaves the second unblocked. The defending formation keeps its gap.

rules.text: When an effect creates a unit, or puts one into play, “in my formation” or “in formation” without naming a position, the effect's controller chooses the position as the effect resolves.
examples: Hooba-Lin's host attacks, and its trigger creates a 1/1 “in my formation”. As the trigger resolves, Hooba-Lin's controller chooses where in the formation the 1/1 goes.

rules.text: The positions such a unit may take are: a new column at either end of the line; the back slot of any column that holds exactly one unit; and the front slot of a hole left after blocks (rule 602.5a).
examples: An attacking line has two columns, the first with two units and the second with one. The legal positions are a new column at the left end, the back slot of the second column, and a new column at the right end.

rules.text: “Either side of the existing units” means the two ends of the line. A unit is never put into a new column between two existing columns.
examples: An attacking line has three columns. A unit placed “in my formation” may open a new column at the left or right end, but never between the first and second columns.

rules.text: A defending formation never gains a new column at its ends this way. A unit placed into a defending formation may go into the back slot of a blocking column that holds one unit. After blocks have been declared, and until combat damage has been dealt, it may also stand in front of an attacking column that still has an attacker and no blocker, and that column is then blocked (see rule 606).
examples: The defender's only blocking column already holds two units. An effect that puts a unit into the defender's formation has no position for it.
After blocks, the defender plays Tiderunner Initiate in front of an unblocked attacker. That column is now blocked, and the attacker deals its combat damage to the Tiderunner.

rules.text: If exactly one position is legal, the unit goes there and no choice is asked. If no position is legal, the effect places nothing.
“My formation” means the formation the effect's source is in. If the source is in play but not in any formation when the effect resolves, the effect places nothing and creates nothing.
examples: Hooba-Lin's host attacks, then is stolen before the trigger resolves, so it is in play but out of the formation. No 1/1 is created.

rules.text: If the effect's source has left play while its effect is on the stack, “my formation” means the formation the source was in when it left play, and the effect still places the unit there.
examples: Hooba-Lin attacks and is killed with its trigger on the stack. The 1/1 is still created, in the formation Hooba-Lin was in.

rules.text: An effect whose text says “if I am still in formation” does nothing if its source is no longer in the formation when the effect resolves, including when the source has left play.
examples: Hooba-Nan attacks and is killed with its trigger on the stack. The trigger creates no 1/1s.

rules.text: An amount that counts units in “my formation” is counted as the effect resolves. Units that have left the formation by then are not counted. If the source itself has left play, the amount counts the formation it was in.
examples: Embermaw Fledgling attacks and dies in combat. Its after-combat trigger still counts the attacking units of the formation it was in.

rules.text: If an effect lets a player play a spell unit into a formation (as Hooba-Pon does), the spell part happens first. If it resolves, the unit then spawns into the formation.
examples: Hooba-Pon attacks and its controller plays a spell unit from hand through it. The spell resolves, and then the unit appears in the chosen position.

rules.text: After blocks, while the defending formation still holds at least one unit, a unit placed into it may also take the front slot of a blocking column whose blockers have all left it. The unit then blocks that column.
examples: The defender's only blocker in the second column dies after blocks. An effect that puts a unit into the defender's formation may put it in front of the second attacking column.

rules.text: A player with no unit standing in a formation in the battle, because they have not formed one or because every unit in it has left, is offered no position in it, not even a hole, and a unit cannot be played or placed into it. Rules 602.6c and 602.6f are the exceptions.
examples: The attacker has attacked and the defender has not yet declared blocks. The defender stands in no formation, so an effect that puts a unit into the defender's formation has nowhere to put it.
After blocks, every attacking unit dies. The attacker then plays Tiderunner Initiate; it cannot be played into the attacking line, not even into a hole, and enters play outside any formation.

The defender declares no blockers. An effect that puts a unit into the defender's formation may still put it in front of the unblocked attacking column (rule 602.6c); the attacker is offered no such spot.

rules.text: Some cards say they may be played into a formation (Tiderunner Initiate, Trench Stalker). The position is chosen as the card is cast, from the positions rule 602.6 allows, and the unit is already in that position when it enters play.
examples: Tiderunner Initiate's spot is asked for while it is being cast, and it enters play already standing in that spot.
No moment exists in which the Tiderunner is in the region but outside the formation, so the opponent cannot respond to it there.

rules.text: If the chosen position no longer exists when the card resolves, the unit enters play in the region, outside the formation.
examples: Tiderunner Initiate is cast to go behind an attacker, and the attacker dies before it resolves. The Tiderunner enters the region outside the formation.

rules.text: Playing such a card into the formation is optional. Its controller may instead play it so that it enters the region outside the formation.
examples: When casting Tiderunner Initiate, its controller may choose to have it stay out of the formation.

rules.text: Such a card can be played into a formation only if its controller has a formation in that battle that still holds at least one unit: they attacked, or they declared blocks, and not every unit in it has left. As an exception, after blocks are declared and until combat damage has been dealt, the defending player may play it in front of an unblocked attacking column (rule 602.6c) even if they declared no blockers. Otherwise it is played normally, outside any formation.
examples: Before blocks, the defending player has no formation. They cast Tiderunner Initiate; nothing is asked and it enters play outside any formation.
After blocks, the defender plays a unit in front of an unblocked attacking column. That column is blocked, and stays blocked when the unit is removed.
After blocks, every attacking unit dies. The attacker plays Tiderunner Initiate; nothing is asked and it enters play outside any formation.

rules.text: A column is one file of the battle line: the attacking units in it and the defending units placed in front of it. Each side of a column holds at most two units. A defending unit placed in front of an attacking column blocks that whole column.
examples: One unit blocks a column of two attackers. Neither attacker deals damage to the defending player.

rules.text: Combat attributes are shared by the units in the same column of a formation, and are not shared with units to their left or right (see rule 802.1).
examples: A unit with Flying attacks in the front of a column. The unit behind it has Flying too; the unit in the next column does not.

rules.text: A defending unit may also block in a column where there is no attacker (a side-block). Side-block columns stand beside the attacking line, on either side of it (see rule 606). Any number of units may side-block, and each may stand in a column of its own.
examples: Two defending units block where no attacker is, each in its own column beside the attack.
A single 2/5 attacks; the defender side-blocks to its left with a 1/1. The 1/1 stands in a new column left of the attack, the attacking column stays unblocked, and it deals 2 to the defender.

rules.text: Two side-blocking units may stand in the same side-block column, one in its front slot and one in its back slot.
A unit in a formation is adjacent to its left, right, front and back neighbours in that formation.
examples: Inspiration gives +2/+2 to its controller's units adjacent to it in formation, and to no others.
The defender blocks the first and third attacking columns and leaves the second unblocked. The two blockers are not neighbours, so an Inspiration in one does not buff the other.

rules.text: A unit in a formation has at most three adjacent positions: the same row of the column to its left, the same row of the column to its right, and the other slot of its own column. The other row of a neighbouring column is diagonal, and is not adjacent. Where a line ends, there is a position past the end only as rule 603.3 allows.
examples: Hooba-Nan stands in the front row of a middle column. Its adjacent slots are the front rows of the columns on either side and the slot behind it, and nothing diagonal.

rules.text: Adjacency exists only in a formation. A unit that is not in a formation has no adjacent units and no adjacent slots.
examples: During deployment, Throwing Boulder stands in its region beside an allied unit, but neither is in a formation. Its ability (“only if I have an adjacent ally”) cannot be activated.

rules.text: An amount based on adjacency, such as the number of adjacent allies, is counted as the effect resolves.
examples: Flamebreath Initiate attacks with one ally in the column beside it. X is 1, so it creates a Fireball 2. Attacking alone, X is 0 and the Fireball is 1.
Flamebreath Initiate attacks beside an ally, and the ally is destroyed while the trigger waits. X is 0 when the trigger resolves.

rules.text: A unit that has left play has no adjacent units. If it left play with its effect on the stack, an amount counting the units adjacent to it is 0.
examples: Flamebreath Initiate attacks and is removed with its trigger on the stack. X is 0, so the trigger still creates a Fireball 1.

rules.text: The empty column just past each end of an attacking line exists. For a unit in the front row at either end of an attacking line, the front-row slot of a new column past that end is an adjacent slot.
examples: Hooba-Nan stands alone in an attacking line. Its trigger creates three 1/1s: one in a new column on each side and one behind it.
Hooba-Nan is at the right end of a longer line, with a unit to its left. Its trigger creates two 1/1s: one in a new column past the right end and one behind it.

rules.text: Past the end of the line, only the front-row slot is adjacent. A unit in the back row at the end of the line has no adjacent slot past that end, because the front row must be filled first (rule 602.3).
examples: Hooba-Nan stands in the back row of the column at the end of the line. Its trigger creates no 1/1 past the edge.

rules.text: A defending formation has no adjacent slots past its ends.

Text that names positions relative to the unit itself, such as “my empty adjacent slots” or “the empty slot behind me”, refers to exactly those positions. Its controller does not choose among positions as they do under rule 602.6.
examples: Rousing Spirit attacks, and a cheap unit from its controller's bin is put into the empty slot behind it.

rules.text: A formation can grow at either end without limit.
When the columns of a line move (a new column opens at the left end, or the line closes up under rule 602.5), each block and each effect that applies to a particular column moves with that column.
examples: A new column opens at the left end of a line that has already been blocked. Every blocker still blocks the same attackers as before.

A Swift column led by Dune Drifter has already dealt its damage first. Its controller then plays Tiderunner Initiate into a new column on the left; the Drifter's column shifts right but still counts as having struck, so it does not deal damage again.

rules.text: Attacking is how a player brings units, and the spell tokens that travel with them, into a neighbouring enemy region for battle. Attacks are declared in the attack step, the first step of a battle round (see 505).
examples: The initiative player declares an attack with one unit. That unit moves into the other player's region, and at regroup it returns home.

rules.text: Units attack players directly. They do not attack individual units unless a spell directs them to.

In a two-player game and in team games, each team gets one chance to attack per turn. In the first battle round the initiative player attacks into the non-initiative player's region; in the second battle round the non-initiative player attacks with the units it sent to counterattack or, if the first round had no attack, with any of its units (see 505, 610 and rule 604.4a).
examples: The initiative player attacks with a 2/2. The non-initiative player sends a 4/3 to counterattack while declaring blocks. After the first round's combat, the 4/3 attacks in the second round.

rules.text: To attack, the attacking player chooses which of its units go and places them in an attacking formation (see 602). The attacking formation is set in the attack step, and from then on its units are locked in position.
examples: A player with three units attacks with two of them, side by side in two columns. The third stays at home.

rules.text: Attacking is optional. A player may declare no attack.
examples: The initiative player has a unit that could attack and declares no attack. The battle moves to the second round.

rules.text: There is no summoning sickness. A unit may attack, or block, however recently it entered play.
examples: A 2/2 enters play during the battle phase, just before attacks are declared. It may attack at once, and it deals 2 to the defending player.

rules.text: Spell tokens may go with an attack, but only together with at least one unit, and only spell tokens the attacking player controls in the region the attack leaves from.
examples: A player sending a counterattack names a Poison token and no unit when declaring blocks. The declaration is refused.
A player declares an attack naming a Poison token and no unit. The Poison does not go: with no unit, the declaration is no attack at all.

rules.text: Bringing a spell token into another region with an attack cannot be undone.
examples: A Poison token goes along with an attack into the enemy region. In the counterattack, fought in its owner home region, the token is still in the enemy region and cannot be cast.

rules.text: A unit targeted by an Alluring trigger may not be declared as an attacker, or sent to counterattack, for the rest of the battle phase (see 802.15).
examples: An Alluring attacker targets a defending unit. That unit cannot be sent out to counterattack when blocks are declared.

rules.text: In the second battle round, the attacking player may attack only with the units it sent to counterattack in the first round, unless the first round had no attack (see 604 and 610).
examples: The non-initiative player sent one unit to counterattack and kept another at home. In the second round, only the sent unit may attack.

rules.text: When an attack is declared, the attacking units, and the spell tokens with them, move into the region attacked. They remain there until the regroup phase, when they return to their own region (see 506).
examples: A unit that counterattacked into the initiative player's region is back in its own region once regroup is over.

rules.text: Once a player has sent attacking units into an enemy region, that player is present there and may interact with things in that region using spells and effects (see 601).
examples: After an attack, both players are present in the battle region, so each sees every death in it.

rules.text: The units in the attacking formation are the attacking units. A unit that arrives in the battle region outside the formation, such as one created there during the battle, is not attacking.
examples: Aberrant Populace attacks and creates two Wisps. The Wisps are in the battle region but not in the formation, so they are not attacking.

rules.text: Abilities that trigger when a unit attacks trigger as the attack is declared. They are put on the stack before the attack window opens, so players can respond to them in that window (see 605 and 706).
examples: Tempest Wrangler attacks and its Alluring trigger goes on the stack. In the attack window the defending player negates it with Containment Protocol, and no unit is lured.

rules.text: A unit attacks alone when it is the only unit in its attacking formation. Spell tokens that travel with it do not count as company.
examples: Whispering Mantid (Sneaky) attacking by itself cannot be blocked; attacking beside another unit, it can.

rules.text: If the attacking player declares no attack, there is no combat in that round: no attack window, no block step, no block window, no combat damage step and no after combat step.
examples: Both players decline to attack. The whole battle phase passes with no priority window at all.

rules.text: If the initiative player declares no attack in the first battle round, the non-initiative player may still attack in the second battle round, and may attack with any of its units.
examples: The initiative player declines to attack. The non-initiative player, who sent nobody to counterattack, attacks in the second round with a unit that stayed at home.

rules.text: The attack window is the priority window that follows the declaration of an attack, in the region attacked.
examples: An attack is declared. Priority goes to the initiative player, then to the other player; when both pass, the step moves on.

rules.text: The initiative player receives priority first in the attack window (see 703).
When all players pass priority in succession with the stack empty, the attack window ends and the block step begins (see 606).
examples: Luminous Arc is cast in the attack window; two passes resolve it and a new window opens. Two more passes on the empty stack end the attack window.

rules.text: Until blocks are declared, a column of the attacking formation that loses its last unit closes up: the columns on its sides move in to fill the gap (see 602).
examples: The middle column of a three-column attack is killed in the block step, before blocks are declared. The right-hand column slides left into the gap, and the attack is two columns wide.

rules.text: If every attacking unit is removed during the attack window, the attacking player is still present in the region for the rest of the battle phase.
examples: The only attacker is destroyed in the attack window. Its controller may still cast spells in that region later in the battle phase.

rules.text: Blocking is how a player who has been attacked defends. In the block step, the defending player may place its units in front of the attacking formation.
examples: Two columns attack, a 3/5 and a 4/5; the defending player places a 2/5 in front of the 3/5. That column is blocked and the two units deal damage to each other; the unblocked 4/5 hits the player.

rules.text: The blocking units form the defending formation. Like any formation, it has a front row and a back row (see 602).
examples: Two units block one attacking column, one in the front row and one behind it. The attacker damages the front one.

rules.text: Unlike an attacking formation, the defending formation may have empty columns: the defending player need not block every attacking column, and an empty blocking column is never closed up.
examples: Against a three-column attack, the defending player blocks only the third column. The first two columns are unblocked, and the attack stays three columns wide.

rules.text: The defending player may declare no blockers at all.
examples: The defending player declares no blocks and sends a unit to counterattack; the attacker's unblocked column hits the defending player.

rules.text: Blocks are declared once. Once declared, the defending formation is set and its units are locked in position. A unit can join it later only by an effect that puts a unit into formation (see 607).
examples: After declaring blocks, the defending player cannot declare them again to move a blocker from one column to another.

rules.text: A blocking unit stands in one slot of the defending formation, so it blocks only the attacking column it stands in front of.
examples: One blocker cannot block two attacking columns at once; to block both, the defending player needs a unit in front of each.

rules.text: An empty blocking column keeps its place in the defending formation. Two blockers with an empty blocking column between them are not neighbours, so they are not adjacent (see 603).
examples: Against a three-column attack, the defending player blocks the first and third columns. The two blockers are not adjacent: the empty middle blocking column lies between them.

rules.text: The defending player may block with units it controls in the battle region.
examples: A unit created in the enemy region during the first round's attack is not in its controller's region when the counterattack arrives, so it cannot block it.

rules.text: A unit may block however recently it entered play (see 604).
examples: A unit that entered the defending player's region during the attack window may be declared as a blocker.

rules.text: Whether a unit is able to block a column depends only on that unit and that column. It never depends on what the defending player chose to do with its other units, except where two Alluring duties name the same unit (see 802.15).
examples: An Alluring column lures a defending unit. The defending player cannot excuse it by putting it on another column instead; it is still able to block the Alluring column, so it must.

rules.text: These attributes change which units may block a column, or how many it takes: Flying (802.2), Feeble (802.12), Evasive (802.13), Sneaky (802.14), Alluring (802.15) and Pure (802.25).
examples: Only a Flying unit can block a Flying column, but a Pure unit ignores Flying and can block it too.
Wisps are Feeble and cannot block.
Curio Drifter is Evasive, so its column needs two blockers.

rules.text: A unit sent to counterattack leaves the region and is treated as if it does not exist until the first battle round is over, so it cannot also block (see 610).
examples: The defending player has one unit. It may block, or it may be sent to counterattack, but not both.

rules.text: A unit targeted by an Alluring trigger must block that Alluring column if it is able to. If the column is blocked at all, the lured unit must be one of its blockers (see 802.15).
examples: An Alluring column lures unit A. The defending player tries to block that column with unit B instead. The declaration is refused.
The Alluring column is also Evasive and the defending player has only the lured unit. It cannot block an Evasive column alone, so it need not block it, and may block another column.

rules.text: Alluring duties never leave the defending player without a legal block declaration. However many Alluring triggers have resolved, the game offers the defending player at least one block declaration, and every declaration it offers is legal.
examples: Two attacking columns both have Alluring, and their triggers targeted the same defending unit. The defending player is still offered a legal declaration.

rules.text: An attacking column is blocked once a defending unit has been placed in front of it. The whole column is blocked, however many attacking units it holds.
examples: A column of two attackers is blocked by one unit. Neither attacker deals combat damage to the defending player.

rules.text: A blocked column stays blocked for the rest of the battle round, even if every unit blocking it leaves, whether it dies, is recalled, is erased or changes control.
examples: The only blocker dies in the block window. The vanilla attacker's column is still blocked and deals no damage to the defending player.
The only blocker is stolen by Download mid-combat. The column is still blocked.

rules.text: A blocked column deals no combat damage to the defending player, except as Piercing allows (see 608 and 802.16).
examples: A blocked non-Piercing column whose blocker died before damage deals nothing to the defending player.

rules.text: A defending unit may be placed blocking where no attacker is. This is a side-block, and the blocking column it makes is a side-blocking column.
examples: One unit attacks. The defending player places two units to the side of it, each in its own column, and leaves the attacker unblocked.

rules.text: Side-blocks may stand on either side of the attacking formation.
examples: A unit side-blocks to the left of a one-column attack. A new column opens before the attacking column, and the attacking column is still unblocked.

rules.text: Any number of units may side-block, each as its own column.
examples: Two units side-block beside a one-column attack; each makes its own side-blocking column.

rules.text: A block declaration may reach no further out from the attacking formation than it has blocking columns, so a single side-block stands next to the attacking formation.
examples: Against a one-column attack, a single side-block may stand right beside the attack on either side, but not three columns out.

rules.text: A side-blocking column counts as a blocked column.
examples: Roving Quillback attacks alone and two units side-block beside it. Quillback deals 1 damage to the defending player for each blocked column: 2, for the two side-blocking columns.

rules.text: A side-block blocks no attacker. It does not count as blocking a lone Sneaky attacker, and no Flying or Evasive rule applies to it.
examples: A lone Sneaky unit attacks. A unit side-blocking beside it is allowed, and the Sneaky unit is still unblocked.

rules.text: A side-blocking column deals no combat damage, Piercing included, because no attacker stands in front of it (see 608).
examples: A 5/5 Piercing unit side-blocks. It deals no combat damage to the attacking player.

rules.text: Side-blocking units are part of the defending formation, so they are adjacent to their neighbours in it (see 603).
examples: A unit side-blocks next to a unit blocking the attacking column. The two are adjacent, which matters to cards that count adjacent units.

rules.text: In the first battle round, the defending player declares at the same time as its blocks which of its units it sends to counterattack (see 610).
examples: The non-initiative player declares no blocks and sends one unit; that unit takes no part in the first round and attacks in the second.

rules.text: Spell tokens may go with the counterattacking units, under the same conditions as with an attack (see 604).
examples: The defending player sends a unit to counterattack and names a Poison token to go with it. The token leaves with the unit and arrives with it for round 2.

rules.text: In the second battle round the defending player declares blocks only. There are no further counterattacks.
examples: In the second round the initiative player blocks the counterattack; it cannot send units to attack back.

rules.text: Abilities that trigger when a unit blocks trigger as blocks are declared. They are put on the stack before the block window opens (see 607 and 706).
examples: Spewing Mushroom says 'When I attack or block'. Declared as a blocker, it creates its Poison.
Palewing blocks and its controller discards a card.

rules.text: If no attacking unit is left when the block step begins, the block step still takes place: the defending player declares blocks, which may be none, and the battle round continues.
examples: The only attacker is destroyed before blocks and the attack collapses to nothing. The defending player declares no blocks, and the block window follows.

rules.text: The block window is the priority window that follows the declaration of blocks.
When all players pass priority in succession with the stack empty, the block window ends and the combat damage step begins (see 608).
examples: After blocks, the first pass deals no damage; the second pass starts the combat damage step.

rules.text: Once blocks have been declared, a column that loses its last unit is not closed up; the columns stay where they are for the rest of the battle round (see 602).
examples: After blocks, the middle attacking column dies. It stays as a hole, and the columns beside it do not move.

rules.text: A unit behind a removed unit still moves up to the front row after blocks have been declared (see 602).
examples: After blocks, the front unit of a column dies; the unit behind it moves to the front.

rules.text: After blocks have been declared, a unit that joins the defending formation (for example Tiderunner Initiate, played into an open spot) may be placed in front of an attacking column that has no blocker. That column is then blocked.
examples: The defending player declares no blocks, then plays Tiderunner Initiate in front of the unblocked attacker. The attacker deals its damage to the Tiderunner, not to the player.

rules.text: A column blocked this way stays blocked if that unit later leaves, like any blocked column (see 606).
examples: Tiderunner Initiate is played in front of an unblocked attacker and is then removed. The column is still blocked.

rules.text: The defending player may block this way even if it declared no blockers.
examples: The defending player declared no blocks; Tiderunner Initiate is still offered the spot in front of the attacker.

rules.text: Only a unit joining the defending formation can be placed this way. A unit joining the attacking formation is never placed in a blocking position.
examples: After blocks, the attacking player is offered no blocking spot; the defending player is offered one, in front of the unblocked column.

rules.text: A unit can be placed this way from the block window until the combat damage step is over.
examples: In the window between the Swift and normal damage sub-steps, the defending player plays Tiderunner Initiate in front of an unblocked attacking column. The column is blocked for the normal sub-step.

rules.text: A unit placed this way was not declared as a blocker, so the events of the block declaration do not happen for it.
examples: After blocks, the defending player plays Tiderunner Initiate in front of an unblocked attacker. It now blocks that column, but it was never declared as a blocker, so nothing that happens when blocks are declared happens for it.

rules.text: An ability that triggers "after the blocking step" triggers once blocks have been declared, and resolves in the block window.
examples: Roving Quillback attacks and two units side-block. Once both players pass in the block window, its trigger resolves and the defending player loses 2 life, before any combat damage.

rules.text: The combat damage step is the step of a battle in which the units in formation deal combat damage. It begins once blocks have been declared and all players have passed priority in the window that follows them, and it is followed by the after combat step (see rule 609).
examples: A 2/5 attacks and is blocked by a 2/5. After blocks, the block window opens; once both players pass, each deals 2 to the other, and then the after combat step begins.

rules.text: The combat damage step takes place separately in each region where a battle takes place. A region that was not attacked has no combat damage step.
examples: The first attacker declares no attack, so the defending player's region has no combat damage step. The second player then attacks, and the only combat damage step of the turn is in the first player's region.

rules.text: All combat damage is dealt simultaneously, unless an ability changes when a column deals its damage. Swift and Sluggish are the attributes that do (see rule 608.2).
examples: A 3/3 attacks and is blocked by a 3/3. Both are dealt 3 at the same time, so both die.

rules.text: Combat damage is dealt by columns. The attacking units of one column deal their combat damage together, as one source, and so do the blocking units of one column. In this section, each of these two groups is called a half-column: a column has an attacking half and a blocking half.
examples: Two Slinks (Thieving) attack in one column and are not blocked. The column is one source of combat damage, so its controller draws one card, not two.

rules.text: The combat damage step has three damage sub-steps, taken in this order: the Swift sub-step, the normal sub-step and the Sluggish sub-step. Each half-column strikes (deals its combat damage) only in the sub-steps that rule 608.2a gives it. The two halves of one column are scheduled separately.
examples: Dune Drifter (2/1, Swift) is blocked by a 1/5, and Ambling Mountaintop (Sluggish) attacks unblocked. The Drifter deals 2 in the Swift sub-step, the 1/5 strikes back in the normal sub-step and kills it, and the Mountaintop deals its damage last.

rules.text: A half-column that has Swift strikes in the Swift sub-step. A half-column that has Sluggish strikes in the Sluggish sub-step. A half-column that has neither strikes in the normal sub-step.
examples: Dune Drifter (2/1, Swift) and Rune Channeler (4/3) attack in one column and are blocked by a 2/2. The attacking half deals its 6 damage in the Swift sub-step; when that sub-step ends the 2/2 has been destroyed and the attackers are undamaged.

rules.text: Whether a half-column has Swift or Sluggish depends on the combat attributes its units share: an attribute of any unit in a column is shared by every unit in that column (see rule 603). When a unit leaves a column, the other units in it lose the attributes that unit was sharing at once.
examples: Dune Drifter (Swift) and Lithoghul attack in one column, so Lithoghul would strike in the Swift sub-step. If Dune Drifter is recalled, Lithoghul at once strikes in the normal sub-step instead.

rules.text: A half-column that has both Swift and Sluggish strikes twice: once in the Swift sub-step and once in the Sluggish sub-step. It does not strike in the normal sub-step.
examples: Rime Wraith (2/1, Swift and Sluggish) and Vroot (4/4) attack in one column and are not blocked. The column deals 6 in the Swift sub-step and 6 more in the Sluggish sub-step.
Rime Wraith attacks alone and is not blocked. It deals 2 in the Swift sub-step, nothing strikes in the normal sub-step, and it deals 2 more in the Sluggish sub-step.

rules.text: If either half of a column contains a Pure card, neither half of that column has Swift or Sluggish for that exchange, so both halves strike in the normal sub-step.
examples: A printed Swift column blocked by a Pure unit strikes in the normal sub-step.

rules.text: A half-column that has struck in the Swift sub-step does not strike in the normal sub-step, even if the unit that gave it Swift has since left the column, and even if a new unit has since been put into that column. A half-column that has struck in the normal sub-step does not strike in the Sluggish sub-step, even if it has since gained Sluggish. A half-column that struck in the Swift sub-step and has Sluggish in the Sluggish sub-step strikes again then (rule 608.2c). This record belongs to the half-column, not to the units in it, and it stays with that column if the columns are renumbered (for example, when a new column is opened to its left).
examples: Dune Drifter (2/1, Swift) and a 3/3 attack in one column; a 1/1 attacks in another. The Swift column deals 5 in the Swift sub-step. Dune Drifter is then recalled. In the normal sub-step only the 1/1's column strikes.
After Dune Drifter's column strikes in the Swift sub-step, Dune Drifter is recalled and Tiderunner Initiate is played into the emptied column. Tiderunner Initiate deals no normal combat damage.

rules.text: Whether a half-column strikes in a sub-step is determined as that sub-step begins, from the units then in the column and the attributes they then share.
examples: A column strikes in the Swift sub-step and then gains Sluggish. It strikes again in the Sluggish sub-step.

rules.text: A combat damage step is split if, when the step begins, half-columns are scheduled to strike in two or more different sub-steps. Otherwise it is unsplit. Only Swift and Sluggish can split a step.
examples: Dune Drifter (Swift) is blocked by a unit without Swift or Sluggish. The attacking half strikes in the Swift sub-step and the blocking half in the normal one, so the step is split.

rules.text: In an unsplit step, all combat damage is dealt at once, as one step. No player receives priority during it, and abilities that trigger during it wait until the after combat step (see rule 608.9b).
examples: Lithoghul (4/4) and Geode (1/1) attack in separate columns and are not blocked. Neither has Swift or Sluggish, so the step is unsplit; the 5 damage is dealt at once and the game goes straight to the after combat step.

rules.text: In a split step, each sub-step that was scheduled, when the step began, to have a half-column strike in it is a separate step. After each such sub-step except the last scheduled one, the abilities that triggered during it are put on the stack and players receive priority; the next sub-step deals no damage until that stack has resolved and all players have passed priority in succession with it empty. State-based changes (deaths, back-row units moving forward, lost shared attributes) have already happened when this window opens.
examples: Bripp (4 power) and Bloated Manablub (2 power) attack in normal columns, and Adversary of the Deep (2/2, Sluggish; 'Whenever a player loses life, put that many +1/+1 counters on me') attacks in a third column. None are blocked. The normal sub-step deals 6; the step stops, Adversary's trigger resolves with priority, and Adversary strikes in the Sluggish sub-step for 8.
At the boundary, the stack holds Adversary of the Deep's trigger and priority is with the player who does not control it.

rules.text: A sub-step in which no half-column was scheduled to strike when the step began is not a separate step: no window opens after it. A scheduled sub-step keeps its window even if every half-column scheduled for it has since been destroyed. No window opens after the last scheduled sub-step; a half-column that still strikes in a later sub-step (rule 608.2f) strikes without a window before it, and then the after combat step begins.
examples: Dune Drifter (Swift) and Lithoghul attack in separate columns and are not blocked. Half-columns strike in the Swift and normal sub-steps and nothing strikes in the Sluggish sub-step, so there is exactly one window, between the Swift and normal sub-steps.

Dune Drifter (Swift) and a 1/1 attack in separate columns and are not blocked. At the window after the Swift sub-step, Dune Drifter's column gains Sluggish. The 1/1 strikes in the normal sub-step and no window follows; Dune Drifter's column then strikes in the Sluggish sub-step, and the after combat step begins.

rules.text: Which sub-steps are separate steps is determined once, when the combat damage step begins. A unit that dies, leaves or loses an attribute during the step does not make a split step unsplit.
examples: Dune Drifter (Swift) attacks beside Lithoghul and is blocked by another Dune Drifter. Both Swift units destroy each other in the Swift sub-step; the window before the normal sub-step still opens, and the death triggers can be answered there.

rules.text: Between sub-steps, the game's state is updated before anything else: units with lethal damage are destroyed, a unit behind a removed unit moves to the front row, and attributes shared by a removed unit are lost. A unit destroyed in an earlier sub-step deals no damage in a later one, and damage in a later sub-step is assigned to the formation as it then stands. Columns do not close gaps after blocks have been declared.
examples: Dune Drifter (2/1, Swift) is blocked by a 2/2 in front of a 4/3. Its Swift damage destroys the 2/2; the 4/3 is already in front when the boundary window opens, and in the normal sub-step it destroys Dune Drifter while taking no damage.
A blocking column whose attacker was destroyed in an earlier sub-step deals nothing in a later sub-step.

rules.text: Each attacking half-column deals its combat damage either to the defending player or to the blocking half-column in front of it, and each blocking half-column deals its combat damage to the attacking half-column it blocks. Piercing can also carry combat damage to a player (see rule 802.16). An attacking column is blocked once a blocking unit has been placed in front of it, normally in the block step (see rule 606) or later as rule 608.4d allows.
examples: A 3/5 and a 4/5 attack in two columns; a 2/5 blocks the 3/5. The 3/5 deals 3 to the blocker, the blocker deals 2 to the 3/5, and the 4/5 deals 4 to the defending player.

rules.text: An attacking half-column that is not blocked deals its combat damage to the defending player.
examples: Slink (2/3) attacks and is not blocked. The defending player is dealt 2 combat damage.

rules.text: An attacking half-column that is blocked deals its combat damage to the units of the blocking half-column in front of it, and that blocking half-column deals its combat damage to the units of the attacking half-column. A blocked attacking half-column deals no combat damage to the defending player, except as Piercing allows (see rule 802.16).
examples: The column of Living Forge and A Pile of Rubbish deals a combined 3 damage to the Tiderunner Initiate blocking it; the Tiderunner deals 2 back, all to Living Forge because it is in the front. (from the Manual p.23)

rules.text: Once an attacking column is blocked, it remains blocked for the rest of the battle, however its blockers leave the blocking half-column: destroyed, recalled, erased or stolen. If no blocking unit remains when that column strikes, an attacking half-column without Piercing deals no combat damage at all, and one with Piercing deals all of its damage to the defending player (see rule 802.16).
examples: A vanilla attacker is blocked; the blocker is then recalled before damage. The column stays blocked and the defending player is dealt no damage.
Good Whale (7/5, Piercing) is blocked by a 1/1 that dies before damage. All 7 of its damage is dealt to the defending player.
A 7/5 without Piercing is blocked by a 1/1 that dies before damage. It deals nothing to the defending player.

rules.text: If, after blocks have been declared and before combat damage is over, a unit is put into the defending formation in front of an unblocked attacking column, that column becomes blocked, and it stays blocked if that unit later leaves. The defending player may do this even if they declared no blockers.
examples: Tiderunner Initiate is played in front of an unblocked attacker after blocks; the attacker deals its damage to the Tiderunner instead of the defending player.

rules.text: A blocking half-column with no attacking unit left in front of it when it would strike deals no combat damage, even if it has Piercing.
examples: Good Whale (7/5, Piercing) blocks a column whose only attacker is destroyed in the block window. Good Whale deals no damage to the attacking player and takes none.

rules.text: A unit blocking where no attacking unit is (a side-block) forms a blocking half-column with no attacker in front of it. It deals no combat damage, even if it has Piercing, and it never makes the combat damage step split.
examples: A Piercing unit side-blocks. It deals no combat damage to the attacking player.

rules.text: A half-column's combat damage is the combined power of the units in it when it strikes, counted as rule 608.5c describes.
examples: A 1/1 and a 2/2 attack in one column beside a Swift column. In the window after the Swift sub-step the 1/1 gets two +1/+1 counters, so the column deals 3 + 2 = 5 in the normal sub-step.

rules.text: A unit with 0 power deals no damage, but it does not stop its column from dealing the combined power of the other units in it. A half-column whose combined power is 0 deals no combat damage.
examples: Zephyrzoa, reduced to 0 power, is in a column with a powered unit. The column deals combat damage and Zephyrzoa's 'when my column deals combat damage' ability triggers.
Zephyrzoa, reduced to 0 power, attacks alone. Its column deals no combat damage and its ability does not trigger.

rules.text: Powerful doubles a half-column's combined power once, before that damage is divided among its recipients (see rule 802.10). Vulnerable does not change the amount a half-column deals; it doubles what a Vulnerable unit is dealt (see rule 802.11).
examples: Chitin Shredder (Powerful) attacks unblocked; the defending player is dealt double its column's power.

rules.text: When a half-column's combined power is counted, a unit with negative power counts as 0: it deals no damage and does not reduce its column's damage. In an exchange in which Unaware applies, each unit's printed power is used.
examples: Lithoghul (4/4) and a -2/3 token attack in one column and are not blocked. The column deals 4.

A Robot token with nine +1/+1 counters (a 9/9) attacks and is blocked by Bubb, which is Unaware. In that exchange both read their printed stats: the Robot is a 0/0, so it dies and deals Bubb no damage.

rules.text: When a half-column deals combat damage to the units of the opposing half-column, its damage is divided among those units, starting with the front unit and then the unit behind it.
examples: Living Forge and A Pile of Rubbish attack in one column and are blocked by Tiderunner Initiate. All 2 of the Tiderunner’s damage goes to Living Forge, in front; none goes to A Pile of Rubbish behind it. (from the Manual p.23)

rules.text: The controller of the half-column dealing the damage divides it: the attacking player divides an attacking half-column's damage among the blocking units, and the defending player divides a blocking half-column's damage among the attacking units.
examples: A 4-power attacker is blocked by two 1/1s. The attacking player is asked how to divide the 4.
The defending player divides a blocking half-column's damage and may put all of it on the front attacker.

rules.text: Lethal damage (rule 608.6e) must be assigned to a unit before any damage is assigned to the unit behind it.
examples: Rune Channeler (4 power) is blocked by a 2/3 in front of a 1/1. Its controller may put 3 or 4 on the 2/3, but not less than 3, since 3 is the 2/3's lethal damage.

rules.text: A unit may be assigned more than lethal damage. The dealing player may assign all of a half-column's damage to the front unit and none to the unit behind it, even if there is enough to destroy both.
examples: A 4-power attacker is blocked by a 1/1 in front of a 1/1. The attacking player assigns all 4 to the front 1/1; the back 1/1 is untouched.

rules.text: All combat damage assigned to a unit is dealt to that unit, including any beyond its lethal damage; none of it is lost. A half-column without Piercing that has at least one unit to deal damage to assigns all of its damage to those units, so none of it reaches the player; any of its damage still unassigned when the last unit is reached is assigned to that unit.
examples: Rune Channeler (4/3, no Piercing) is blocked by a 1/1. All 4 damage is dealt to the 1/1; none is lost and none reaches the player.
An overkill combat hit on Mirage Scuttler marks the whole amount, not only the lethal part.

rules.text: Lethal damage, for assignment, is the smallest amount of the half-column's damage that would destroy the unit, given the damage already marked on it: its remaining defense; half of that, rounded up, if the unit is Vulnerable; 1 if the half-column has Deadly. In an exchange in which Unaware applies, the unit's printed defense, less the damage already marked on it, is used. In an exchange involving a Pure card, neither Vulnerable nor Deadly changes lethal damage.
examples: A 10-power Piercing half-column blocked by a Vulnerable 3/8 must assign 4 to it, and the other 6 may go to the player.

rules.text: If the opposing half-column has only one unit, all of the damage is assigned to that unit; with Piercing, the dealing player may instead send damage beyond that unit's lethal damage to its controller (see rule 802.16).
examples: A Piercing attacker with 10 power is blocked by a lone Vulnerable 3/8. It may assign all 10 to that unit (dealt as 20), and then none reaches the player.

rules.text: Damage prevention on a unit does not change its lethal damage. Lethal damage is worked out as if the unit were not protected, and the prevention applies when the damage is dealt (rule 608.7a).
examples: A shielded 0/5 Awoken Tomb is in front of a 5/6. At least 5 must be assigned to the Tomb before any is assigned to the 5/6.

rules.text: In each sub-step, every half-column's damage is divided before any damage in that sub-step is dealt.
examples: Two 10/20 attackers are each blocked by two 1/3s. Both attackers are asked how to divide their damage, and no damage is dealt until both have answered.

rules.text: All the combat damage of one sub-step is dealt simultaneously. Damage dealt to a unit is marked on it; a Vulnerable unit is dealt double the damage assigned to it (see rule 802.11), and a Poisonous source deals its damage to units in the form of -1/-1 counters (see rule 802.18).
examples: Crumbling Ancient (Vulnerable) is marked with double the combat damage assigned to it.

rules.text: Prevention applies as combat damage is dealt. Damage that is prevented is not dealt: it is not marked, it places no -1/-1 counters, it does not trigger abilities that trigger on a unit being dealt damage, and it cannot destroy a unit through Deadly.
examples: A 12-power half-column is blocked by an Awoken Tomb under Phytochemical Protection in front of a 5/6. The 5 combat damage assigned to the Tomb is prevented: none is marked, and the Tomb’s “when I am dealt damage” ability does not trigger.
A Deadly half-column cannot destroy a unit whose damage is prevented.

rules.text: After a sub-step's damage has been dealt, units with lethal damage, and units dealt damage by a Deadly source, are destroyed before the next sub-step begins.
examples: A Swift half-column destroys its 2/2 blocker in the Swift sub-step; the blocker never strikes back in the normal sub-step.

rules.text: Damage marked on units remains until the regroup phase, when it is removed.
examples: An attacker and its blocker each have 2 damage marked in the first battle of the turn. Both still have 2 damage marked when the second battle begins; it is removed in the regroup phase.

rules.text: Combat damage is dealt to a player in two ways: by an unblocked attacking half-column (rule 608.4a), and as Piercing excess from an attacking half-column, or from a blocking half-column with an attacker in front of it (see rule 802.16). Combat damage dealt to a player causes that player to lose that much life, unless an effect replaces that damage or changes the life lost.
examples: A Piercing attacker is not blocked; all of its damage is dealt to the defending player.
A blocking Piercing half-column with an attacker in front of it deals its excess to the attacking player.

rules.text: Combat damage to a player that an effect replaces (for example, Blightsea Polyp's rot) was still dealt. An ability that triggers when a column deals combat damage to a player still triggers, and reads the damage dealt, even if the player lost no life.
examples: A fully replaced combat hit still counts as dealt: Vroot's 'that much' pays out the damage its column dealt, not the life the player lost.

rules.text: Damage dealt by an ability that a source's combat damage causes, such as Resonant's extra damage, is not combat damage, even when it is dealt during or because of combat.
examples: Resonant's extra damage to a player is not combat damage, so Oorblak does not take it; the player does.

rules.text: If combat damage that would be dealt to a player is dealt to a unit instead (as Oorblak's ability does), the replacement applies to that damage once. Without Piercing, all of that damage is dealt to the unit. With Piercing, the damage beyond the unit's lethal damage is dealt to the player, and it is not redirected again.
examples: 10 Piercing combat damage that would be dealt to a player is redirected into a 2/4 Oorblak. 4 destroy it, and the other 6 are dealt to the player.
A non-Piercing overkill redirected into Oorblak is absorbed whole; nothing reaches the player.

rules.text: An ability that triggers on combat damage, or on something combat damage causes (such as a unit being destroyed), triggers when that event happens, during the combat damage step, and its trigger condition is checked then. It is put on the stack later, as rules 608.9b and 608.9c describe, and only then are its targets chosen.
examples: Lithoghul attacks and is blocked by a Geode. In the damage step the Geode deals 1 to Lithoghul, and Lithoghul's 'whenever I am dealt damage' ability triggers then; nothing goes on the stack or resolves until the after combat step.

rules.text: An ability that triggers 'when my column deals combat damage' triggers in each sub-step in which its own column deals combat damage, and only for damage its own column dealt; another column's damage does not trigger it. A 0-power unit with such an ability triggers if its column's combined power is greater than 0.
examples: A Swift and Sluggish column with Vroot strikes twice, and Vroot's ability triggers twice.
Vroot's 'that much' is its own column's damage, not the total dealt to the player by every column.

rules.text: In an unsplit step, every ability that triggered during the combat damage step is put on the stack in the after combat step, together with the abilities that trigger at the start of the after combat step, as one batch. The initiative player puts all of theirs on the stack first, in the order they choose, and then the other player puts theirs; each player may interleave the two kinds in any order. All players may respond to them.
examples: One player's combat-damage trigger and after-combat trigger are put in order together, in one choice.
The initiative player's triggers go on the stack first and sit at the bottom.

rules.text: In a split step, the abilities that triggered during a sub-step other than the last scheduled one are put on the stack, in the same order as in rule 608.9b, at the window after that sub-step, and resolve before the next sub-step deals damage (rule 608.3b). The abilities that trigger during the last sub-step in which damage is dealt join the after combat batch as in rule 608.9b.
examples: In a split step, a death trigger from the Swift sub-step resolves at the window before the normal sub-step, not after combat.
With Sluggish last, a death in the Sluggish sub-step joins the after combat batch.

rules.text: Abilities that trigger during the combat damage step trigger during battle, so an effect that makes abilities cost more to trigger during battle applies to them.
examples: Crevice Lurker taxes a combat-damage trigger; on the same board without the Lurker there is no tax.

rules.text: An ability that works only while its card is in the bin can trigger on combat damage only if the card is already in the bin when that damage is dealt. A unit destroyed by combat damage is not in the bin while that same damage is dealt, but a unit destroyed in an earlier sub-step is.
examples: Cinder Scuttler is destroyed in the same sub-step in which another of its controller's columns deals combat damage to the opponent. It does not return.
A Swift unit destroys Cinder Scuttler in the Swift sub-step; in the normal sub-step its controller deals combat damage to the opponent, and it returns.

rules.text: The after combat step is the last step of a battle round. It follows the combat damage step, in the region where that battle is fought, and it is the last priority window for interaction in that region before regroup.
A region in which no battle takes place has no after combat step. A battle round in which no attack is declared has no after combat step.
examples: Both players decline to attack. Neither region has a combat damage step or an after combat step, and the battle phase opens no priority window at all.

rules.text: In a game with two battle rounds, each round that has a battle has its own after combat step, in the region where that round is fought: the first round's in the non-initiative player's region, and the second round's in the initiative player's region.

The after combat step is a priority window. The initiative player receives priority first, then priority passes to the non-initiative player in the region. When all players pass priority in succession with the stack empty, the after combat step ends.
examples: After combat, the initiative player passes, the non-initiative player casts a spell, and both then pass. The spell resolves and the initiative player receives priority again. When both pass with the stack empty, the step ends.

rules.text: When the after combat step of the first battle round ends and units were sent to counterattack, the battle phase does not end: the second battle round begins (see rule 610).
examples: With counterattackers sent, passing in round 1's after-combat window does not end the battle.

rules.text: When the after combat step of the last battle round ends, the battle phase ends and regroup begins. The last battle round is the second round, or the first round if no units were sent to counterattack.
examples: When the last player passes in the final after-combat window, the game goes through regroup and into deployment; no one is given priority in between.

rules.text: An ability that triggers "after combat" triggers when the after combat step begins. It is put on the stack in the after combat step, and players may respond to it there.
examples: Smouldering Inferno, played as a unit, sacrifices itself after combat.

rules.text: An "after combat" ability of a unit triggers if that unit is present in the region where the battle is happening. The unit need not be in a formation.
examples: A unit with an after-combat ability that stands in the battle region outside the formation still triggers.

rules.text: An "after combat" ability does not trigger in a region where no battle took place. A unit in a region other than the one where the battle is fought does not trigger.
examples: A unit with an after-combat ability that stays in another region does not trigger.

rules.text: Abilities that triggered during the combat damage step and are still waiting are put on the stack in the after combat step together with the "after combat" abilities, as one batch. The initiative player puts all of theirs on the stack first, then the non-initiative player puts theirs, so the non-initiative player's resolve first. Each player chooses the order of their own and may interleave the two kinds.
examples: One player's combat-damage trigger and after-combat trigger are put in order together, in one choice.
The initiative player's triggers go on the stack first and sit at the bottom.

rules.text: When Swift or Sluggish splits the combat damage step, only the abilities that triggered in the last sub-step in which damage is dealt join the after combat batch. Those that triggered in an earlier sub-step have already resolved before the next sub-step (see rule 608.9c).
examples: With Swift in the battle, a unit that dies in the last (normal) sub-step has its death trigger in the after-combat batch.
With Sluggish last, a death in the Sluggish sub-step joins the after-combat batch.
In a split damage step a death trigger from an earlier sub-step resolves at the boundary, not after combat.

rules.text: A counterattack is the non-initiative team's attack in a battle phase with two battle rounds. The non-initiative team sends its counterattacking units out during the block step of the first battle round, and they attack in the second battle round.
Units are sent to counterattack only in the first battle round, at the same time as the non-initiative team declares its blocks. Sending counterattackers is optional.
Counterattacking units leave their region as soon as they are sent. From then until the first battle round ends they are in no region, and they are treated as if they do not exist.
A sent counterattacker's static abilities apply to nothing while it is away, not even to itself.
examples: Bubb carries Towering Colossus ("Enemies gain +2/+2"), so an enemy 1/1 attacking into Bubb's region is a 3/3. When Bubb is sent to counterattack, the attacker is a 1/1 again at once.
A sent Prickly Protector ("I gain +1/+1 for each other ally") does not give itself that bonus while it is away.

rules.text: A sent counterattacker cannot be targeted and cannot be sacrificed while it is away.
examples: The initiative player casts a spell that targets a unit in the round-1 battle region. A unit that was sent to counterattack is not offered as a target.

rules.text: A sent counterattacker does not count as a unit in the region it left. A unit that stays behind does not count a sent counterattacker as an ally.
examples: Prickly Protector, carrying a -1/-1 counter, is alive only because it has one other ally. When that ally is sent to counterattack, the Protector stays home, no longer counts it, and dies.

rules.text: Spell tokens sent with counterattackers are away with them, and cannot be cast until they return.
A sent counterattacker is not checked for death while it is away. It is checked as soon as it returns at the start of the second battle round.
examples: Prickly Protector with a -1/-1 counter, alive only through its own static, survives being declared as a counterattacker.
A Prickly Protector sent out alone survives the send, and dies on arrival in the enemy region, where it has no ally to count.

rules.text: Spell tokens may go with counterattacking units, under the same conditions as with an attack (see rule 604.2c). A counterattack made only of spell tokens is not allowed: spell tokens need at least one counterattacking unit to go with.
The second battle round begins only once the first battle round has completely finished, its after combat step included. In a two-player game it is fought in the initiative player's region.
When the second battle round begins, the sent counterattackers, and the spell tokens sent with them, reappear in the region they are attacking.
examples: The non-initiative player sent two units. When round 1's after combat step ends, both appear in the initiative player's region, ready to be put into formation.

rules.text: If the first battle round had a battle, only the units sent to counterattack can attack in the second battle round. In its attack step, the non-initiative team puts them into formation.
examples: The non-initiative player sent Conduit of Pain at block time. In round 2 it is the only unit they can attack with.

rules.text: If the first battle round had a battle and no units were sent to counterattack, there is no second battle round. The battle phase ends after the first round's after combat step.
examples: With no counterattack sent, no battle is fought in the initiative player's region.

rules.text: If the initiative team declared no attack in the first battle round, the non-initiative team may still attack in the second battle round. It may attack with any of its units, since it never had a block step in which to send counterattackers.
examples: The initiative player could attack and declines; the non-initiative player may then attack with any unit.

rules.text: The non-initiative team may decline to attack in the second battle round, even if it sent units to counterattack. Then the second round has no battle and opens no priority window, and the battle phase ends.
examples: One unit was sent to counterattack. In round 2 both attacking with it and declining are legal.
The initiative player's spell tokens at home cannot be cast in any round-1 window. If the non-initiative player then declines to attack in round 2, those tokens never become castable this battle.

rules.text: In the second battle round the initiative team declares blocks only. It cannot send units to counterattack, because each team gets only one chance to attack.
In every priority window of the second battle round, the initiative player receives priority first, although it is now the defending player.

While the second battle round is resolved, units in the region where the first round was fought are treated as if they do not exist. They include the units the initiative team attacked with and any unit created there during the first round, so none of them can block in the second round.
examples: Tidelurker's 2/2, created mid-attack in the enemy region, stays there and cannot block the counterattack.
A spell token the initiative player keeps at home cannot be cast in any round-1 window, and can be cast in round 2's windows.

rules.text: A battle phase has at most two battle rounds. After the second round's after combat step, battle ends and regroup begins.
examples: In round 2 the initiative player cannot send units out to counterattack, and the battle phase ends after round 2.

rules.text: In team games, combat is first resolved completely in every region the initiative team attacked. Then combat is resolved in the regions the non-initiative team counterattacked.
examples: In a 2v2 game the initiative team attacks both non-initiative regions. Both of those battles are resolved, one region at a time, before any counterattack battle in an initiative region begins.

rules.text: An effect is anything on the stack. Whenever a card is played, or an ability is activated or triggered, it is added to the stack as an effect. A unit or spell unit on the stack is an effect too.
examples: a {Battle} unit being played sits on the stack and can be chosen by an effect that says "target effect" (Dematerialize).

rules.text: A spell effect is an effect that is a spell: a spell, a spell unit or a spell token on the stack, or an ambush. A unit on the stack is an effect but not a spell effect, so a card that says "spell effect" cannot affect it.
examples: Null Drone ("target spell effect") cannot choose a plain unit on the stack, but can choose a spell unit.

rules.text: A nonspell effect is any effect that is not a spell effect: a triggered ability, an activated ability, a Virus being applied, or a unit on the stack.
examples: Nothyr ("negate up to one target nonspell effect") can choose a {Battle} unit on the stack.

rules.text: Casting a spell is playing it. The printed rules use "cast" and "play" for the same act, and casting a spell token is playing a spell.
Players interact by playing cards and activating abilities in response to one another. All interaction uses the stack (rule 703).
Only units and spells are played, whatever zone they are played from. Applying a modification is not playing a card (701.2).
examples: Godray and Monke played from hand, and Trench Stalker played from the bin, are plays; a Virus applied to the attacker is not.

rules.text: Playing a spell unit is playing a spell.
examples: a spell unit played through Hooba-Pon counts as a spell played.

rules.text: Casting a spell token is playing a spell. A spell token is never in a hand; it is cast from play, so it is played from somewhere other than the hand.
examples: casting a Fireball token triggers Stalwart Sentinel ("when you play a card from anywhere other than your hand").

rules.text: A token is not a card. An ability or cost modifier that refers to a "card" being played does not apply to a spell token being cast; one that refers to a "spell" does; one that refers to a "nontoken spell" does not.
examples: Arbiter of Armistice ("Cards played during battle gain [Pay 2 life]") does not make a spell token cost life.

rules.text: Creating a token is not playing it.

An ability that triggers whenever its controller plays a unit works only while its card is in play. A card that is being played is on the stack, not in play, so its own play does not trigger it, whether or not the ability says "another".

Applying a modification (an augment, a graft, or a Virus) is not playing a card. A modification is applied, whether it comes from a hand, a bin, a cache or elsewhere. Applying a modification is a special action.
An ability that triggers when a player plays a unit, a spell or a card does not trigger when a modification is applied, including one applied from the bin.
examples: Ravenous Fireslinger does not trigger when its controller applies an augment, and does trigger on a real spell.
Applying a Virus during battle is not playing a card, so Void Mandible does not react to it.

rules.text: A modifier to the cost of playing cards does not change the cost of applying a modification. A modification still needs its own affinity and its own mana cost to be applied.

Tides of the Cosmos is the one exception. Although it says "play", it may put a Virus card onto a unit as a Virus, and it may play a card as an Ambush or a Prophecy. It cannot graft a card or apply a non-Virus augment.
examples: a Virus card that Tides of the Cosmos plays as a Virus is attached to a unit and never enters play.

rules.text: Putting a card into play is not playing it. Whether an effect plays a card or puts it into play is decided by the verb the effect prints.
examples: Covenant of the Damned puts a unit from the bin into play; only Covenant itself was played.

rules.text: A spell unit that enters play without being played (for example, one put into play from a bin) does not produce its spell effect.
examples: Covenant of the Damned puts Lonely Forager into play from the bin; Forager does not draw a card.

rules.text: A card played during the resolution of another effect is played. During battle it is put on the stack and can be responded to (rule 703.5), and abilities that trigger on a play see it.
examples: Tides of the Cosmos plays a unit, and Bloomcaster's "Whenever you play a unit" triggers on it.

rules.text: A card played by an effect is played from the zone it came out of. If it came out of a hand, it is played from the hand. If it came out of the cache, a bin, the deck or anywhere else, it is not played from the hand.
examples: Tides of the Cosmos plays a card off the top of the deck, so Proph and Stalwart Sentinel see a play from somewhere other than the hand.
Hooba-Pon plays a unit from its controller's hand, so neither Proph nor Stalwart Sentinel triggers.

rules.text: A copy of a spell is not played. It does not trigger abilities that trigger on playing, and it is not counted as a played spell.
examples: Earthbound Replicator does not copy its own copy.

rules.text: To play a card, a player must meet its affinity requirement, pay its mana cost, select its targets as it is played, and resolve whatever is inside its brackets (an additional cost to pay or a mode to choose).
examples: Arc Lightning (rr, cost 4) cannot be played with four water resources (no affinity) or with only two fire resources (not enough mana); with two fire and two water it can.

rules.text: A player must meet a card's affinity requirement to be able to play it, unless an effect lets it be played ignoring affinity.
examples: Tides of the Cosmos plays a fire unit for a player who has only water resources.

rules.text: To pay a card's mana cost, the player expends a number of unexpended resources equal to that cost.
examples: playing Arc Lightning, cost 4, expends four of the player’s unexpended resources.

rules.text: A card can be played only when its timing allows (rule 207). A card with no timing icon can be played only during deployment.
examples: Lonely Forager has no timing icon: it can be played in deployment but not in battle.

rules.text: A card in the cache under a live permission may be played in every way it could be played from the hand. It is still not in the hand.
examples: a glimpsed Virus in the cache can be applied onto an enemy unit in battle.

rules.text: A card played from the cache or a bin under a permission still obeys its own printed timing; the permission itself never waives timing. Apart from the timing grants that also work from the cache (rule 702.2d), only an effect that says the card may be played now, such as Tides of the Cosmos, lets it ignore its timing.
examples: Tides of the Cosmos plays a deploy-timing unit in battle.

rules.text: A card that says it can't be played from your hand is restricted from that zone only. It may still be played from another zone that allows it.
Permission to play a card "as if it had [Haste]" does not let a {Battle} card be played outside battle.
examples: Dispatch Courier cannot let a {Battle} spell unit be played in the haste step.

rules.text: The rules that widen a card's timing when it is played from hand also widen it when it is played from the cache: a haste grant such as Dispatch Courier's, the erase-funded haste play of Writhing Host, Ambush, and the battle {Virus} augment window.
examples: a glimpsed {Virus} card in the cache can be augmented onto a unit in a battle window, as it could from hand.

rules.text: Playing a card follows the steps below, in order. Everything the play needs is declared and paid before the card is put on the stack, so no player can respond to an undeclared or unpaid play.
examples: while Sacrificial Burst’s target and sacrifice are being chosen, nothing is on the stack and the opponent has no action; it reaches the stack only once both are done.

rules.text: Step 1: if the card has an X, the player chooses X. A variable additional cost (one whose amount is X) is paid at this step, and the amount paid is X. The card's mana cost is paid at the start of the play.
Step 2: the player chooses any {Modular} modifications for the card.
examples: Spellbind asks for its {Modular} mods as it is played; the chosen mod goes on the stack with it.

rules.text: Step 3: the player declares every target the card's text names (rule 110).
Step 4: if a bracket in the card's text offers a choice of modes, the owner of the effect chooses one.
examples: Wither and Bloom declares which half it is before anyone may respond.

rules.text: Step 5: a card that may be played into a formation has its place in the formation chosen.
examples: Tiderunner Initiate’s place in the formation is chosen as it is played, before it is on the stack.

rules.text: Step 6: the player pays the card's fixed additional costs, after everything else has been declared.
examples: Sacrificial Burst asks for its target before its sacrifice; Trench Stalker asks for its formation spot before its two discards.

rules.text: Step 7: options that a card offers "as you play" a spell (Maelstrom Charger) are taken. Such an option is not an effect: it never goes on the stack and cannot be responded to.
examples: the Maelstrom Charger option is asked while the spell is played and never reaches the stack.

rules.text: Step 8: the card is put on the stack as an effect (rule 703).
examples: once Arc Lightning has been declared and paid, it is on the stack as a spell effect controlled by its player, and no longer in hand.

rules.text: Every cost of playing a card is paid before the card is put on the stack. No player can respond to the payment, or between a cost and the effect it pays for.
A card whose costs cannot all be paid cannot be played.
examples: with nothing to sacrifice, Tides of the Cosmos does not offer Volatile Toxicity.

rules.text: Negating a card does not refund the costs paid to play it.
A unit sacrificed to pay a cost is gone before the card is played, so it does not see that card being played.
examples: Ravenous Fireslinger sacrificed to pay for Sacrificial Burst does not trigger on it.
