rules.text: A cost cannot be paid with something that does not exist yet: not with units the effect itself would create, and not with a unit played by the same effect, which is on the stack and not in play.
examples: Volatile Toxicity played by Tides of the Cosmos cannot sacrifice a Towering Colossus played by the same Tides.

rules.text: A card played during another effect's resolution pays its bracketed additional cost exactly as if it were played from a hand.
examples: a Trench Stalker played through Hooba-Pon discards two cards.

rules.text: A printed square bracket in a card's text is either an additional cost or a choice of modes. The owner of the effect pays that cost or chooses that mode, when the effect is played or put on the stack, and at no other time.

A payment an effect's text asks for without brackets, such as "unless its controller pays [x]", is not a cost of playing. It is made while the effect resolves, by the player the text names (rule 704.1).
X is chosen when the card is played, before it is put on the stack. Only values the player can pay may be chosen, and responses see the X already fixed.
If a card says X can't be zero, X must be at least 1. A player with less open mana than the smallest legal X cannot play the card.
A variable additional cost sets X. The player pays it one unit at a time until they stop, and the amount paid is X.
examples: a player removes two +1/+1 counters for Discharge, one at a time, then stops; X is 2 and Discharge deals 2 damage.

rules.text: An X spell released for free by a fulfilled prophecy is cast with X = 0. A variable bracketed cost on it is still collected.
examples: a fulfilled prophecy releases an X spell; no X is asked, X is 0 and no mana is paid.

rules.text: A spell token is cast from play, and only in the region the token is in. Otherwise it is cast the same way as a spell from the hand.
examples: In the attack window the defending player casts their Fireball 3 token in the battle region. They choose its target, the attacking player, and it goes on the stack, where the attacker may respond; when both pass it deals 3.

rules.text: A modifier to the cost of playing spells applies to casting a spell token, and a spell token cast counts as a spell played.
examples: Tranquility makes a spell token cost [1] more in battle.

rules.text: A spell token with Burst is cast together with all of its controller's spell tokens of the same name in the same region as it. They are still separate spells.
examples: A player with two Fireballs in the battle region casts one; both go on the stack. A Fireball the same player has in another region is not cast.

rules.text: A card or ability that needs targets can be played only if every target it requires can be chosen at the same time, each one legal and different from the others.
examples: Fight cannot be played unless the region holds an ally and another unit.
Tidal Reversion cannot be played while one player has no unit to recall.

rules.text: A card that targets nothing has no target requirement.
examples: Rebalance can be played by a player with no unit.

rules.text: A triggered graft composite whose targeted part has no legal target is not put on the stack at all, and its untargeted parts do not happen either.
examples: Megadeath grafted with Resurrect, and no unit of cost 2 or less in the bin: no Poison 5 is made.

rules.text: The stack is "first in, last out". A new effect is put on top of the effects already there. When it is time to resolve, the top effect resolves first, so the effect put on last resolves first.
examples: Mycelial Mentor is played with Bloomcaster out. Bloomcaster's trigger goes on the stack above the Mentor, so its 1/1 is made before the Mentor arrives and the Mentor never sees it.

rules.text: An effect put on the stack does not resolve immediately. This gives the other players in the region a chance to respond to it.
examples: Luminous Arc is cast at a unit; the unit is undamaged while the Arc waits on the stack, and the other player may respond.

rules.text: New effects can be added on top of the stack after it has started resolving, between the resolutions of the effects on it.
examples: two Luminous Arcs are on the stack; after the top one resolves, a third Arc is cast and resolves before the one still waiting.

rules.text: A triggered ability put on the stack can be responded to like any other effect.
examples: Xenopod Progenitor's trigger is negated on the stack, and its controller is never asked to pay its [1].

rules.text: Priority is the ability to take game actions such as playing cards or activating abilities. A player with priority can take such actions; a player without priority cannot.
examples: In the attack window only the initiative player, who holds priority, may play a card; the other player cannot until they receive priority.

rules.text: A player who uses priority to take an action may keep priority and take further actions. Each action goes on the stack as an effect; none of them happens immediately.
When a player passes priority after taking one or more actions, each other player receives priority, so that they can respond. This continues until all players pass priority in succession.
examples: after a cast the other player receives priority and responds; the first player then receives priority again, and the top item resolves only after both pass in succession.

rules.text: A player cannot respond to another player passing priority. A player who passes may not get another chance to act.
examples: the defender passes on an Arc and the attacker passes; the Arc resolves at once, with no further chance for the defender.

rules.text: All players on a team share priority and can act in whichever order they choose among themselves. Teams pass and receive priority as one.
A priority window is a sequence in which the players (or teams) each receive priority in order.
examples: in an empty attack window the initiative player receives priority, then the other player; when both have passed the step ends.

rules.text: In a priority window the initiative player receives priority first. If they decline to act, priority passes clockwise to the next non-initiative player in the region. If the initiative player is not in the region, priority begins with the player nearest to the initiative player, clockwise.
examples: the defender casts a spell, which resolves; the new window opens with the initiative player, not the caster.

rules.text: In each region, the attack step, the block step and the after combat step each have a priority window. The combat damage step has a priority window only between its sub-steps, and only when Swift or Sluggish units split it (rule 608).

When all players pass priority in succession with an effect on the stack, the top effect resolves. All players then receive priority in order again, which is a new priority window. When all players pass priority with the stack empty, the game moves to the next step.
examples: two passes resolve Luminous Arc; a new window opens in the same step with the initiative player; two passes on the empty stack end the step.

rules.text: When several effects are put on the stack at the same time, each player chooses the order of their own. The initiative player puts all of theirs on first, then the non-initiative player, so the non-initiative player's effects resolve first.
examples: with one trigger per player, the initiative player's trigger is at the bottom of the stack.

rules.text: Cards played by one effect at the same time are separate effects, put on the stack at the same time in an order their controller chooses.

A Burst group of spell tokens goes on the stack all at once. Its caster chooses the order, one token at a time, and aims each; the token chosen first resolves first. The other players receive priority only when the whole group is on the stack.
examples: the first Fireball picked ends on top of the stack.

rules.text: A card played during another effect's resolution waits on the stack until that resolution has finished. Only then do players receive priority, and they may respond to the played card before it resolves.
examples: a card Tides of the Cosmos plays for free can be answered on the stack.

rules.text: Once an effect has begun to resolve, no player can respond to it. It can no longer be targeted, negated or augmented.
examples: while Premonition is resolving, the other player is offered nothing, it is not a legal target, and a negation or a Virus aimed at it is refused.

rules.text: Deployment uses the stack, but each player has a stack of their own there. Only that player sees it and holds priority over it; no other player can respond to it or is made to wait on it.
examples: In deployment a player plays a deploy-timing spell at their Earthbound Replicator; the spell goes on that player's own stack, so the Replicator can copy it.

rules.text: There is no priority in the haste step. Haste cards are played there as special actions.
examples: Molten Upheaval played in the haste step makes its Fireball at once; no one has priority and nothing waits on a stack.

rules.text: When an effect resolves, its instructions are carried out in the order printed, and a later instruction sees the results of an earlier one. The exception is target legality: it is judged once, as the effect begins to resolve (rule 704.5), so an earlier instruction cannot make a later instruction's target illegal.
examples: Finality ("Negate all other effects. Erase all cards in bins.") erases the cards it has just negated, because they are in bins by its second sentence.

rules.text: Choices an effect makes that are not targets (how to divide damage among a player's units, which card to discard, whether to pay an optional amount inside the effect) are made while it resolves.
examples: Xenopod Progenitor's trigger goes on the stack with no payment asked; its [1] is asked as it resolves.

rules.text: No priority window opens around a payment or choice made while an effect resolves.
examples: while Premonition asks its controller which card to cache, the other player has no action; the choice made, Premonition finishes without any pass.

rules.text: When a spell resolves it goes to its controller's bin. When a spell unit resolves it enters play as a unit instead.
examples: a resolved Luminous Arc is in its controller’s bin; a resolved Jelly is in play as a unit.

rules.text: A card that goes to a bin from the stack is not trashed.
examples: two Luminous Arcs reach the bin from the stack, one resolved and one fizzled; neither is trashed.

rules.text: A spell token never goes to a bin; it is erased.
A spell that is Unstable, or that carries a Virus applied to it on the stack, is erased instead of going to a bin, whether it resolves, fizzles or is negated.
examples: a spell played from the bin under Abyssal Evocation is Unstable, so it is erased and not put back in the bin.
a spell played from the bin under Abyssal Evocation that fizzles is erased too.

rules.text: A copy of a spell has no card. When it resolves or leaves the stack, nothing goes to a bin.
examples: a resolved copy of Suspend bins nothing, and its "Erase me." erases nothing.

rules.text: A spell unit's spell effect happens first; if it resolves, the unit then enters play. If the spell unit is prevented from resolving (negated, or with its targets made invalid), the unit does not enter play and the card goes to the bin.
examples: a spell unit played through Hooba-Pon has its spell part happen, then spawns into the formation.

rules.text: A negated effect is removed from the stack at once, when the effect that negates it resolves. It does not resolve.
examples: one mass negate removes all its victims from the stack together, with no extra priority rounds.

rules.text: A negated spell, spell unit, unit, ambush or Virus goes to its controller's bin, and a negated Virus cannot be used as a Virus again. A negated spell token is erased. A negated triggered or activated ability just leaves the stack, because it has no card of its own.
A negated unit or spell unit never enters play.

As an effect begins to resolve, each target it declared is checked again by the rule it was chosen under: its kind, its printed restriction, its region, and being different from the other targets. A target that fails the check is lost, exactly like a target that has left play.
examples: an Ambush whose ally was stolen in response recalls nothing.

rules.text: The check is made once, as the effect begins to resolve. An earlier part of the effect cannot make a later part's target illegal in the middle of its resolution.

A target remains the same object while it stays where it is. A target that changes zone (to a hand, a bin, and so on) is gone, and the effect does not follow it to a new object. A target that stays put is still a legal target even if another effect also targets it.
examples: Organic Exchange may target two of its controller's own units, and another spell aimed at one of them still resolves.

rules.text: Several effects may target the same unit, even if together they would do more than destroying it takes. If an earlier one removes it, the later ones lose that target.
Changing an effect's targets before it resolves can save it from fizzling.
An effect fizzles if, as it resolves, it has lost all of its targets. A fizzled effect does nothing, and a fizzled spell goes to the bin.
examples: Arc Lightning’s only target dies before it resolves; Arc Lightning fizzles, deals no damage and goes to the bin.

rules.text: When an effect fizzles, none of it happens, including parts of it that had no target.
examples: Spewing Mushroom carries the grafts Biotoxicity ("create three Poison 1") and Technological Superiority, which targets the Mushroom itself. The Mushroom attacks, and the opponent deletes it with Leaping Lillik before its trigger resolves. Its only target is gone, so the whole trigger fizzles: not even Biotoxicity's Poisons are made.

rules.text: If an effect has lost some but not all of its targets, it resolves as best it can against those that remain, untargeted parts included.
examples: Tidal Reversion still recalls the other unit when one of its targets is removed.
Twin Flame loses one of its two targets before it resolves; the remaining target still takes its 2 damage.

Spewing Mushroom carries Biotoxicity and two Technological Superiority grafts; when it attacks, the two targeted parts aim at the Mushroom and at an enemy 1/1. The 1/1 dies before the trigger resolves. One target remains, so it still resolves: all four Poison tokens are made.

rules.text: An effect that needs two of its targets together (a fight or an exchange) does nothing if it loses one of them. It does not fizzle.
examples: Fight that loses one of its two targets does nothing to the survivor.
Organic Exchange that loses one of its two targets exchanges nothing; the survivor stays with its controller.

rules.text: An effect that has no targeting part anywhere cannot fizzle. Nor can a part whose target was optional ("up to") and was left empty: declaring no target was a legal choice, and the rest of the effect still happens.
An ambush is a targeted effect. If its target is removed, the ambush fizzles and the ambushing unit is put into the bin.
examples: the ally targeted by Lurking Slimebeast’s ambush dies; the ambush fizzles and Slimebeast goes to the bin.

rules.text: A Virus whose target has become invalid when it resolves is put into the bin, and cannot be used as a Virus again.
examples: a Virus’s host dies before the Virus resolves; the Virus goes to the bin and is not offered as a Virus from there.

rules.text: An effect with a required target that never had a legal candidate fizzles, although it declared no target.
An effect stays on the stack, and still resolves, if its source leaves play.
Where such an effect reads its source (its attributes, power, defense, or the formation it stood in), it uses the source's last-known state: what the source was at the moment it left play.
examples: Bellowing Boulder dies with its ping on the stack; the ping is still Deadly, from its last state.

rules.text: An effect that acts on its source itself, or that says "if I am still in formation", does nothing if the source is gone.
examples: Hooba-Nan dies with its attack trigger on the stack; the trigger creates no 1/1s.

rules.text: An activated ability is written with a colon (":"). Everything before the colon is the cost of activating the ability; everything after it is the effect the ability has.
examples: Glook's "[once] Discard X cards: Glimpse 1, X times" — discarding X cards is the cost, and glimpsing X times is the effect.

rules.text: An activated ability may print a timing icon of its own. An ability marked {Battle} can be activated only during battle, and one marked {Deployment} only during deployment. The icon is checked when the ability is activated.
examples: Grox's ability is marked {Battle}, so it cannot be activated during deployment.
Cadaverous Cultivator's {Battle} ability is refused when activated outside battle, rather than doing nothing when it resolves.

rules.text: To activate an ability, the player takes the steps below, in order. Everything is chosen and paid before the ability is put on the stack, so no player can respond between the payment of its cost and the ability going on the stack.

Step 1: the game checks that the ability can be activated: its timing allows it, any printed condition on it ("Activate this ability only if …") is met, every part of its cost can be paid, and every target it requires has a legal choice. If any check fails, the ability cannot be activated and nothing is paid.
examples: Instrument of Reassignment costs [x] and "sacrifice another nontoken unit". With only a token beside it, it cannot be activated, and the 3 open mana are not spent either.

rules.text: Step 2: if the cost has a variable part (a printed [x], "Discard X cards", "Sacrifice X units"), the player pays it, one at a time, until they stop. The amount paid is X.
examples: Celestial Shifter's "[x]" is paid while activating, so the opponent sees X before deciding whether to respond.

rules.text: Step 3: the player declares the ability's targets.
examples: Slag Spewer's target is declared before its mod is erased to pay the cost.

rules.text: Step 4: the player pays the rest of the cost: its mana, including any tax on activating abilities (rule 111.10f), and any life, debt, sacrifice or other fixed part.
examples: Auric Ascendant's "Recall another ally" is paid before the ability is on the stack, so the opponent already knows which ally left.

rules.text: Step 5: the ability is put on the stack as an effect, and players receive priority as rule 703 describes.
examples: Infernal Cultivator's sacrificed units are gone while the ability waits on the stack, so negating it refunds nothing.

rules.text: If a part of an ability's cost names something that is not there to pay with (no other ally to recall, no mod to erase), the ability cannot be activated. Nothing is paid, and a [once] on the ability is not used.
examples: Auric Ascendant with no other ally cannot be activated, so its [one] is not paid and its [once] is kept.

rules.text: An activated ability that a mod gives its host is an ability of the host. The host's controller activates it, and "I" and "me" in it mean the host.
examples: Living Forge augmented onto another unit lets that unit's controller activate "[three]: create a Robot 2" through the mod.
Aurozoa's "[Augment] Pay 1 life: Recall me" recalls the host when Aurozoa is a mod.

rules.text: Some actions are not activated abilities, and rules and effects that apply to activating abilities do not apply to them: applying a mod (an augment or a graft), playing a card as an Ambush, casting a spell token, using a resource, and taking an option a card offers as a spell is played (rule 109.6).
examples: during battle Crevice Lurker taxes activated abilities, but applying an augment costs nothing extra.

rules.text: A triggered ability is an ability that happens when something else takes place. "When" and "Whenever" mark a triggered ability. A triggered ability can also happen at a stated time, such as "After combat" or "At the end of turn".
examples: Embermaw Fledgling's "after combat" ability creates an X/X unit after combat.

rules.text: A triggered ability triggers at the moment its event happens, and whether it triggers is decided then (rule 109.3a). It is put on the stack afterwards, at one of the times this section gives, and its targets are chosen and its costs paid only as it is put on the stack.
examples: a "whenever I am dealt damage" ability triggers inside the combat damage step, but is put on the stack, and has its target chosen, after the step.
the {Alluring} trigger chooses its target as it goes on the stack, and can then be negated.

rules.text: Triggered abilities that have triggered are put on the stack at the times below, depending on when they triggered.
examples: Eminence of the Barrens damaged by a spell in battle has its trigger on the stack as soon as the spell has resolved, while Lithoghul damaged in combat triggers inside the damage step and is put on the stack only in the after combat step.

rules.text: During battle, outside the combat damage step: as soon as the action or resolution that made them trigger is complete, on top of anything already on the stack. Players then receive priority and may respond to them.
examples: Eminence of the Barrens dealt damage by a spell in battle puts its trigger on the stack, and the opponent may respond to it.

rules.text: During the combat damage step: they wait. They are put on the stack in the after combat step, or at a window between damage sub-steps, as rules 608.9b and 608.9c describe.
examples: a "when I die" ability of a unit killed by combat damage waits with the others and goes on the stack after combat.

rules.text: During deployment: on the deployment stack of the player who controls them (rule 703.7). All the abilities that trigger at the same moment are put on that stack before any of them resolves.
In the end-of-turn step: they resolve as special actions. No player can play cards in response to them (rule 508.1a).
examples: while an end-of-turn trigger is asking its controller a question, neither player may play a card.

rules.text: An ability that triggers on a card being played, or on something being targeted, is put on the stack above the effect that made it trigger, so it resolves first. It still resolves if that effect is negated afterwards.
examples: Mycelial Mentor is played while Bloomcaster is in play. Bloomcaster's 1/1 is created before the Mentor arrives, so the Mentor does not see that token being created.
a spell unit that is negated after Bloomcaster triggered still leaves Bloomcaster's 1/1 behind.

rules.text: Triggered abilities that are put on the stack at the same time are put there in the order of rule 703.4: each player orders their own, the initiative player puts all of theirs on first, and the non-initiative player's resolve first. A player may order their own abilities in any way, whatever made each of them trigger.
examples: a player with a "when I die" ability triggered by combat damage and an "after combat" ability orders the two in one choice.

rules.text: A triggered ability triggers once each time its event happens. If one action makes the event happen several times, the ability triggers that many times.
examples: an enemy spell that targets two allies triggers Earnest Defender twice, and two 1/1s are created.

rules.text: Several cards that enter a hand together in one move are one event. An ability that triggers when a card, or one or more cards, enters a hand triggers once for that move.
examples: Rider of the Tides is attacking. Its controller plays Tilling the Graves, returning Curio Drifter and Bumblecrab from the bin to hand in one move. That is one entry into the hand, so the Rider triggers once and gets +2/+2, not +4/+4.

rules.text: Each mod that Reconfigure moves onto a new host is applied to that host separately. An ability that triggers whenever a mod is applied triggers once for each of them.
examples: Reconfiguring a unit carrying three mods onto Perpetual Construct triggers it three times.

rules.text: A triggered ability triggers only on events in the region its card is in. An event in another region does not trigger it, even when the event involves its controller.
examples: Refuse Reclaimer does not grow when a unit dies in a region it is not in.

rules.text: An "after combat" ability triggers only in a region where a battle took place.
examples: A unit with an "after combat" ability in a region where no battle happened does not trigger.
a unit with an "after combat" ability that stands in the battle region but in no formation still triggers.

rules.text: An ability of a unit that triggers on its own death ("When I die") triggers when the unit dies, although the unit has then left play. The ability is put on the stack in the region where the unit died.
examples: A "when I die" ability of a unit that died in the battle region can target things in the battle region, not in its controller's home region.

rules.text: An ability that triggers when its unit despawns ("When I despawn"), including one a mod gives its host, triggers whichever way the unit leaves play: when it dies, when it is recalled, and when it is cached.
examples: a host carrying Growing Plague that is recalled to its hand triggers Growing Plague's despawn ability.
the same host cached triggers it too.

rules.text: Moving a unit and its mods onto another unit (Reconfigure) is not a despawn: the unit does not change zones, so its "When I despawn" abilities do not trigger.
examples: Bubb wearing Growing Plague is Reconfigured onto a Robot; Growing Plague does not trigger.

rules.text: Units that die together hear each other. A unit destroyed in the same batch of deaths as other units still triggers on their deaths, and on their cards being trashed, as it would have had it survived.
examples: Muck Rummager killed by combat damage alongside two allies still draws for its controller trashing those allies.

rules.text: An ability that triggers when a spell is played targeting something reads the targets the spell declared as it was played. A target changed onto that thing later does not make the ability trigger, and a target changed away from it later does not undo the trigger.
examples: a spell played at another unit and then retargeted onto Earthbound Replicator makes no copy.
a spell played at Earthbound Replicator and then retargeted away still makes its copy.

rules.text: An "If you do" clause in a triggered ability is part of that ability, not a separate triggered ability. It resolves as part of the ability, and it is not put on the stack or taxed separately.
examples: Eminence of the Barrens attacks under an enemy Crevice Lurker and is damaged by a spell. Its controller is asked the Crevice Lurker tax once for the trigger, and the [one] to fight is asked while that same trigger resolves, and is never taxed itself: each trigger costs 2 in all, the tax plus the fight.

rules.text: {Alluring} and {Resonant} work as triggered abilities of the unit or source that has them. What they do is put on the stack, so it can be responded to and negated, and an effect that taxes triggered abilities applies to it.
examples: Crevice Lurker taxes the {Alluring} trigger, and declining the tax stops the lure.
Containment Protocol negates an {Alluring} trigger waiting on the stack.
a {Resonant} source's extra damage waits on the stack after combat as that source's ability, and can be negated.

rules.text: Some triggered abilities choose a unit without targeting it, such as a Wraith's start-of-deployment ability choosing "an ally". The unit is chosen as the ability is put on the stack. Several such abilities may choose the same unit, even if together they would do more than destroying it takes; if the chosen unit has left play when one resolves, that one fizzles.
examples: three Wraith abilities all choose one 1/1 ally. The first kills it, and the other two fizzle.
a Wraith with no other ally is its own only ally. Its ability chooses it without asking, resolves on it (it shrinks to 2/2), and nothing fizzles.

rules.text: Choosing a unit this way is not targeting it. It does not trigger "when I become targeted" abilities, and it cannot be redirected.
examples: a Wraith ability choosing Mohruung does not give its controller a Crystal.

rules.text: An ability that triggers on a card being played, and then acts on what was played ("negate that effect"), acts on the item that play put on the stack. Another item with the same name and the same controller is not it, whether it is older or newer. A copy of the played spell is not it either, because a copy is not played (see rule 701.5).
examples: Two Burgeons by the same player are on the stack, and only the second one's play makes Void Mandible trigger. The Mandible negates the second Burgeon, not the first.
A copy of Burgeon sits below a newly played Burgeon. Void Mandible negates the played Burgeon and leaves the copy alone.
Origon negates the spell whose play made it trigger, even with an identical spell above it on the stack.

rules.text: A static ability states a change that its card continuously makes to the game for as long as the card is in play.
examples: Prickly Protector's "+1/+1 for each other ally" is counted again whenever its stats are read.

rules.text: A static ability does not use the stack. It cannot be responded to or negated, and an effect that changes what abilities cost to activate or trigger does not apply to it.
examples: Crevice Lurker does not tax Tranquility's "spells cost [one] more"; Tranquility still adds exactly one.
Aetherflux Golem's "I gain +2/+2" never goes on the stack, so Containment Protocol cannot negate it.

rules.text: Only triggered abilities and activated abilities put anything on the stack. A triggered ability says "When" or "Whenever" or names a time such as "After combat"; {Alluring} and {Resonant} also work as triggered abilities; an activated ability is written with a colon. A sentence that states a standing fact ("I gain +2/+2", "Spells cost [one] more to play during battle") is a static ability, and a sentence that says "instead", "as" or "if" and names no target is a replacement effect. Neither goes on the stack, except that a replacement whose substitute names a target puts that substitute on the stack.
A static ability applies continuously to everything it describes, including units that enter play after it began to apply. When its source leaves play, the change ends.
examples: a unit that enters play while Transmogrifant is in play has no attributes, and gets them back when Transmogrifant leaves.

rules.text: A unit that enters play while a static ability applies to it enters with the change already made. An ability that triggers on the unit entering play sees the unit as changed.
examples: under Sandstone Defender a 1/1 enters as a 1/3, so Nectar Ridge Oracle ("an ally spawns with greater defense than power") draws.
under Infernal Wispweaver a 0/1 Wisp enters as a 2/2, so Nectar Ridge Oracle does not draw.
Animated Spark's +X/+0 applies to a unit that spawns mid-battle from the moment it spawns.

rules.text: A static ability that changes stats ("I gain +2/+2") puts no counters on the unit. Effects that count, move, double or remove counters do not see the change, and it ends as soon as its source stops applying it.

A card's statement that it enters play with counters ("I spawn with two +1/+1 counters") is not a triggered ability. The unit enters play already holding those counters; nothing goes on the stack, and an ability that triggers on the unit entering play sees it with them.
examples: Aethercap Siphoner (printed 4/4, "I spawn with three -1/-1 counters on me") is seen as a 1/1 by an ability that triggers when it spawns.
neither Powerforge Synergist's nor Aethercap Siphoner's counters can be responded to.

rules.text: Replacement effects that change how many counters are put on a unit apply to those counters. But no player puts them on the unit, so abilities that trigger when a player puts counters on a unit do not trigger.
examples: under an allied Flux Resonator a Robot 2 enters as a 3/3.
Aethercap Siphoner's own -1/-1 counters do not count as its controller putting counters on an ally.

rules.text: A static ability applies only in the region its source is in.
examples: Rotspore Herald ("Everything is {deadly}") in its home region does not make a spell resolving in the battle region deadly.

rules.text: A static ability applies to everything its text names, with no limit its text does not state. "Everything" means every unit, spell and spell token in its region, on both sides.
examples: with Rotspore Herald in the region, a spell that deals 1 damage destroys a 7/5.
a Fireball 1 spell token in Rotspore Herald's region is {Deadly} too.

rules.text: A static ability that names "spells" applies to spell tokens too, because spell tokens are spells.
examples: Emberflame Enlightener says "Your units and spells gain {Powerful}". Its controller's Fireball token is a spell, so it has {Powerful} too.

rules.text: A static ability that applies to effects with a number of targets ("spell effects with a single target") counts the targets the effect declared as it was played, including targets that have since become illegal.
examples: Twin Flame played at two units is not "a single target" for Envoy of Lightning, even after one of them is removed.

rules.text: A static ability or replacement effect that a mod gives its host works from the host. "I" and "me" mean the host, "you" and "your" mean the host's controller, and it applies in the host's region.
examples: Transmogrifant as a mod gives "your other units +2/+2" from its host.
Crevice Lurker as a mod taxes abilities in its host's region.

rules.text: A permission a card grants ("You may play one unit with no abilities from your bin each deployment") is a standing fact, not an ability that goes on the stack. Using it cannot be responded to, and an effect that negates activated or triggered abilities cannot stop it. (engine differs, see F-U15-1)
examples: Containment Protocol cannot stop a player using The Bonesculptor's permission, because there is nothing on the stack to negate.

rules.text: A replacement effect is an ability that changes an event as it happens, written "If … instead". It replaces the event, rather than triggering in response to it.
examples: Flux Resonator ("if one or more counters would be put on a unit by an allied source, put that many counters plus one instead") makes a counter put on an ally one more.

rules.text: A replacement effect does not use the stack. It cannot be responded to, and an effect that negates triggered and activated effects (Containment Protocol) cannot stop it or undo what it did.
examples: Containment Protocol on the stack cannot negate Nullbringer's life-gain replacement.
Conduit of Pain's extra damage never reaches the stack, so nothing can negate it.

rules.text: A replacement effect whose substitute names a target is the one exception (rule 109.5a): the event is replaced at once, and the substitute goes on the stack as a triggered ability. If the substitute later has no legal target or fizzles, the replaced event still does not happen.
examples: Beyond, Codex Incarnate replaces its controller's rot damage with -1/-1 counters on a target unit; the damage never lands, whatever becomes of the counters.

rules.text: The event a replacement effect replaces does not happen, and the substitute happens instead. Abilities that trigger on the replaced event do not trigger. When the substitute is still damage (damage dealt "as" rot), the damage was still dealt (rule 112.12).
examples: under Nullbringer a player who would gain life loses that much instead; nothing that triggers on gaining life triggers.
a Robot that Cosmic Conspirator replaces with a Fireball is never created, so nothing that triggers on a unit spawning triggers for it.
with Blightsea Polyp in play, Zephyrzoa's column still deals combat damage to the opponent, although the opponent gains rot instead of losing life.

rules.text: A replacement effect applies to an event only once. What it produces is not replaced again by the same effect, unless a new event occurs.
examples: 10 {Piercing} combat damage redirected into a 2/4 Oorblak: 4 destroy it, and the other 6 reach the player and are not redirected again.
two Nullbringers turn one life gain into one loss, not into a gain again.

rules.text: If two or more effects could each replace or redirect the same event (two Nullbringers, two Counter Thieves, two Oorblaks), only one of them does. An event a redirect produces is not redirected again by another such effect. (engine differs, see F-U15-3)
examples: two Counter Thieves do not pass the same counters back and forth.

rules.text: Replacement effects that only change an amount ("that many plus one instead") all apply: each applies once, and their changes add up. A modifier does not apply to its own change, but two copies of the same card are two modifiers and both apply.
examples: two Conduits of Pain make 1 damage from an allied source into 3.
two allied Flux Resonators make a Robot X spawn with X plus 2 counters.

rules.text: Effects that double an amount ("Double all life gain and life loss") multiply together. With n of them applying to the same amount, it is multiplied by 2 to the power n.
examples: three Arbiters of Vitality multiply a life loss by 8.

rules.text: When modifiers that add to an amount and an effect that doubles it apply to the same amount, the additions are made first and the result is doubled.
examples: a {Powerful} Bellowing Boulder with Conduit of Pain deals (1+1)x2 = 4 damage to each unit.
Conduit of Pain and Arbiter of Vitality: the 1 is added before the life loss is doubled.

rules.text: A multiplied life loss is lost all at once, as one loss of the whole amount, and only then does the game check whether the player has lost.
examples: Arbiter of Vitality doubles a lethal loss before the game checks whether the player has lost.

rules.text: When a replacement that changes the number of counters and a replacement that redirects them both apply to the same placement, the number is changed first, and the redirect then moves the whole changed number.
examples: a Counter Thief beside a Flux Resonator steals the extra counter too.

rules.text: A replacement effect applies only to what its own text names. One that applies when counters "would be put on" a unit does not apply when counters are removed.
examples: Proliferating Slime does not change how many counters Burn the Blight removes.

rules.text: Counters of either sign are counters. A replacement effect that adds to counters being put on a unit adds -1/-1 counters to -1/-1 counters, as it adds +1/+1 counters to +1/+1 counters.
examples: Flux Resonator makes two -1/-1 counters its controller puts on a unit into three.

rules.text: Whether counters are put "by an allied source", or put by "you", depends on whose effect put them, not on whose unit they land on. Counters that a redirect moves are still put by the player whose effect put them.
examples: counters an opponent's effect puts on your unit do not get your Flux Resonator's extra counter.
counters your effect puts on an enemy unit do.

rules.text: All the tokens one resolution of one effect creates are created together. A replacement effect that acts on "each unique token you created" sees all of them at once, and a token is unique by its name and its X together.
examples: Automaton of Abundance with Manufacture (a Robot 3, a Robot 2 and a Robot 1) creates three extra Robots.
three identical Robot 2s created together are one unique token and yield one extra.

rules.text: When an effect says a player's life total can't change, a gain or loss of life for that player does not happen at all, and no replacement effect applies to it.
examples: with the life total locked by Suspend, Nullbringer has no gain of life to turn into a loss.

rules.text: A prevention effect ("if damage would be dealt …, prevent it") is not a replacement effect. Prevented damage is not dealt at all (rule 112.11), while damage a replacement effect changes is still dealt (rule 112.12).
examples: a unit shielded by Phytochemical Protection and hit by a {Poisonous} unit takes no -1/-1 counters and does not trigger on being dealt damage.

rules.text: A prevention effect on a unit prevents all the damage dealt to it, including any beyond what would destroy it.
examples: a lone shielded blocker is assigned the whole of a column's damage, and all of it is prevented.

rules.text: Prevention applies to the damage as it would be dealt, after the recipient's own doubling ({Vulnerable}). It does not change how damage is assigned or how much is lethal (rule 608.6g).
examples: a shield changes what is dealt to a unit, never how much of a {Piercing} hit goes past it.

rules.text: A continuous effect changes the game for a period of time rather than once. It comes either from a static ability, and lasts as long as that ability is in play, only in its region; or from an effect that says how long it lasts, such as "until regroup".
examples: Sudden Bloom gives your units in its region +1/+1 until regroup, and the bonus is gone after regroup.

rules.text: A continuous effect applies to a unit that enters play while the effect applies, from the moment it enters. The unit enters play already changed, so an ability that looks at the unit as it enters sees the changed unit.
examples: under Sandstone Defender ("Your other units gain +0/+2") a 1/1 enters as a 1/3, so Nectar Ridge Oracle ("When another ally with greater defense than power spawns, draw a card") draws.
under Infernal Wispweaver a 0/1 Wisp enters as a 2/2, so Nectar Ridge Oracle does not draw.

rules.text: When the source of a static ability leaves play, its continuous effect ends at once. The units it was changing are again what they would be without it, and they get back any attributes and abilities it had removed.
examples: a unit that entered play under Transmogrifant has no attributes; when Transmogrifant leaves play it has them again.
when Infernal Wispweaver leaves play, Wisps sacrifice themselves after combat again.

rules.text: A unit's stats are worked out layer by layer, in the order of rule 206.4. Every effect in one layer applies before any effect in the next layer, whatever order the effects began in. Within one layer, effects apply in timestamp order (rule 113).
examples: An effect that makes a unit base 4/4 applies over Apex Prime's copy effect whether the copy began before it or after it, because base stats are a later layer than the copy.

rules.text: Before those layers, a copy effect decides which card the unit's printed stats come from. A unit that is a copy of a card has that card's printed stats as its layer 1, and every later layer applies to them (rule 710).
examples: a Unit Token that becomes a copy of Good Whale and is Unaware reads as a 7/5, Good Whale's printed stats.

rules.text: In layer 4, Tough and Balanced apply in the order the unit has them, from top to bottom. A Tough unit that attacks with a Balanced unit behind it has its defense doubled, then its stats balanced. Where a Balanced unit gets Tough from a mod, the Manual's answer gives both orders: Tough "augmented onto" a Balanced unit doubles, then balances; Tough "applied to" a Balanced unit balances, then doubles (D-U16-1). The engine takes a unit's printed attributes first, in type-line order, then those from its mods in the order the mods were applied, then those its column shares with it, front to back, so it balances first (R19 calls this order its own; engine differs from the "augmented onto" reading, see F-U16-4).
An attribute is either present or not. A unit that has the same attribute from several sources has it once, and it applies once.
examples: two Reality Benders on one unit make it Inverted once; they do not cancel out.

rules.text: Inverted (layer 5) applies after all of layer 4, whatever order the unit gained its attributes in. A unit that is Tough and Inverted has the same stats whichever of the two it gained first.
examples: a 1/4 that is Tough and Inverted is a 1/0, in either grant order.

rules.text: A unit's stats are worked out all at once. A unit whose stats would reach 0 defense partway through the calculation does not die for that; only the final result counts (rule 713).
examples: a 1/1 with a -1/-1 counter that is Inverted is a 2/2, never a dead 0/0 on the way.

rules.text: An effect that exchanges the base stats of two units (Body Swap) gives each unit the other's base stats as they are when it resolves. It is a base rewrite of its own, later than any base rewrite already applying, so it wins over one.
examples: your 1/1 and an enemy Wisp that Aberrant Statweaver makes base 3/3 are exchanged: your unit becomes base 3/3 and the Wisp base 1/1, until regroup.

rules.text: An effect that doubles a unit's power or defense until regroup gives the unit a temporary stat change (layer 3) of the size that makes the final stat, after every layer, twice what it was. Because the change is in layer 3, it is still there if an attribute in a later layer stops applying.
examples: a 1/10 Tough unit (a 1/5, doubled) doubled by Burgeon gets +0/+5 and is a 1/20. If it then loses Tough to Monke, it is a 1/10.

rules.text: Where an effect that switches a unit's power and defense until regroup (Invasive Reassignment) applies in the stat layers is an open ruling. The engine applies it as a temporary stat change worked out from the unit's stats when it resolves, so a stat change that comes afterwards applies on top and is not switched.
examples: An 8/3 unit switched by Invasive Reassignment is a 3/8; if it then gets +2/+0 it is a 5/8, not switched again.

rules.text: A unit that becomes a copy of a card takes that card's name, printed stats, attributes and text in place of its own. The physical card does not change: in every zone other than play it is still its own card (rule 410.3a).
examples: a Borrower of Forms that copies a unit takes its name, its attributes and its text.
a unit that is a copy dies and its own card goes to the bin, not the copied card.

rules.text: While a unit is a copy, its mana cost and its card type are those of the card it copies. A Borrower of Forms that copied a Robot costs 0, and while it copies a unit it is not a spell unit.
examples: a Borrower of Forms that copied a Robot costs 0, so Lumengrove Lurker can recall it.
while it copies a unit, Cosmic Reversal's "and spell units" does not recall it.

rules.text: Counters and marked damage belong to the unit, not to the card it copies. A unit keeps them when it becomes a copy, and keeps them when the copy ends.
examples: a 1/1 that becomes a 7/5 until regroup and takes two -1/-1 counters dies when the copy ends at regroup.

rules.text: A unit that becomes an "exact copy" (Borrower of Forms) also takes the stat changes and the counters of the unit it copies, and its card text including the text of its mods. Its layer-1 stats are the copied unit's base stats.
examples: Borrower of Forms erases its target and takes its stats and counters.

rules.text: A copy of a modded unit has what the mods say, but no mod is copied. The copy is not modded, so it is not Unstable. Its copied grafts run as part of its graft cause, and each copied augment gives it that augment's [Augment] box.
examples: a Borrower of Forms that copied a unit carrying a Powerful virus is Powerful, and is not modded or Unstable.
A Borrower of Forms that copied a Bellowing Boulder with Flame Juggle grafted has the Boulder's whole trigger, Flame Juggle's grafted part included.

rules.text: More grafts may be added to a copy of a grafted unit, but they go underneath the copied grafts.
examples: A graft added to a Borrower of Forms that copied a grafted unit resolves below the copied grafts.

rules.text: When a copy of a modded unit leaves play, only its own card goes anywhere. Nothing is binned or erased for the mods it copied, because it has none. A mod later put on the copy is a real mod, and makes it Unstable as usual.
examples: a Borrower of Forms that copied a unit with a virus dies, and only Borrower of Forms goes to the bin.

rules.text: A [once] ability from a copied augment can be used once per turn on the copy, exactly as if a real mod of that card were on it.
examples: a Borrower of Forms that copied a Graxxlid-augmented unit can use Graxxlid's ability once per turn.

rules.text: If a unit becomes a copy more than once, the latest copy applies. It does not have two faces.
examples: an Apex Prime copy made when attacking and another made when blocking leave the unit one copy, the later one.

rules.text: A copy of a unit that is itself a copy copies what that unit currently is, not the card printed on it.
examples: a copy of a Borrower of Forms that copied a virused unit carries the copied virus's text too.

rules.text: An effect that creates a copy of its own source ("create a copy of me") creates a token copy of what the source currently is. The token has none of the source's counters and none of its mods.
examples: Hooba-God, killed under its own attack trigger, still creates a copy of what it was.

rules.text: A copy that lasts until regroup (Apex Prime) ends at regroup. The unit is its own card again, still with its counters, and it dies if its own stats cannot survive them.

An ability that gives a unit "all abilities" of other units (Ancient One) gives it everything in those units' text boxes, including the text their mods give them, but not their attributes, their name or their stats. The unit has the text only while the other units qualify, and loses it the moment they stop.
examples: Ancient One has an adjacent ally's static ability, and loses it when the column breaks.
an adjacent ally's attributes are not given to Ancient One.
Ancient One keeps its own name and stats.

rules.text: In text a unit gets this way, "I" and "me" mean the unit that has the text, not the unit it came from.
examples: next to Gatekeeper of Souls ("I must be targeted if able"), it is the Ancient One that must be targeted.

rules.text: A copy of a spell is put on the stack above the spell it copies, so it resolves first. It is an effect on the stack like any other: players may respond to it, and it can be targeted and negated.
examples: Earthbound Replicator's copy goes on the stack above the original, so it resolves first.
the copy can be chosen as a "target effect" and negated by Dematerialize.

rules.text: A copy of a spell keeps what the original declared when it was cast: its X, its mode and its targets. Additional costs the original paid are not paid again. The copy is given new targets only if the card that makes it says so.
examples: Maelstrom Charger's copy of Volatile Toxicity uses the original's sacrifice, which is not paid again.
A copy of Fight keeps both targets the original declared.

rules.text: A copy of a spell targets what it targets: an ability that triggers when something becomes a target sees the copy's targets, although the copy was not played.
examples: an enemy plays Burgeon on an attacker beside Earnest Defender and copies it with Maelstrom Charger, keeping the targets. Earnest Defender triggers twice, once for the spell and once for its copy.

rules.text: A copy of a spell has no card. An instruction on it to erase itself erases nothing, and however many copies resolve, only the original card goes to a bin.
examples: a resolved copy of Suspend puts nothing in a bin and its "Erase me." erases nothing; the original Suspend is erased once.

rules.text: A copy of a spell carries the {Modular} mods the original was cast with, so their [Augment] attributes apply to the copy too.
examples: Spellbind cast with Primordial Coalescence as a Modular mod and copied with Maelstrom Charger: the copy on the stack carries the same mods as the original.

rules.text: A card that transforms in play is the same unit with its other face up: its name, stats and text are those of the face that is up. It keeps that face while it stays in play, and turns back over as it leaves play (rule 410.3).
examples: Scholar of the Void transforms into Beyond, Codex Incarnate and is still the same unit.

rules.text: When a player gains control of a unit, the unit changes sides: it becomes that player's unit, an ally of that player's units and an enemy of its former controller's. Its owner does not change.
examples: a stolen unit recalled goes to the hand of the player who controls it, and its owner is unchanged.

rules.text: A unit's mods change controller with it. The unit's new controller controls the mods and their text, so text a mod gives the unit refers to the new controller.
examples: Mindspore Fiend gives away a modded blocker, and its mods go with it.

rules.text: A unit whose controller changes leaves its formation. If this happens during a battle, the unit stays in the battle out of formation for the rest of that battle: it attacks for nobody and blocks for nobody. It joins its new controller's side at regroup.
examples: a Robot token stolen by Download mid-battle is out of the formation for the rest of the battle.
the stolen Robot joins its new controller's side at regroup.

rules.text: If a unit that was blocking changes controller, the attacking column it blocked stays blocked.

A unit given to a player who is not present in the region where it stands (for example, during deployment) goes at once to that player's home region, with its mods. During a battle both players are present in the battle region, so the unit stays there.
examples: Mindspore Fiend gives away a modded blocker after combat, and it stays in the battle region.

rules.text: An effect that exchanges control of two units and swaps their positions (Organic Exchange) leaves both units in formation: each takes the other's place, which is on its new controller's side.
examples: Organic Exchange swaps control, and the attack slot passes to the exchanged unit.

rules.text: An effect that would give control of a unit to the player who already controls it, or of a unit that has gone, changes nothing. An "If you do" that depends on the handover does not happen (rule 101.5a).
examples: Amphivore carries the grafts Flame Juggle and Ralph, and its trigger runs them three times. The first time, Ralph gives Amphivore to the opponent and creates three 1/1s. The second and third times the opponent already controls it, so nothing changes hands and no more 1/1s are made; Flame Juggle still runs all three times.

rules.text: A unit that leaves play goes to the zones of the player who controls it, not of its owner, unless the effect names another player's zone (rule 405.3).
examples: a stolen unit recalled goes to the thief's hand.

rules.text: A mod is controlled by the controller of the unit it is on. When a mod is moved onto another unit (Rotbeast, Reconfigure), its controller becomes that unit's controller.
examples: an augment Rotbeast moves onto an enemy takes its Unstable and its static ability with it.

rules.text: Some effects make a unit lose all its attributes, all its abilities, or both ("loses all attributes and abilities"). While the unit has lost them, they do not apply.
examples: Monke makes other units lose all attributes and abilities during battle.

rules.text: Losing all abilities takes everything the unit's text does by itself: its triggered abilities, its activated abilities (which cannot be activated), its static abilities and cost changes, and its replacement effects, whether printed on it, given by its mods or granted to it. A unit that loses its abilities stops applying its static abilities at once, whether a one-time effect (Suppression Field) or a continuous one (Transmogrifant, Monke) took them; two continuous strips that each fall under the other are rule 712.5. Engine differs, see F-U16-3: a unit that a continuous effect strips keeps applying its static abilities.
examples: a copy silenced by Suppression Field stops applying the static it copied.
With Transmogrifant and Sandstone Defender in play, Sandstone Defender has lost its abilities, so a 1/1 token gets only Transmogrifant's +2/+2 and is a 3/3.

rules.text: Stats are not abilities. A unit that has lost its abilities keeps its stats, its counters and its stat changes; Tough and Balanced stop changing its stats only because they are attributes. It can still be targeted, block, die, and be grafted onto.
Erasing a unit's mods is a separate instruction from making it lose its abilities. Losing abilities silences the text its mods give it; erasing the mods removes them.

A strip takes what the unit has when the strip applies. An attribute or ability the unit gains afterwards (a mod attached later, an attribute or ability granted later, a static ability that starts applying later) is not taken.
examples: after Suppression Field resolves on Bubb, Protective Adaptations gives Bubb Piercing, and it has it.
a virus applied after Monke still gives its attribute.
A continuous strip takes a mod attached before it began, and leaves one attached after.

rules.text: When an effect that removes attributes (Formless, Suppression Field) is aimed at a unit in a formation, every unit in that unit's column loses its attributes, whichever unit they came from. Only the loss of attributes reaches the column: the rest of the effect, such as the loss of abilities or Formless's "base 4/4", applies to the target alone.
examples: Formless takes Blessed off the whole column, not just its target.
Suppression Field aimed at either unit of a column takes both Unaware and Flying from both.
Formless's base 4/4 still hits the target alone.

rules.text: A target that is not in a column (outside battle, or out of formation) loses only its own attributes.
Each unit in the column loses its attributes as its own state, until the effect ends. A unit that leaves the column does not get them back, and a unit that joins the column afterwards keeps its own.
examples: Formless is aimed at a unit whose column-mate is Blessed. The column-mate loses Blessed, stays without it for the rest of the battle after combat damage is over, and gets it back at regroup.

rules.text: A unit that has lost its attributes can still get attributes from a column it joins later, by sharing. It does not share the attributes it lost.
examples: a stripped Bubb that later joins a Balanced unit's column is Balanced, and the column is not Unaware.

rules.text: An effect that switches off one named behaviour stops only that behaviour; it does not take the unit's other abilities. Only "loses all abilities" takes them all.
examples: Infernal Wispweaver stops a Wisp sacrificing itself after combat, and the Wisp keeps an ability it was given.

rules.text: Two continuous strips whose sources each fall under the other (two Monkes, each another's "other unit") both apply. Each source loses its abilities, and neither stops the other.

The Everywhere's controller names a card during the haste step. Every unit with that name in The Everywhere's region loses all abilities, for as long as The Everywhere is in that region. Naming another card replaces the first, and a card that is not in play may be named.
examples: an enemy copy is silenced only once The Everywhere attacks into its region.

rules.text: Text a copy has from the mods of the unit it copied is part of the copy's own card text. An effect that makes the copy lose all attributes and abilities takes it, and "erase all of its mods" finds no mod to erase.
examples: Suppression Field strips the augment text a Borrower of Forms copied.

rules.text: Units in the same column of a formation share their combat attributes: each unit in the column has every combat attribute any unit in it has.
A unit in a column has the column's attributes for everything it does while it is in the column, not only for combat damage. An ability it activates, or damage it deals by an effect, uses them too.
examples: an ability fired by a unit in a Blessed column gains its controller life.
Powerful from the column doubles that damage too.

rules.text: Columns exist only in battle. Outside battle a unit shares no attributes with anything.
Attributes are shared only within a column, never with the units to the left or right.
examples: Good Whale attacks with a unit behind it in its column and another unit in the next column. The unit behind it has Piercing; the unit in the next column does not.

rules.text: When a unit leaves a column, the other units in it lose at once the attributes it was sharing with them.
examples: once the Deadly unit leaves Bellowing Boulder's column, the Boulder's ping is not Deadly.

rules.text: Non-combat attributes, such as Unstable, Burst and Modular, are not shared. A modded unit is Unstable, but the units in its column are not.
Two questions are each unit's own, whatever its column shares: a unit with Feeble cannot block even in a column with other units, and an Alluring trigger comes from the unit that has Alluring.
State checks are made by the game itself, at safe points. In a state check, every unit that should be dead dies, and every token that is in a zone where it cannot exist ceases to exist.
examples: a lethally damaged unit and a dead unit token both go at the next safe point; the card reaches the bin, the token is erased, and a token recalled to a hand is erased from it.

rules.text: A unit dies in a state check if its defense is 0 or less, or if the damage marked on it is greater than or equal to its defense.
examples: the turn's draw takes Dreadspawn Horror ("I gain -1/-1 for each card in your hand") to 0 defense, and it dies.

rules.text: The end of every action is a safe point, so no action ends with a unit standing that should have died: not a draw, a draft, a recycle or a resource activation. An action that is waiting on a player's decision has not ended and is not at a safe point; it is checked when the answer comes and the action finishes. The one exception is Constructed's draw phase, where drawing 4 and putting 2 back are judged as one step: a player's units are not checked while that player still has the 2 cards to put back.
examples: in Constructed, Dreadspawn Horror with 3 cards in hand is still in play after the draw of 4, and dies once its controller has put 2 back (5 cards in hand).
in Constructed, Dreadspawn Horror with 1 card in hand is a 4/2 after the draw phase and lives.

rules.text: Deaths are also checked while an effect is still resolving, not only at safe points. Each time an effect puts counters on a unit, and after each part of an effect made of several parts, units that should be dead die at once, before the rest of the effect happens.
examples: Pestilent Titan attacks and its trigger puts a -1/-1 counter on each unit. A 1/1 token dies as soon as it gets its counter, before the next unit gets one.

rules.text: A unit can die in a state check from a change no damage caused: a new base, a stat change, a mod it loses, or a combination of attributes (Tough and Inverted) that leaves its defense at 0 or less.
examples: Rampart Guardian makes a unit Tough, then Reality Bender makes it Inverted, and it dies with no damage on it.

rules.text: Pure does not save a unit from a state-check death. Pure hides attributes in a combat exchange; it does not change the unit's stats.
examples: a Pure 1/3 that is also Tough and Inverted reads 1/0 and dies in the state check.

rules.text: In a state check, a token that is in any zone other than play or the stack (a hand, a bin, a cache) ceases to exist. This happens before anything its arrival there caused to trigger is put on the stack.
examples: A Hooba-Mon token is exchanged out of play by Skittering Blight. It goes to the bin, and the state check then erases it from there.

rules.text: Units that die in the same state check die together. Each of them still sees the others leave: an ability of one that triggers when another unit dies, or when a card is trashed, triggers for the others in the same batch.
examples: Muck Rummager dies from combat damage in the same batch as an ally, and still triggers on that ally being trashed.

rules.text: A unit that dies in the batch does not see its own departure that way, and it is not a legal target or an ally for a count while the batch is dealt with.
examples: Cthyrian Culler dying alone makes nobody lose life for its own trash; dying beside an ally, it triggers once, for the ally.
Splort dies in the same batch as an ally; its trigger for the ally cannot target either dead unit.

rules.text: A unit sent out to counterattack, which does not exist until round 1 ends, is not checked for death while it is away. It is checked as it comes back.
examples: Prickly Protector, alive only through its own static, survives being declared as a counterattacker.
a counterattacker sent out alone survives the send and dies on arrival.

rules.text: A unit that stays home does not count a unit that has gone to counterattack as an ally.
examples: Prickly Protector, carrying a -1/-1 counter, is alive only because it has one other ally. When that ally is sent to counterattack, the Protector stays home, no longer counts it, and dies.

rules.text: A unit that is destroyed dies: by a state check, by being sacrificed, or by being deleted. An {Unstable} unit that is destroyed still dies. A unit that leaves play any other way, by being recalled, cached, exchanged or erased, does not die.
examples: Banishment erases a unit, and no death is recorded.

rules.text: A unit's last-known state is what it was at the instant it left play: its card and the face it showed, its controller, its region, its attributes (including those its column shared with it), its power and defense, and the formation it stood in.
examples: Deathglow Strider, sharing Piercing in a Good Whale column with a +1/+1 counter, is destroyed before its after-combat trigger resolves; the trigger remembers a 3/4 Piercing Deathglow Strider of its controller, in that region and formation.

rules.text: An effect whose source has left play has the attributes its source had when it left, including attributes shared with it by its column then.
examples: Bellowing Boulder dies with a Deadly unit beside it and its ping on the stack; the ping is still Deadly.

rules.text: An effect whose source has left play that uses its source's power or defense uses the power or defense the source had when it left.
examples: Deathglow Strider (printed 2/3) with a +1/+1 counter is a 3/4. It leaves play before its after-combat trigger resolves; the trigger deals 4 to each opponent, its last-known defense, not its printed 3.
Spewing Mushroom (printed 1/3) gets +2/+0 and leaves play before its attack trigger resolves; the trigger creates a Poison 3, from its last-known power 3.

rules.text: An effect whose source has left play that refers to the source's formation ("in my formation", "attacking units in my formation") uses the formation the source stood in when it left, for the rest of that battle.
examples: Hooba-Lin, killed under its own attack trigger, remembers its formation and the 1/1 joins it.
Embermaw Fledgling, gone before its trigger resolves, still counts the attackers it stood with.

rules.text: A count of the allies adjacent to a source that has left play is 0.
examples: Flamebreath Initiate removed before its trigger resolves still makes a Fireball 1 (X = 0).

rules.text: An effect whose source has left play that makes a copy of the source copies what the source was when it left.
examples: Echo of Despair, gone before its after-combat trigger resolves, still makes its copy.

rules.text: While its source is still in play, an effect reads the source as it is when the effect resolves, not as it was when the effect was put on the stack.
examples: Deadly given back to Bellowing Boulder before its ping resolves makes the ping Deadly again.

rules.text: A source that is still in play but out of formation (for example, a unit stolen mid-battle, rule 711.3) stands in no formation. An effect that places units in its formation, or counts it, does nothing.
examples: a Hooba-Lin alive but out of the formation makes no token.

rules.text: The facts of how a unit left play are fixed as it leaves: the region it left from, the counters it carried, whether it was a token, how it left, and where its card went. Abilities that trigger on its leaving use those facts.
An ability that triggers on its own source leaving play ("when I die") resolves in the region the source left from, not in its controller's home region.
A modification (mod) changes a card's abilities by combining cards together. A card that can be a mod carries one of two mod symbols: the augment symbol (721) or the graft symbol (722).
examples: Aetherflux Golem (augment) and Flame Juggle (graft) are offered as mods; The Foretold, with neither symbol, is not.

rules.text: Virus and Modular are not further kinds of mod. A Virus is a card that can also be applied as an augment during battle (723). Modular lets mods be applied to a card as it is played (724).
Applying a mod is a special action, which a player may perform during the deployment phase.

A timing icon other than Virus does not change when a card can be applied as a mod. A Battle card cannot be applied as a mod during battle, except under a card that lets cards be augmented as if they were Viruses (723.5) or to a Modular card as it is played (724).
examples: Burning Vengeance, a Battle card, is not offered as a mod during battle, but it is offered to Spellbind, a Modular card, played in battle.
Hooba-Lin, a Haste augment card, cannot be applied as a mod in the haste step when no card such as Slurpr allows it.

rules.text: A mod can be applied outside deployment only where a rule or a card says so: a Virus during battle (723.2); a card augmented in battle under a card that lets it be augmented as if it were a Virus, such as Rook (723.5); a mod applied in the haste step under a card that allows it, such as Slurpr (504.8a); and a mod applied to a Modular card as it is played (724). No other card widens the window.
An effect that lets a player play cards does not let them apply mods. Tides of the Cosmos cannot graft a card or apply a non-Virus augment; it may only put a Virus card onto a unit as a Virus.
Applying a mod is not playing a card, from whatever zone the mod comes. An ability that triggers when a player plays a unit, a spell or a card does not trigger when a mod is applied.
examples: Stalwart Sentinel counts a spell played from the bin, but not a mod applied from the bin.
A Virus applied during battle is not a spell: Origon does not negate it, and it does not count as a spell played.

rules.text: To apply a mod, a player must meet the mod card's affinity requirement and pay its mana cost, wherever the mod comes from.
A modifier to the cost of playing cards or spells does not change the cost of applying a mod, and a modifier to the cost of activating or triggering abilities does not apply to applying a mod either.
examples: Under Crevice Lurker, applying an augment during battle costs only its own mana.

rules.text: A mod applied from the cache is priced by the permission that lets it be used. Under a fulfilled prophecy it costs nothing and ignores affinity. Under a glimpse this turn it costs its mana but ignores affinity.
A mod may be applied from the player's hand or from their bin.

A mod may also be applied from the cache, but only while a permission to use that card is live: a fulfilled prophecy, or a glimpse this turn. A cached card with no live permission cannot be applied as a mod.
A mod becomes part of the card it is applied to, its host. A modified card is treated as a single card with all of the additional text from its mods; the mods are not separate from it.
examples: Aetherflux Golem augmented onto a unit gives that unit +2/+2 and is not a unit of its own.

rules.text: A mod is controlled by its host's controller. A player who augments a card onto an opponent's unit gives that opponent control of the mod and all of its text.
examples: In battle, a player applies Corrupting Blight as a Virus to an opponent's Bubb. The opponent now controls the Blight, so its "you" is the opponent: after combat, a player who doesn't control Bubb gains control of it, and Bubb ends up with the player who applied the Blight.

rules.text: On a mod's text, "you" means the host's controller.
examples: Oorblak applied as a Virus to an opponent's unit: the combat damage that would be dealt to that opponent is dealt to their own unit instead.

rules.text: On a mod's text, "I", "me" and "my" mean the host.
examples: Life Leech applied as a Virus gives its host, not the Leech, +3/+3 when its controller pays 5 life.

rules.text: On a mod's text, "other" and "another" exclude only that mod itself, not other mods made from copies of the same card.
examples: A host wearing two Rotbeast augments: each Rotbeast moves the other.

rules.text: When a unit changes controller, its mods change controller with it.
examples: Download steals a unit token that carries an augment; the augment changes controller with it.

rules.text: There is no limit to the number of mods a card can have.
examples: Six Aetherflux Golems augmented onto one unit give it +12/+12.

rules.text: As long as a card is modded, it has {Unstable}: when it dies or is erased, it and all of its mods are erased.
examples: A unit carrying Ephemeral Skywalker as an augment dies; both cards are erased and neither reaches the bin.

rules.text: If a modded card leaves play without dying or being erased, for example when it is returned to a hand, its mods are put into the bin and the card goes on alone.
When a modded unit is cached, its mods do not follow it into the cache; they go to the bin.
A token mod has no card of its own. It never enters a bin: however its host leaves play, the token mod is erased.
examples: A unit carrying a Wraith token as an augment is recalled, cached or killed. Whichever way it leaves, the Wraith goes to no bin and is not trashed: it is erased.

rules.text: The {Unstable} that a mod gives goes with the mod. A unit stops having {Unstable} for this reason when its last mod leaves it, and a unit a mod is moved onto has it from then on.
examples: Rotbeast moves its host's other augments onto an enemy; the enemy becomes Unstable and the augment's static goes with it.

rules.text: A copy of a modded unit (Borrower of Forms) is not itself modded and does not have {Unstable} for that reason. A mod applied to the copy afterwards makes it {Unstable} in the ordinary way.
examples: A Borrower of Forms that has resolved becomes Unstable when a mod is attached to it.

rules.text: When a host is recalled or cached and its nontoken mods are left in a bin, each of those mods is trashed, and the host's controller is the player who trashes it.
A nontoken mod erased together with its {Unstable} host is not trashed. The host's single trash counts for the whole unit.

An effect or a cost can erase a mod off a host that stays in play. The mod card goes to the erased pile of the mod's controller. The host stays in play, and can die if losing the mod leaves it unable to survive.
examples: Return to Nature negates everything on the stack and erases all mods in the region.
A mod on a stolen unit is erased off it; it goes to the erased pile of the player who stole the unit, not its owner's.

rules.text: A token mod erased off a host that stays in play is not recorded on the erased pile, because a token is not a card.
examples: A Wraith token mod erased off a host that stays in play, as the payment of a cost, is not filed on the erased pile.

rules.text: An effect can move a mod from one host to another (Reconfigure, Rotbeast). Moving a mod is not a zone change: the mod never leaves play, and nothing despawns.
examples: Reconfigure moves Bubb and its Growing Plague onto a Robot; Growing Plague's "when I despawn" does not trigger.

rules.text: A moved mod is controlled by its new host's controller.
examples: Rotbeast moves augments onto an enemy unit; the enemy now controls them, along with their text.

rules.text: Moving a mod does not refresh it. A once-per-turn ability on the mod that was already used this turn stays used on the new host.
examples: A Graxxlid used this turn and moved by Reconfigure cannot be used again this turn.

rules.text: Moving a mod is not applying it. An ability that triggers when a mod is applied does not trigger when a mod is moved, unless the moving effect says the mods are augmented (721.5a).
examples: Rotbeast moves its Curio Drifter augment onto an enemy Perpetual Construct, which makes no unit.

rules.text: A mod's effects take their timestamp from when the mod was applied. A mod applied after an effect that removes attributes and abilities on the same layer (Monke) still gives its attribute and ability.
examples: A Virus applied after Monke's effect began still gives its attribute.

rules.text: An ability that triggers when a mod is applied to its unit triggers once for each mod applied.
examples: Perpetual Construct makes an X/X for an applied mod, X the mod's cost.
Reconfigure moves three mods onto Perpetual Construct: three triggers, a 1/1, a 3/3 and a 4/4.

rules.text: Augment is a modification. An augment adds the text that follows its augment symbol to the card it is applied to.
examples: Aetherflux Golem, a 1/1 whose augment text is "I gain +2/+2", gives its host +2/+2.

rules.text: An augment symbol at the start of a paragraph in the text box gives the host that whole paragraph.
examples: Growing Plague applied as an augment gives its host "When I despawn, each other player draws two cards."

rules.text: An augment symbol on the type line gives the host the attributes on that type line. It gives no stats.
examples: Bubb ([Augment] {Unaware}) gives its host Unaware, and not its 5/6.

rules.text: On a host, only the augment's own augment text works. The rest of the augment card's text, including body text printed outside the augment paragraph and attributes printed before a text-box augment symbol, does nothing for the host.
examples: Infernal Wispweaver played as a unit gives your wisps +2/+1. Applied as an augment, it gives its host only "At the end of turn, create a wisp"; the +2/+1 for your wisps, printed outside the augment paragraph, does nothing.

Smouldering Inferno has {Piercing} on its type line and "[Augment] After combat, sacrifice me" in its text box. Applied as a Virus to an attacking Rune Channeler, it does not give the Channeler Piercing, and after combat the Channeler sacrifices itself.

rules.text: A card that is played normally reads its whole text, its augment text included.

Augment text keeps its kind on the host. A static ability given by an augment ("I gain +2/+2") is a continuous effect on the host for as long as the mod is attached; it is not a triggered ability and does not use the stack.
Augment text that triggers on the host's own departure ("When I despawn") triggers whichever way the host leaves play: when it dies, is recalled or is cached.
A card can be applied as an augment if it prints the augment symbol, in its text box or on its type line, whether or not its augment text does anything.
examples: Chitin Shredder prints the augment symbol only on its type line and has no text box, and it can be applied as an augment.
