rules.text: To apply an augment, the player takes these steps in order: (1) meets the augment's affinity requirement; (2) pays its mana cost; (3) selects a target to apply it onto; (4) places the augment card beneath the target, with its text box visible beneath the target's.

During deployment a player can augment only their own units. An opponent's unit can be augmented only with a Virus during battle (723.2), or under a card that lets cards be augmented as if they were Viruses (723.5).
examples: In deployment Curio Drifter can augment your own unit but not an opponent unit; in battle Aetherflux Golem (a Virus) can augment the attacking enemy.

rules.text: During deployment a player may also augment a spell token they have in play, with any augment, not only a Virus. The token gains only the augment's attributes.
examples: An augmented token deals {Powerful} damage when cast.

rules.text: An augment applied to a spell, on the stack (723.4) or as it is played through Modular (724), gives the spell only its type-line attributes. Augment text and static abilities give a spell nothing, but applying such an augment is still legal.
examples: An augment-text mod applied to Spellbind is accepted and does nothing.

rules.text: Reconfigure augments a unit and all of its mods onto another unit. Its first target must have the augment symbol.
Each mod Reconfigure moves is applied to the new host. An ability that triggers when a mod is applied to that unit triggers once for each moved mod.
examples: Bubb with two mods reconfigured onto Perpetual Construct makes three tokens, one per mod applied.

rules.text: A unit that has become a copy of a card with the augment symbol does not have that symbol, so it cannot be Reconfigure's first target.
examples: A Borrower of Forms that copied an augment unit cannot be chosen as Reconfigure's first target.

rules.text: An effect can augment a card onto a unit when it resolves. When the effect augments a token ("Augment a Wraith onto an ally"), the token is created directly as a mod of that unit.
examples: An augmented Wraith gives its host its first line: at the start of deployment the host puts a -1/-1 counter on an ally, here itself, its only ally, so a 4/4 host becomes 3/3.

rules.text: Graft is a modification that combines several effects under a single cause. It is marked by the graft symbol, written [Switch] (unbounded) or [Switch1] (bounded) in the card text this document quotes.
examples: Flame Juggle grafted onto Oracle of the Flame: one sacrifice of the Oracle creates its own Fireball 1 and Flame Juggle's three Fireball 1s.

rules.text: A graft card's ability has a cause, before the graft symbol, and an effect, after it. Oracle of the Flame's cause is "Sacrifice me" and its effect is "Create a Fireball 1".
When a card is grafted, only what follows its graft symbol is added to the host. Everything printed before the symbol, its cost and cause included, is ignored.
examples: A grafted Omniwield Evoker adds "Put a +1/+1 counter on me" to the host's ability; its own cost of three, printed before the graft symbol, is not paid.

rules.text: A graft card still works as written when it is played normally. A spell or spell unit with a graft symbol resolves normally when it is played, and can later be grafted from the bin.
examples: Once Leaping Lillik has died, it can be grafted from the bin.

rules.text: Both cards must have the graft symbol. The host must be a unit in play with a graft cause of its own.
Applying a graft follows the same cost and timing as an augment: from the hand or the bin, during deployment, paying the card's cost and meeting its affinity.

A graft is applied only in deployment, never in the haste step or in battle, even when the graft card has Haste. The exceptions are a card that allows mods in the haste step, such as Slurpr (504.8a), and a Modular card, to which a graft card may be applied as the Modular card is played, in battle too (724).
examples: With Slurpr in play, a graft can be applied during the haste step.

rules.text: A card that lets cards be augmented in battle as if they were Viruses (Rook) does not let a card be grafted in battle.
examples: With Rook in play, Curio Drifter is offered as an augment in battle, but Flame Juggle is not offered as a graft.

rules.text: Applying a graft targets the host. An ability that triggers when its unit becomes targeted (Mohruung) triggers first, before the graft is attached.
examples: Grafting onto Mohruung targets it, so it makes its Crystal.

rules.text: A player applying a new graft may insert it at any position below the host's own card, but may not re-order the grafts already applied.
examples: A new graft slides between two already applied, whose order stays fixed.

rules.text: Each grafted effect is added to the cause of the host's own card. The host's ability then reads "cause: effect 1 AND effect 2 AND effect 3 …", in the order the grafts sit.
examples: Accelerated Germination grafted onto Oracle of the Flame reads "Sacrifice me: Create a Fireball 1 AND (once per turn) create two 1/1 units."

rules.text: The host's own graft cause decides when the whole composite triggers or can be activated.
The composite is a single ability. It goes on the stack as one item, resolves all at once, and a single negation stops all of it.
The composite resolves from top to bottom: the host's own effect first, then each graft in the order it sits.
examples: On a Mohruung host, Overbloom grafted above Spewing Mushroom makes a Poison 8; grafted below it, a Poison 1.

rules.text: Every target of the composite is declared when it is put on the stack. A part that requires a target must take one if any is legal, even one of the player's own units.
examples: Plodding Pebble, with Leaping Lillik ("Delete target unit") grafted under it, attacks into an empty region and is hit by a Fireball 1. As its trigger goes on the stack, the delete must take a target: with no enemy unit there, Plodding Pebble itself is legal, and the player cannot choose no target.

rules.text: A triggered composite with a part that requires a target, when that part has no legal target, is not put on the stack at all. Its untargeted parts do not happen either.
examples: Megadeath with Resurrect grafted attacks with no cheap unit in the bin: no Poison 5 either.

rules.text: A composite fizzles when it has lost all of its targets, and then none of it happens, its untargeted parts included. While at least one target remains, every part resolves as far as it can. Only a composite that was never targeted cannot fizzle: one with no part that calls for a target, or one whose only target was optional ("up to one") and none was chosen (see rule 704.6g).
examples: Spewing Mushroom carries Biotoxicity and Technological Superiority as grafts. It attacks, and its composite trigger targets Spewing Mushroom, the only target it declares. The opponent deletes the Mushroom with Leaping Lillik in response: the composite fizzles, and Biotoxicity's untargeted Poisons are not created either.

rules.text: A graft composite is a triggered or activated ability like any other. A modifier to the cost of activating or triggering abilities (Crevice Lurker) applies to it.
A graft is either unbounded ([Switch]) or bounded ([Switch1]). An unbounded graft can trigger any number of times; a bounded graft can trigger only once per turn.
examples: Plodding Pebble's bounded graft gives one counter per turn.

rules.text: Under an unbounded cause, the composite can fire any number of times, but each bounded graft in it is included only the first time in a turn.
Under a bounded cause, the whole composite fires only once per turn, its unbounded grafts included.
Each grafted card has its own use. Two copies of the same bounded graft on one host each have one use.
A unit that leaves play and comes back is a new object, so its bounded graft can be used again the same turn.
examples: A recalled and replayed Engorged Caudex draws from its bounded graft again the same turn.

rules.text: A graft printed "{graft} [cost]: effect" adds a cost to the composite. That cost must be paid; it cannot be declined.
examples: A grafted Immolate's sacrifice is paid as the composite goes on the stack, and the player cannot decline it.

rules.text: If a grafted cost cannot be paid, the whole composite stays off the stack: the host's own effect and every other graft with it.
The cost is paid as the composite goes on the stack. No player can respond to the payment, and units the composite itself would create cannot pay it.
Some graft causes trigger several copies of the graft ability as one single trigger: Lost Guardian two, Amphivore and Witness of the Crossing three. The copies are one effect on the stack.
examples: Amphivore's combat damage to an opponent triggers its grafts three times, in one trigger.
Lost Guardian's after-combat trigger runs each graft twice as one trigger.

rules.text: The copies run top to bottom, then top to bottom again, once for each copy.
examples: Amphivore with Plodding Pebble and Bellowing Boulder goes counter, damage, counter, damage, counter, damage.

rules.text: A bounded graft under a multiplier is repeated too.
examples: Amphivore triples a bounded "Create three" graft into nine Fireballs.

rules.text: Each copy of a targeted graft chooses its targets separately.
A cost in a repeated graft is paid once for each copy. If the multiplied cost cannot be paid in full, none of it is paid, and the composite stays off the stack (722.6a).
examples: With one card in hand, a doubled [Discard a card] cannot be paid: nothing is paid and nothing happens.

rules.text: A copy that cannot do part of its effect does the rest. Ralph grafted under a multiplier gives the host away and makes three 1/1s on the first pass only; the later passes cannot give it away, and the rest of the composite still runs every time.
examples: Amphivore with Ralph grafted: the first pass gives the host away and makes three 1/1s, the later passes give nothing, and the other graft runs three times.

rules.text: A unit that has become a copy of a grafted unit runs the whole copied composite. More grafts may be added to it, but only below the copied grafts.
examples: A Borrower that copied a Bellowing Boulder with Flame Juggle grafted runs the whole copied composite.
A graft added to that Borrower resolves below the copied grafts.

rules.text: Virus is a timing icon. A Virus card can be applied as an augment from the hand during battle, as well as being played and augmented normally during deployment.
examples: Aetherflux Golem augments the attacker from hand during battle; in deployment it may be played as a unit or augmented.

rules.text: A Virus applied in battle is an augment: it gives its host its augment text or its type-line attributes (721.1), and an ability that triggers when a player applies an augment triggers on it.
examples: Morphic Mentor's controller applies an augment in battle and the Mentor gets +2/+2; an enemy's augment does not count.

rules.text: Virus changes when a card may be augmented, not what it may be augmented onto. In deployment a Virus is applied like any other augment.
examples: In deployment Aetherflux Golem, a Virus, can augment your own unit but not an opponent unit.

rules.text: During a battle, a player who has priority may apply a Virus from their hand onto any unit in the battle's region, their own or an opponent's.
examples: A player applies Smouldering Inferno from hand to the opponent's attacker; the Virus goes on the stack and the host is modded when it resolves.

rules.text: A Virus may also be applied in battle from the cache, while a permission to use it is live, at the cache's price (720.4b). With no live permission it cannot.
examples: A glimpsed Virus in the cache goes onto an enemy unit in battle, ignoring affinity.

rules.text: A Virus in a bin cannot be applied during battle by its Virus ability. From the bin it can be applied as an ordinary mod during deployment, and outside deployment only where another card opens a window: augmenting in battle under a card such as Rook (723.5), applying to a Modular card as it is played (724), or applying in the haste step under a card such as Slurpr (504.8a).
examples: Bumblecrab, a Virus, is offered from the hand in battle but not from the bin; in deployment it is offered from the bin.
With a Rook in the battle's region, a card is augmented out of the bin during battle.

rules.text: A Virus applied to an opponent's unit is controlled by that opponent, with its ability (720.6a). A Virus whose text works against its host's controller therefore works against the opponent.
examples: Smouldering Inferno augmented onto an opposing unit forces it to sacrifice itself after combat.

rules.text: Applying a Virus in battle uses the stack. The Virus goes on the stack as an effect that targets its host, and it can be responded to, redirected and negated.
examples: A Virus being applied to Graxxlid is an effect targeting Graxxlid, which Graxxlid can negate.

rules.text: A Virus that is negated, or whose target has become invalid, is put into the bin and cannot be used as a Virus again.
examples: A Virus aimed at a spell on the stack: the spell leaves the stack first, so the Virus fizzles and goes to the bin.

rules.text: A Virus being applied is not a spell. An effect that negates spells, or counts the spells played, does not see it.
examples: Origon does not negate a Virus applied in battle, and its first-spell count is untouched.

rules.text: During battle a Virus may be augmented onto a spell on the stack, the player's own or an opponent's. The spell gains only the Virus's attributes (721.4b).
examples: Chitin Shredder on Arc Lightning doubles its damage.

rules.text: Spells, spell units and spell tokens on the stack are legal hosts for a Virus.
A spell carrying a Virus is modded, so it is {Unstable}: the spell and the Virus are erased instead of going to a bin, whether the spell resolves, fizzles or is negated.
A spell unit carrying a Virus is not erased when it resolves. It enters play with the Virus attached as an augment, and so has {Unstable}.
A spell that has begun to resolve cannot have a Virus applied to it.
Triggered and activated abilities, Viruses, units being cast and Ambushes on the stack are not legal hosts for a Virus.
A card can let other cards be augmented during battle as if they were Viruses. Rook: "You may augment cards from hand and bin during battle as if they were [Virus]."
examples: Applying a non-Virus augment from hand during battle is not allowed without Rook, and is with it.

rules.text: Such a card gives the augmented card the Virus ability itself, so the augment may go onto an opponent's unit or onto a spell on the stack.
Such a card reaches only the zones it names. Rook names the hand and the bin, so a non-Virus card in the cache cannot be augmented in battle through Rook.
Such a permission belongs to the controller of the card that grants it (the host's controller, when it is a mod), and works only in that card's region.
Modular is an attribute. A player may apply mods from their hand and/or bin to a Modular card as it is played, paying their costs.
Spellbind is the only card that prints Modular.
Any card in the player's hand or bin whose cost they can pay may be applied to a Modular card: a graft, an augment, a Virus, or a card that can do nothing on a spell.
A mod that does nothing on a spell is still a legal choice, and its cost is still paid.
examples: Sparkwraith's augment text applied to Spellbind is accepted and does nothing.

rules.text: Each mod's cost is paid as it is applied, while the Modular card is cast. Applying it is not playing it.
The mods are chosen and paid for while the Modular card is being cast, before it reaches the stack, and they go on the stack with it. The caster may apply none.
A graft applied to a Modular spell adds its effect to the spell's ability as an extra part.
examples: A player casts Spellbind and applies Primordial Coalescence from their bin to it. When Spellbind resolves, Primordial Coalescence's graft effect happens too: three Wraiths, and its 2 Rot on top of Spellbind's one.

rules.text: A type-line augment applied to a Modular spell gives its attributes to the spell's effect.
examples: {Powerful} turns a Spellbind-carried Twin Flame from 2 damage into 4.

rules.text: Augment text and static abilities applied to a Modular spell do nothing, because a spell has no body for them to work on.
examples: Sparkwraith on Spellbind: a spell played while it rides the stack puts no counter anywhere.

rules.text: A grafted cost on a Modular spell's graft part must be paid if it can be. If it cannot, only that part is skipped, and the spell still resolves.
examples: Spellbind carrying a grafted Immolate with no unit to sacrifice: the Immolate part is skipped, and Spellbind still gives its rot.
Spellbind carrying a grafted Immolate, with a unit to sacrifice: the cost is paid, the unit is sacrificed and a card is drawn. Declining is not offered.

rules.text: A Modular card with any mod applied is modded, so it has {Unstable}: it and all of its mods are erased instead of going to a bin, whether it resolves, fizzles or is negated.
examples: A graft card replayed from the bin by Spellbind is erased, so it cannot be used that way twice.

rules.text: A Modular card with no mod applied does not have {Unstable}, and goes to the bin like any other spell.

Card text uses some verbs with a fixed game meaning: these are keyword actions, defined in this section. Where a card prints reminder text for a keyword action, the printed reminder states its meaning, and it wins over any paraphrase of it.
A card is trashed when it enters a bin from any zone except the stack.
examples: A card discarded from a hand enters a bin from the hand, so it is trashed.
A card that leaves a cache for a bin is trashed.

rules.text: Discarding a card, sacrificing it, milling it and a card dying into a bin are all ways of trashing it.

A card that goes to a bin from the stack is not trashed, whether it resolved, was negated or failed to resolve. A card played for free during another effect's resolution and then put into the bin counts as coming from the stack.
examples: A spell Tides of the Cosmos plays for free off the deck goes to the bin afterwards and is not trashed.

rules.text: Erasing a card is not trashing it: an erased card never enters a bin.
examples: Banishment erases a unit: no death and no trash happen.

rules.text: A token is never trashed, because only a card can be trashed. A unit token that dies still enters the bin and still dies, but its trip through the bin is not a trash: no "when I am trashed" ability triggers for it, its own included.
examples: A token copy of Dropslime that dies does not trigger its own "When I am trashed".

rules.text: The player whose bin the card enters is the player who trashes it. A unit that dies goes to its controller's bin, so its controller trashes it; when an effect sends the card to another player's bin, that player trashes it.
examples: A stolen unit that dies goes to the bin of the player who controls it, and that player trashes it.
Pull Under deletes an enemy unit and puts it into the caster's bin: the caster trashes it.

rules.text: When a modded unit is recalled or cached, each nontoken mod it carried is left behind in a bin and is trashed there. The host's controller trashes it, not the mod's owner.
A nontoken mod that is erased together with its {Unstable} host is not trashed. The host's departure is the whole unit's; the mod has no trash of its own.

An {Unstable} card that dies in play is erased instead of entering the bin, so it is not trashed. An {Unstable} card that goes to a bin from an inactive zone (a hand, the deck or a cache) enters the bin and is trashed.
examples: Aberrant Statweaver (printed {Unstable}) discarded from a hand goes to the bin and is trashed: the hand is inactive.

rules.text: An effect that counts cards trashed counts only cards. A token dying never adds to the count.
examples: Dropslime deals damage equal to the cards trashed this battle, and the tokens that died in it do not count.

rules.text: To discard a card is to put it from a hand into the bin. A discarded card is trashed. Discarding is not playing the card, and a cached card cannot be discarded.
To sacrifice a unit is for a player to choose a unit they control and put it into their bin. A sacrificed unit dies.
examples: Immolate sacrifices a unit to draw a card.

rules.text: A player can sacrifice only something they control. An effect may make an opponent sacrifice something; that opponent sacrifices one of their own units and chooses which.
examples: General Smof: after combat each present player sacrifices a unit of their own choice.

rules.text: A player can sacrifice only a unit in the region where the effect or cost happens, never one of their units in another region.
examples: Ghord's sacrifice makes each opponent in Ghord's region sacrifice a unit there, and reaches no other region.

rules.text: A player told to sacrifice a unit who has no unit in the region sacrifices nothing.
examples: Cull's "each player sacrifices a unit" with nobody holding a unit in the region kills nothing.

rules.text: To delete a unit is one way for it to die: the unit dies, and it is removed from play into the bin. Abilities that trigger when a unit dies, its own "When I die" included, trigger. Unless the effect names another bin, it goes to the bin a dying unit would go to.
examples: Throw off a Cliff deletes a unit with 4 or more defense: it goes to the bin, as a death.

rules.text: An effect that deletes a unit and names where it goes overrides the usual bin. Pull Under puts the deleted unit and all of its mods into its caster's bin, where they stay.
To erase a card is to take it out of the game: it goes to the erased pile. When card text says "erase", the erased pile is where the card goes.
examples: Celestial Purge erases its target unit: it goes to no bin.

rules.text: Erasing a unit is neither a death nor a trash. It is a despawn.
examples: Banishment erases a unit: it does not die and is not trashed, but it does despawn.

rules.text: To recall a card is to put it into a hand. Printed recalls take a card from play, from a bin, from the stack or from a cache.
examples: Vaporweave Eidolon recalls itself from play to its controller's hand, at no cost.
Eldritch Reclaimer recalls a unit from its controller's bin to their hand.
Prismatic Observer recalls an enemy's cached card to its owner's hand.

rules.text: A unit recalled from play goes to the hand of the player who controls it, not necessarily its owner, unless the effect names another hand. Recalling does not change who owns the card.
examples: A stolen unit that is recalled goes to the thief's hand, not its owner's.
Cosmic Reversal recalls a stolen spell unit to the hand of the player who controls it.

rules.text: A recalled {Unstable} unit goes to the hand as a card. {Unstable} changes only a move into a bin, so a recall is not affected by it.
Recalling a card from a bin moves it from that bin to its player's hand. "Recall target unit in your bin" can reach only a card in that player's own bin.
examples: Delver of Mysteries recalls a chosen spell from its controller's bin.
Eldritch Reclaimer, cast with both players in the battle, can pick a unit in its caster's own bin, never one in the opponent's bin.

rules.text: Recalling a spell effect on the stack negates it and puts the card into its controller's hand. A recalled spell token enters its controller's hand and is then erased.
examples: Cosmic Reversal recalls the other spell effects on the stack to their controllers' hands.
Dream Lapse recalls a cast Fireball token: it enters its controller's hand, so Rider of the Tides grows, and then it is erased.

rules.text: When an effect tells a player to recall a unit and they have none to recall, the recall does nothing, but the rest of the effect still happens unless it depends on the recall ("If you do").
examples: Recall ("Each player recalls a unit and loses 2 life"): a player with no unit to recall still loses 2 life.
Shoreline Specter: if the recall is declined, the life drain that follows "If you do" does not happen.

rules.text: To cache a card is to put it into a player's cache. A unit cached from play goes to its controller's cache unless the effect names another, and its mods go to the bin.
examples: A stolen unit that is cached goes to the thief's cache.
Grob caches a stolen unit into its controller's cache, as its text says.

rules.text: Caching a card does not by itself let anyone use it. A cached card can be played or used as a mod only while a permission on it is live: a glimpse that cached it this turn, a fulfilled prophecy, or the text of the effect that cached it.
examples: Murkdrop Distiller caches a trashed card; its own text then lets its controller play it until end of turn.

rules.text: Glimpse N means: reveal the top N cards of the deck, cache one of them, and recycle the rest.
examples: Oracle of Foretelling's Glimpse 5 caches one of the five revealed cards.

rules.text: The player who glimpses chooses which of the revealed cards to cache.
examples: In a Glimpse 3, choosing the last revealed card caches it and recycles the two above it.

rules.text: Glimpse 1 reveals the top card of the deck and caches it. There is no choice to make and nothing to recycle.
"Glimpse 1, X times" is X separate glimpses of one card each, not one Glimpse X.
examples: Glook discards X cards when activated and then glimpses 1, X times.

rules.text: A glimpse reveals from the glimpser's own deck. When an effect makes another player glimpse ("Its controller Glimpses 3"), that player reveals from their own deck, not from the deck of the player who controls the effect. In live draft every player's deck is the one shared deck.
examples: Celestial Purge cast by one player erases an enemy unit; that unit's controller glimpses, chooses the card to cache and caches it in their own cache.
In constructed, a player who glimpses reveals the top of their own deck, caches from it and recycles the rest into their own pile; the other player's deck is untouched.

rules.text: Until end of turn, the glimpser may play the cached card as if it were in their hand, ignoring affinity.
examples: A card with affinity its glimpser cannot meet can be played from the cache, for its mana only.

rules.text: A card played under a glimpse permission still costs its mana, and still obeys its printed timing. Only the affinity requirement is waived.
examples: A glimpsed {Battle} card cannot be played in deployment.

rules.text: The same permission lets the glimpser apply the cached card as a mod, on the same terms (its mana, ignoring affinity): an augment or graft during deployment, and a {Virus} during battle.
examples: A glimpsed {Virus} in the cache goes onto an enemy unit in battle.

rules.text: While the permission is live, a glimpsed card with a prophecy banner may be prophesied where it stands in the cache, in the same window and for the same cost as from the hand. Doing so uses up the glimpse permission.
The permission ends at end of turn. The card stays in the cache, and it can no longer be played, prophesied or applied as a mod there.
examples: Premonition's permission dies with the turn; the card stays cached.

rules.text: To recycle a card is to put it on the bottom of the deck. A recycled card goes past the deck's mark into the recycle pile.
examples: Tides of the Cosmos recycles the revealed cards it did not play.

rules.text: When two units fight, each deals damage equal to its power to the other.
examples: The spell Battle makes two target units fight: each deals damage equal to its power to the other.

rules.text: Each fighting unit is the source of the damage it deals, with its own current attributes. Attributes the fight spell itself has do not apply to that damage.
examples: A fighter that gained {Powerful} deals double damage.
A {Powerful} virus on the Fight spell does not double either fighter's damage.

rules.text: Damage dealt in a fight is dealt by the units, not by the spell or ability that made them fight. Abilities that look for damage dealt by a spell effect do not see it.
examples: Squish's damage is dealt by the unit, so Ember of Life does not trigger; Fight and Battle work the same way.
Fight makes a 3-power unit deal 3 damage, and Ember of Life does not trigger; a spell dealing damage in the same setup does trigger it.

rules.text: A fight needs both of its units. If one of them is gone when the fight would happen, nothing happens: the remaining unit deals and is dealt no damage. The effect does not fizzle.
Rockfall N means: each player chooses one of their units, and the source of the rockfall deals N damage to each chosen unit.
examples: A Fast Pile of Rocks dies and rockfalls 4: each player picks one of their own units, and each takes exactly 4.

rules.text: Rockfall chooses; it does not target. No targets are declared when it goes on the stack, and an effect that stops targeting cannot stop it.
examples: Boon of Protection has nothing to negate when a Meteor Shower falls on its unit.

rules.text: Each player must choose a living unit of theirs in the region. A player with no unit there chooses none, and takes no part in that rockfall.

"Rockfall N, X times" is X rockfalls carried out one after another. Each player chooses again for each of them, and each rockfall is a separate source of damage. Abilities that trigger during one of the rockfalls wait until the whole effect has resolved: none is put on the stack between rockfalls.
examples: Meteor Shower rockfalls 3 three times: each player picks each time, and the damage stacks up.

rules.text: "Exchange" is printed in four senses, each read from its card: exchanging a unit in play for a unit card in a bin (Hooba-Mon, Necromorph), exchanging control of two units (Organic Exchange), exchanging control of a unit for a spell another player played (Hexbane Shiitake), and exchanging the base stats of two units (Body Swap).
examples: Hexbane Shiitake gives itself away and takes control of an enemy spell.

rules.text: When a unit in play is exchanged for a unit card in a bin, the unit leaving play despawns and goes to the bin, where it is trashed, but it does not die.
examples: Necromorph's exchange fires no death trigger, but the unit despawns and is trashed.
Hooba-Mon exchanging an unmodded host: the host goes to the bin and stays there.

rules.text: To prophesy a card is to pay the cost on its prophecy banner and put it into the cache with its prophecy attached. Prophecy itself is 803.

rules.title: General
rules.text: Attributes are qualities that a card or a token can have (see rule 204). An attribute applies whenever the card or token has it, in combat or not. Some attributes change how a unit engages in combat; others change the card in other ways (see rule 802.1b).
Cards with attributes carry reminder text, in italics, to help players remember what each attribute does.

Attributes are combat attributes or non-combat attributes. Combat attributes are printed in gold. Non-combat attributes, such as Burst and Unstable, are printed in purple and generally have nothing to do with combat.
Combat attributes are shared by the units in the same column of a formation: while a unit is in a column, it has every combat attribute that any unit in that column has.
examples: A token attacking in a column behind a Flying unit has Flying too.

rules.text: Attributes are not shared with the units to the left or right of a unit. They are shared only within its column.
examples: A unit attacking in the next column beside a Flying unit does not have Flying.

rules.text: A unit has the attributes of its column for everything it does while it is in the column, not only for combat damage. Damage it deals with its abilities has those attributes too.
examples: Lithoghul stands in a battle column with Flzzz, which is Blessed. An ability of Lithoghul deals 3 damage to an enemy unit: Lithoghul has Blessed from its column, so its controller gains 3 life.
Bellowing Boulder, in a column with a Deadly unit, pings with Deadly.

rules.text: Columns exist only during a battle. Outside a battle no unit is in a column, so no attribute is shared.
examples: Outside battle, a unit standing beside a Blessed unit gains nothing from it.

rules.text: When a unit leaves a column, the other units in that column immediately lose the attributes it was sharing with them.
examples: Once the Deadly unit leaves Bellowing Boulder's column, the Boulder's ping is not Deadly.

rules.text: Non-combat attributes are not shared in formation. A unit that is Unstable, or has Burst or Modular, does not give that attribute to the other units in its column.
examples: A modded (and so Unstable) unit does not make its column-mate Unstable.

rules.text: A card either has an attribute or does not. Having the same attribute from more than one source has no extra effect.
examples: Two sources granting Inverted to one unit invert its stat changes once, not twice.

rules.text: Four attributes change a unit's stats. Tough and Balanced apply in the fourth stat layer, Inverted in the fifth and Unaware in the sixth and last (see rule 206.4).
examples: A 1/4 with Tough, Balanced and Inverted is a -6/0.
A unit with both Inverted and Unaware is read at its printed stats: Unaware applies last.

rules.text: A unit's stats are worked out through all the stat layers before it is checked for death. A unit whose defense would be 0 or less part-way through the calculation, but not at the end of it, does not die.
examples: A 1/1 with a -1/-1 counter and Inverted is a live 2/2, never a dead 0/0.
Child of Aether, a 2/0 with Balanced, is a 2/2 and survives.

rules.text: When Tough and Balanced both apply to a unit, they apply one after the other, from top to bottom. If Tough is augmented onto a Balanced unit, or a Tough unit attacks with a Balanced unit behind it, the unit has its defense doubled, then its stats balanced. If Tough is applied to a Balanced unit, it has its stats balanced, then its defense doubled. Attributes granted by a unit's augments apply in the order the mods were gained, the first attached first, and attributes shared from its column apply from front to back. An attribute the unit has from more than one source takes the position of the first.
examples: A 3/1 augmented with Rampart Guardian (Tough) and then Child of Aether (Balanced) is a 3/3; augmented in the other order it is a 3/6.
Child of Aether prints Balanced and is a 2/0. Augmented with Rampart Guardian (Tough), its defense is doubled (still 2/0), then its stats balanced: it is a 2/2.
Rampart Guardian (0/4, Tough) attacks with Child of Aether (Balanced) behind it: its defense is doubled (0/8), then its stats balanced, and it is an 8/8.

rules.text: A Pure card, and every card interacting with it, ignores all its other attributes in that interaction (see rule 802.25). This includes the attributes that change stats: in an interaction with a Pure card, Tough, Balanced, Inverted and Unaware do not apply.
examples: Rampart Guardian (a 0/4 with Tough) is dealt 5 damage by a Pure source. In that interaction it ignores Tough, so its defense is 4 and it dies.
An Unaware source dealing 3 damage to a Pure unit pumped from 2/3 to 4/5 does not read it at its printed 2/3: it survives, where a pumped non-Pure 2/3 dies.

rules.title: Flying
rules.text: Flying is a combat attribute. Its reminder text reads "Only flying units can block flying units."
examples: A Flying 3/1 attacks; a ground unit may not block it, and a unit with Flying may.

rules.text: An attacking column that has Flying can't be blocked by a unit that does not have Flying.
examples: A ground 2/2 cannot block a column holding Ephemeral Skywalker (Flying).

rules.text: Because Flying is shared, a unit attacking in the same column as a Flying unit has Flying too, and the whole column can't be blocked by units that do not have Flying (see rule 802.1).
If the Flying unit leaves an attacking column before blockers are declared, the other units in that column lose Flying, and the column can then be blocked by units without Flying.
examples: Ephemeral Skywalker (Flying) attacks with a 1/1 token in one column; the Skywalker is destroyed before blocks, the token loses Flying, and Rune Channeler, which does not fly, blocks it.

rules.text: Flying does not restrict a block when the attacking column or the blocking unit includes a Pure card. A Pure unit can block a Flying column.
examples: Just a Unit (Pure, no Flying) blocks a column holding Ephemeral Skywalker (Flying) and kills it.

rules.text: A unit without Flying is not able to block a Flying column, so an Alluring trigger cannot compel it to block that column (see rules 606.2e and 802.15).
examples: A lured unit with no Flying, facing a Flying Alluring column, may leave that column unblocked.

rules.title: Deadly
rules.text: Deadly is a combat attribute. Its reminder text reads "Any damage from a deadly source will kill a unit."
examples: Tidepool Terror (1/2 Deadly) is blocked by a 5/9; its 1 damage kills the blocker.

rules.text: A unit dealt any nonzero amount of damage by a Deadly source is destroyed, whatever its defense. A Deadly source that deals 0 damage destroys nothing.
examples: A Deadly source dealing 2 noncombat damage destroys a 5/6.

rules.text: Deadly does not reduce the damage its source deals. A Deadly source deals all of its damage; Deadly changes only how much of it is lethal.
examples: A 10-power Deadly column blocked by a 1/1 deals all 10 to it.

rules.text: In combat damage assignment, lethal damage for each unit a Deadly half-column deals damage to is 1 (see rule 608.6e). Once the front unit has been assigned at least 1, the dealing player may assign damage to the unit behind it.
examples: A Deadly and Piercing column over two blockers assigns 1 to each, and the rest may go to the player.

rules.text: A unit dealt combat damage by a Deadly source is destroyed in the same damage sub-step, before the next sub-step begins (see rule 608.7b).
examples: Paired with a Swift unit in its column, a Deadly unit kills what it hits before that unit can strike back.

rules.text: Deadly applies to all damage its source deals, not only combat damage, including damage dealt through spells and abilities.
A spell or a spell token can have Deadly. Damage it deals is then Deadly damage.
examples: With Rotspore Herald in the region, a Fireball 1 kills any unit it hits.

rules.text: A source with both Deadly and Poisonous that deals damage to a unit both destroys it and puts the -1/-1 counters on it (see rule 112.10).
If all the damage a Deadly source would deal to a unit is prevented, no damage is dealt, and Deadly does not destroy the unit (see rule 112.11).
examples: A shielded blocker dealt combat damage by a Deadly column is not destroyed.

rules.text: Deadly has no effect on damage dealt to a player.
examples: An unblocked Carapace Devourer (3/3, Deadly) costs the defending player exactly 3 life.

rules.text: Deadly does not apply in an interaction with a Pure card (see rule 802.25).
examples: Just a Unit (Pure) blocking a Deadly unit is not killed by 1 damage.

rules.title: Swift
rules.text: Swift is a combat attribute. Its reminder text reads "Swift units deal combat damage first."
examples: Dune Drifter (2/1 Swift) is blocked by a 2/2; the blocker dies before it strikes, and the Drifter survives undamaged.

rules.text: A half-column that has Swift deals its combat damage in the Swift sub-step, before the normal and Sluggish sub-steps (see rule 608.2a).
A unit destroyed by Swift damage in the Swift sub-step deals no combat damage in the later sub-steps.
examples: A Swift attacker kills a 2/2 blocker, which never strikes back.

rules.text: A half-column with both Swift and Sluggish deals combat damage twice: once in the Swift sub-step and once in the Sluggish sub-step, with normal damage from other units in between (see rule 608.2c).
A half-column that has dealt combat damage in the Swift sub-step does not deal combat damage in the normal sub-step, even if it has since lost Swift (see rule 608.2e).

When a Swift half-column strikes and another half-column will strike in a later sub-step, the combat damage step is split: the abilities that triggered on the Swift damage go on the stack and resolve, with priority, before normal damage is dealt (see rules 608.3b and 608.9c).
examples: Dune Drifter (Swift) and Lithoghul attack in separate columns and are not blocked. The damage step splits once: Dune Drifter strikes, then there is a window to respond, then Lithoghul strikes. No Sluggish unit is in the battle, so there is no second split.
Flowstone Arcanite's counters from the Swift step land at the boundary, in time to save an ally.

rules.text: In an exchange involving a Pure card, Swift does not apply, so the exchange strikes in the normal sub-step (see rule 608.2d).
examples: Dune Drifter (2/1, Swift) is blocked by Just a Unit (2/3, Pure): both strike in the normal sub-step, and the Drifter dies.

rules.title: Sluggish
rules.text: Sluggish is a combat attribute. Its reminder text reads "Sluggish units deal combat damage last."
examples: Ambling Mountaintop (4/5 Sluggish) is blocked by a 5/4; the blocker strikes first and kills it, and is never struck.

rules.text: A half-column that has Sluggish deals its combat damage in the Sluggish sub-step, after the Swift and normal sub-steps (see rule 608.2a).
Because a Sluggish half-column strikes in a later sub-step of a split step, abilities that triggered on the earlier sub-steps' damage resolve before it deals its damage (see rule 608.9c).
examples: Adversary of the Deep (Sluggish) grows from the 6 life lost in the normal sub-step before it strikes, and deals 8.

rules.text: A half-column that has dealt combat damage in the normal sub-step does not deal combat damage in the Sluggish sub-step, even if it has since gained Sluggish. A half-column that dealt damage in the Swift sub-step and has gained Sluggish deals damage again in the Sluggish sub-step (see rule 608.2e).
In an exchange involving a Pure card, Sluggish does not apply, so the exchange strikes in the normal sub-step (see rule 608.2d).
examples: Ambling Mountaintop (4/5, Sluggish) is blocked by Just a Unit (2/3, Pure): both strike in the normal sub-step.

rules.title: Tough
rules.text: Tough is an attribute. A Tough unit's defense is doubled.
examples: Rampart Guardian (0/4, Tough) is a 0/8, and a unit it is augmented onto has its defense doubled.

rules.text: Tough doubles a unit's defense after counters and other +X/+X changes to it have been applied.
examples: Rampart Guardian (0/4, Tough) with a +1/+1 counter is a 1/10.
Rampart Guardian (0/4, Tough) with a -1/-1 counter has defense 6: the counter makes it 3, then Tough doubles it.

rules.text: Tough does not change a unit's power.
examples: A 0/4 Tough unit with a -1/-1 counter is a -1/6: its power is not doubled.

rules.text: If an effect doubles a Tough unit's defense, the defense the unit then has is double what it had. The doubling is a stat change applied before Tough doubles the result, so if the unit later loses Tough, that change stays and is no longer doubled.
examples: Burgeon on a 1/10 Tough unit makes it 1/20 (a +0/+5 under Tough); if Monke then takes its Tough, it is a 1/10.

rules.title: Balanced
rules.text: Balanced is an attribute. Its reminder text reads "The power and defense of balanced units are equal to the greater of the two."
examples: Child of Aether (2/0, Balanced) is a 2/2.

rules.text: Balanced compares the unit's power and defense after its counters and other stat changes, and after any attribute that applied before it, have been applied.
examples: A 1/4 with Tough and Balanced: Tough makes it 1/8, then Balanced makes it 8/8.
A 1/3 with two +1/+1 counters and Balanced is a 5/5.

rules.title: Inverted
rules.text: Inverted is an attribute. Its reminder text reads "Invert the stat changes of inverted units. For example, -1/+2 would become +1/-2."

Inverted inverts the net change to a unit's stats. An Inverted unit's power is its base power minus the net change to its power, and its defense is its base defense minus the net change to its defense. It is worked out on the total change, not on each change separately.
examples: Malformed Monstrosity (10/9) with its -7/-7, in a column with Reality Bender, is a 17/16.

rules.text: The changes Inverted inverts include those that Tough and Balanced make. Inverting Tough removes the defense Tough added; it does not halve the defense.
examples: A 1/4 with Tough and Balanced is an 8/8; with Inverted too it is a -6/0.

rules.text: Setting a unit's base stats is not a stat change that Inverted inverts: the new base stats are what Inverted inverts from.
examples: A unit made base 3/3 by Aberrant Statweaver, with no other changes, is a 3/3 whether or not it is Inverted.

rules.text: If a unit has both Tough and Inverted, its defense is minus twice the net change to its defense from base. So it has 0 or less defense, and dies, unless that net change is a reduction, in which case its defense is twice the reduction.
examples: A 1/4 with Tough and Inverted is a 1/0, in either grant order, and dies.
A 1/3 with one -1/-1 counter, Tough and Inverted survives as a 2/2.
Inverted on the front unit of a column and Tough on the back unit: both units have both attributes, and both die.

rules.title: Unaware
rules.text: Unaware is an attribute. An Unaware card, and every card interacting with it, ignores all stat changes: each is read at the stats printed on it.
examples: Bubb with two +1/+1 counters is still a 5/6. A 3/3 with four +1/+1 counters attacks into Bubb: it deals 3 and dies to 5.

rules.text: An Unaware card's own power and defense are always the ones printed on it, for every purpose, including whether it has died. Counters, temporary changes, continuous effects and the other stat attributes do not change them.
examples: A +1/+1 counter on Bubb (5/6, Unaware) leaves it a 5/6.
Bubb survives 100 -1/-1 counters.
Tough donated onto Bubb does nothing.
Reconfigure moves Bubb onto a Robot token, which gains Unaware: it ignores its own +1/+1 counters and dies as a 0/0.

rules.text: Setting a unit's base stats is a stat change too. An Unaware unit whose base stats an effect sets is still read at its printed stats.
examples: Aberrant Statweaver ("your units are base 3/3") leaves Bubb a 5/6.

rules.text: When an Unaware card deals damage or is dealt damage, every card in that interaction is read at its printed stats: the other card as well as the Unaware one.
examples: Unaware Bubb squishing a Robot 10 kills it: the Robot is read as its printed 0/0.
A Robot 10 squishing Unaware Bubb deals its printed defense, 0.
Two units fight: Bubb reads a Robot 7 as a 0/0 and kills it.

rules.text: In combat, the interaction is the exchange between an attacking half-column and the half-column blocking it. If a unit on either side is Unaware, every unit on both sides deals and is dealt combat damage at its printed stats.
examples: Bubb blocks a 3/3 pumped to 5/5 and takes 3, the attacker's printed power.

rules.text: A unit dealt damage in such an interaction is destroyed if the damage is lethal for its printed defense, even if the stats it has outside the interaction would let it survive.
examples: Bubb blocking a Robot token kills it, however many +1/+1 counters it has.
Haboob's 1 damage kills any unit with a printed defense of 1.

rules.text: Outside such an interaction, an Unaware card does not change the stats of the other cards.
A spell can be Unaware. A spell has no stats of its own, so its Unaware only makes the cards it deals damage to be read at their printed stats.
examples: Haboob (an Unaware spell) deals 1 damage to each unit and kills every unit with a printed defense of 1.

rules.text: Unaware does not stop a card being targeted. An effect can put counters or other stat changes on an Unaware card; they stay on it but do not change its stats while it is Unaware.
examples: Poison with X = 6, targeting Bubb (a 5/6, Unaware), puts six -1/-1 counters on it; Bubb is still a 5/6.
A Robot 10 may Squish Unaware Bubb, targeting Bubb. The Robot, interacting with Unaware Bubb, is read at its printed 0/0, so it deals 0 and Bubb takes no harm.

rules.title: Powerful
rules.text: Powerful is a combat attribute. Its reminder text reads "Powerful sources deal double damage".
examples: When Chitin Shredder (1/2, Powerful) is the source of 3 damage from an effect, 6 is dealt; attacking unblocked, it costs the defending player 2 life.

rules.text: A Powerful half-column's combat damage is doubled once, as a whole, before it is divided among its recipients, whether they are units or a player. A unit without Powerful in a Powerful column has its damage doubled along with the rest (see rule 608.5b).
examples: Chitin Shredder (Powerful) deals double combat damage to a player.
A vanilla unit in front of Chitin Shredder has its damage doubled too.

rules.text: If a modifier that adds to the damage also applies, the addition is made first and Powerful doubles the result (see rule 112.9).
examples: A Powerful Bellowing Boulder's 1 damage with Conduit of Pain is (1+1)x2 = 4 to each unit.

rules.text: Powerful also doubles damage its source deals through spells and abilities, to units and players alike.
A spell can have Powerful. Damage a Powerful spell deals is doubled.
examples: With Emberflame Enlightener in its region, a player's spell deals double damage.

rules.text: When a spell makes a unit deal damage, as Squish, Fight and Battle do, the unit is the source: the unit's own Powerful, including Powerful it shares from its column, applies, and Powerful on the spell does not (see rule 112.6).
examples: Squish makes a Powerful ally deal double its defense.
A Powerful Squish does not double.
Squish on a 1/3 that shares Powerful from Chitin Shredder in its column deals 6.

rules.text: Powerful does not apply in an interaction with a Pure card (see rule 802.25).

rules.title: Vulnerable
rules.text: Vulnerable is an attribute. A Vulnerable unit is dealt double the damage that would be dealt to it.
examples: Crumbling Ancient (Vulnerable) is dealt double the combat damage assigned to it.

rules.text: Because the damage is doubled when it is dealt, lethal damage for a Vulnerable unit, when assigning, is half its remaining defense, rounded up (see rule 608.6e).
examples: Arc Lightning (6 damage, Electric) on a Vulnerable 3/8: 4 of the 6 destroy it, and the other 2 may jump on.
A 10-power Piercing column blocked by a Vulnerable 3/7 assigns it 4 (half of 7, rounded up), and 6 go through.
A Vulnerable 3/8 with 2 damage marked needs 3, so a 10-power Piercing column sends 7 through.

rules.text: Damage assigned to a Vulnerable unit counts as that much of the source's damage; the unit is then dealt double that amount. Any damage the source keeps on a Vulnerable unit, including the rest of a column's damage, is doubled on that unit.
examples: A Piercing attacker may put all 10 of its damage into a lone Vulnerable 3/8, which is dealt 20.

rules.text: Piercing excess past a Vulnerable unit is measured in the source's damage before the doubling: only the source damage beyond what the unit needs is excess (see rule 802.16).
examples: A 10-power Piercing column blocked by a Vulnerable 3/8 assigns 4 to it, and 6 goes to the player.

rules.text: If a Powerful source deals damage to a Vulnerable unit, both apply: the source's damage is doubled, and the unit is dealt double that.
A Pure Vulnerable unit, and a Vulnerable unit in an interaction with a Pure card, is not dealt double damage.
examples: Chitin Shredder (Powerful), made Pure, deals 2 damage to Crumbling Ancient (Vulnerable, 3/8). It is dealt 2: neither Powerful nor Vulnerable doubles it, and the Ancient survives.
Crumbling Ancient (Vulnerable) made Pure is dealt 2 by a 2-damage effect, not 4.

rules.title: Feeble
rules.text: Feeble is an attribute. A Feeble unit can't block.
examples: Spectrogenesis creates three Wisps (Feeble); none of them can block.

rules.text: Whether a unit can block depends on its own Feeble only. A Feeble unit can't block even if it shares a column with units that are not Feeble, and Feeble that a unit would share from its column does not stop it blocking.
A Pure unit that is Feeble can block: Pure makes it ignore its own Feeble (see rule 802.25).
examples: Just a Unit (Pure) granted Feeble can still be declared as a blocker.

rules.text: A Feeble unit is not able to block, so an Alluring trigger that targets it cannot compel it to block (see rules 606.2e and 802.15).

rules.title: Evasive
rules.text: Evasive is an attribute. Its reminder text, printed under the type line, reads "Evasive units require two blockers."
A column with Evasive cannot be blocked by a single unit. To block it, the defending player must place two units in front of it.
examples: An Evasive Curio Drifter attacks. The defender may block it with two units placed in front of it, one behind the other, but not with one.

rules.text: Evasive does not apply if either the Evasive column or the units blocking it include a Pure card. A single Pure unit can block an Evasive column on its own (see rule 802.25).
examples: Just a Unit (Pure) blocks an Evasive column by itself.

rules.title: Sneaky
rules.text: Sneaky is an attribute. Its reminder text, printed under the type line, reads "Sneaky units can't be blocked if attacking alone."
An attacking column with Sneaky cannot be blocked if its unit is the only attacking unit in the attacking formation.
examples: Whispering Mantid attacks alone and cannot be blocked. Attacking with another unit, it can be.

rules.text: Spell tokens that go with an attack do not count as attacking units for Sneaky. A Sneaky unit attacking with only spell tokens beside it is attacking alone.
examples: A Sneaky unit attacks together with two Fireball spell tokens. It is still attacking alone and cannot be blocked.

rules.text: Two Sneaky units attacking together are not alone. Both can be blocked.
examples: Two Whispering Mantids attack in different columns. The defender may block either or both.

rules.text: A side-block does not block a lone Sneaky attacker. The defending player may side-block beside it, and it stays unblocked (see rule 606.4e).
A Pure unit ignores Sneaky, so it can block a lone Sneaky attacker (see rule 802.25).
examples: A lone Sneaky unit attacks. The defender can block it with Just a Unit (Pure), and with no other unit.

rules.title: Alluring
rules.text: Alluring is an attribute. Its reminder text, printed under the type line, reads "When an alluring column attacks, target enemy can't attack and must block it this combat if able."

When an attacking column with Alluring is declared, Alluring triggers. The trigger goes on the stack and targets one enemy unit, chosen by the attacking player from the enemy units in the battle region as the trigger is put on the stack.
examples: Two attacking columns, one Alluring, against one possible blocker: the Alluring trigger targets that blocker, which then must block the Alluring column.

rules.text: Alluring does not stack. An attacking column with Alluring has one Alluring trigger, however many of its units have Alluring.
examples: Two Alluring units attack in one column. Alluring triggers once.

rules.text: Each attacking column with Alluring has its own trigger. Two Alluring columns make two triggers, which may target the same unit or different units.
examples: Two Alluring columns attack. Each triggers, and both triggers may target the same defending unit.
Two Alluring columns target two different units. Each of those units must block its column.

rules.text: Alluring is shared by the units of its column, but the column's Alluring trigger comes from the unit that has Alluring itself, not from the units it is shared with.
examples: Tempest Wrangler attacks in a column with a vanilla unit. The trigger is Tempest Wrangler's.

rules.text: When the Alluring trigger resolves, its target cannot attack: it cannot be declared as an attacker or sent to counterattack for the rest of the battle phase (see rule 604.2e).
examples: A lured unit cannot be sent out to counterattack when blocks are declared.

rules.text: When the Alluring trigger resolves, its target must block the Alluring column in that battle round if it is able to. If the column is blocked at all, the target must be one of its blockers (see rule 606.2e).
examples: The defender has two units able to block and tries to leave the Alluring column unblocked by putting both on other columns. That is not allowed: the lured unit must block the Alluring column.

rules.text: Whether the target is able to block the Alluring column depends only on that unit and that column. If the target could not block the column by itself (because the column is Evasive and needs two blockers, the target is Feeble, the column has Flying and the target does not, or the column is a lone Sneaky attacker), the defending player may leave the column unblocked, and the target may block another column.
examples: A lone lured unit cannot block an Alluring and Evasive column by itself, so it need not block it, and it may block another column.

rules.text: An Alluring and Evasive column can be blocked only by two units, one of which is the target. The defending player chooses between blocking it with the target and one other unit, and not blocking it at all; blocking it with two other units is not allowed.
examples: The target is A and the defender also has B and C. A+B and A+C may block the column; B+C may not.
The defender has only A and B. They block the column with A+B, or leave it unblocked.

rules.text: If, when the Alluring trigger would resolve, the unit with Alluring is no longer in an attacking column, or its column no longer has Alluring, the trigger does nothing.
examples: The attacker's Alluring unit is killed while its trigger is on the stack. The trigger does nothing, and the targeted unit may attack and block freely.

rules.text: Once the Alluring trigger has resolved, removing the unit with Alluring does not undo it: its target still cannot attack. If the Alluring column ceases to exist, the duty to block it ends with it.
examples: After the trigger resolves, the Alluring attacker is killed in the attack window. The lured unit may block another column, but it still cannot be sent to counterattack.

rules.text: If two Alluring triggers have targeted the same unit, it cannot block both columns. Blocking either of those columns with it satisfies both triggers, and the other column may then be blocked by other units or left unblocked.
examples: Two Alluring columns both target unit A. A blocks the first column. The second column may be blocked by B alone, or left unblocked.

rules.text: An Alluring trigger from a lone Sneaky attacker compels no unit, because no unit is able to block that attacker (see rule 802.14), unless its target is Pure.
examples: A lone Sneaky and Alluring unit attacks. The defender declares no blocks, and that is legal.

rules.text: An Alluring column that contains a Pure card does not trigger at all (see rule 802.25).
examples: An Alluring column with Just a Unit in it attacks. No Alluring trigger is put on the stack.

rules.text: A Pure unit ignores the attributes that would stop it blocking, so a Pure target is able to block any Alluring column: it must block even a Flying Alluring column, and it satisfies an Evasive Alluring column by itself.
examples: A lured Pure unit must block a Flying Alluring column.
A lured Pure unit blocks an Evasive Alluring column alone.

rules.text: The Alluring trigger is a triggered ability. It can be negated while it is on the stack, and an effect that makes triggered abilities cost more to trigger (Crevice Lurker) applies to it: if that cost is not paid, the trigger does not happen.
examples: Crevice Lurker is in play. The attacker declines to pay for the Alluring trigger, and nothing is lured.
Containment Protocol negates a waiting Alluring trigger.

rules.title: Piercing
rules.text: Piercing is an attribute. Its reminder text reads "Excess damage from piercing sources is dealt to the recipient's controller."

Excess damage, for Piercing, is the damage a source deals to a unit beyond that unit's lethal damage. A unit's lethal damage is worked out after Powerful has doubled the source's damage; it is reduced for a Vulnerable unit, which is dealt double what reaches it; it is 1 if the source has Deadly; and damage already dealt to the unit counts towards it, including damage dealt to it earlier by the same effect (see rule 608.6e).
examples: A Powerful Piercing source deals 3 to a 1/1. The 3 is doubled to 6; 1 is lethal; 5 is excess.
A 10-power Piercing column is blocked by a Vulnerable 3/8. Lethal damage is 4, which is dealt as 8; the other 6 is excess.
One effect names the same unit twice with Piercing. The unit is given its lethal damage once, and the rest of both hits is excess.

rules.text: A half-column with Piercing that deals combat damage to the units of the opposing half-column must assign lethal damage to each of those units, front to back. Any of its damage that is not assigned to a unit is dealt to the player who controls those units.
examples: A Piercing column with 10 power is blocked by a 1/2 in front of a 1/3. It must assign 2 to the front unit and 3 to the back unit; the other 5 may be dealt to the defending player.

rules.text: Excess is elective. After each unit has been assigned its lethal damage, the dealing player may assign any part of the remaining damage to those units, including all of it, and only the damage no unit is assigned is dealt to the player.
examples: A 10-power Piercing attacker is blocked by a lone Vulnerable 3/8. The attacker may put all 10 into it (dealt as 20), and none reaches the player.

rules.text: An unblocked attacking half-column with Piercing deals its combat damage to the defending player, as any unblocked half-column does.

If an attacking half-column with Piercing is blocked but no blocking unit is left in front of it when it strikes, all of its damage is excess and is dealt to the defending player. A blocked half-column without Piercing deals no damage in that case (see rule 608.4c).
examples: A Piercing column's only blocker dies before damage. The column is still blocked, and its full power is dealt to the defending player.
The same position without Piercing deals nothing to the player.

rules.text: A blocking half-column with Piercing deals excess combat damage to the attacking player only if there is an attacking unit in front of it when it strikes. If no attacking unit is in front of it (its attackers are all gone, or it is a side-block), it deals no combat damage at all (see rules 608.4e and 608.4f).
examples: A Piercing side-blocker deals no combat damage to the attacking player.

rules.text: If the Piercing source also has Deadly, lethal damage is 1 for each unit, so all damage beyond 1 for each unit may be excess.
examples: A Deadly and Piercing column is blocked by two units. It assigns 1 to each, and the rest may go to the player.
A 10-power Deadly and Piercing column is blocked by one unit: 1 kills it and the other 9 may pierce.

rules.text: Damage prevention on a unit does not change how much must be assigned to it before there is excess. Excess is worked out as though the unit were unprotected.
examples: A Piercing column is blocked by a shielded 0/5 in front of a 5/6. It must assign 5 to the shielded unit and 6 to the unit behind; the rest may go to the player.

rules.text: Piercing excess is dealt as part of the same damage as the rest, at the same time. It is not a triggered ability, and no player can act between the damage dealt to the units and the excess dealt to the player.
examples: A Piercing effect deals 5 to a 1/1. The unit's 1 and the 4 to its controller are dealt together, with nothing on the stack in between.

rules.text: Piercing applies to noncombat damage too. A Piercing source that deals noncombat damage to a unit must deal that unit its lethal damage first. The dealing player may then keep any of the excess on that unit; the rest of the excess is dealt to that unit's controller.
examples: Squish makes Bubb, in a column with Good Whale (Piercing), deal 6 to a 1/1. The dealing player may keep all 6 on the 1/1, or send up to 5 to its controller.

rules.text: For noncombat damage, the dealing player is the controller of the source unit, even if another player controls the spell that made it deal damage (for Squish, Fight and Battle the unit is the source; see rule 112.6). If the source is not a unit in play (a spell, or a unit that has left play), the controller of the effect decides.
examples: A Battle makes an opponent's Piercing unit fight. The opponent, who controls that unit, places its excess.

rules.text: Each unit's excess is dealt to that unit's controller. If one effect deals Piercing damage to units controlled by different players, each player is dealt the excess from their own units.
A unit in a column with a Piercing unit has Piercing while that column exists, for the noncombat damage it deals as well as for combat damage (see rule 802.1).
examples: Bubb, in a column with Good Whale, squishes with Piercing: the excess reaches the player.

rules.text: If Piercing combat damage that would be dealt to a player is dealt to a unit instead (as Oorblak's ability does), that unit is dealt its lethal damage and the rest is still Piercing excess. That excess is dealt to the player, and it is not redirected again (see rule 608.8c).
examples: 10 Piercing combat damage is redirected into a 2/4 Oorblak. 4 kill it and the other 6 reach the player.
5 Piercing combat damage is redirected into Oorblak on a 1/1 host. 1 kills the host and the remaining 4 reach the player.

rules.text: If a source has both Electric and Piercing, excess that reaches a unit with no further unit to jump to is Piercing excess: the dealing player may keep any of it on that unit, and the rest is dealt to that unit's controller (see rule 802.17).
examples: A 6-damage Electric and Piercing hit lands on a lone 1/2 with no neighbour. The dealing player chooses how much of the 4 excess stays on it; the rest goes to its controller.

rules.text: Piercing does not apply in an interaction involving a Pure card (see rule 802.25).
examples: A 6-power Piercing column is blocked by Just a Unit (Pure). All 6 are dealt to Just a Unit; none reaches the defending player.

rules.title: Electric
rules.text: Electric is an attribute. Its reminder text reads "Excess damage from electric sources can be directed to an adjacent unit, recursively."

When an Electric source deals a unit more than its lethal damage, the excess may be dealt to a unit adjacent to that unit instead. The unit the excess jumps to is dealt the lethal damage it needs, and any excess beyond that may jump again, to a unit adjacent to it.
examples: Arc Lightning (6, Electric) hits a Vulnerable 3/8. 4 kill it (dealt as 8), and the other 2 may jump to an adjacent unit.

rules.text: The excess never jumps to a unit it has already been dealt to in that chain.
The Electric source's controller chooses where the excess goes at each jump.

Each jump is optional. At any jump, the source's controller may instead keep all the remaining excess on the unit it has reached; it is then all dealt to that unit and goes no further. This is so even when there is only one unit to jump to.
examples: Arc Lightning hits a Vulnerable 3/8 with a unit beside it. Its controller keeps all 6 on the 3/8 (dealt as 12), and nothing jumps.

rules.text: Excess that has no unit to jump to is dealt to the last unit it reached; it is not lost. If the source also has Piercing, that excess is Piercing excess instead (see rule 802.16).
examples: Arc Lightning hits a lone Vulnerable 3/8 with nothing beside it. All 6 land on it, dealt as 12.

rules.text: Adjacency for Electric is adjacency in a formation (see rule 603.2). A unit that is not in a formation has no adjacent unit, so Electric excess dealt to it has nowhere to jump.
examples: During the deployment phase no unit is in a formation, so an Electric spell's excess stays on the unit it hit.

rules.text: The whole Electric chain is part of one damage event. No formation changes happen while the excess is distributed.
examples: An Electric chain of three units is dealt in one damage event; the units it kills die together afterwards.

rules.text: Lethal damage along the chain is worked out as it is for Piercing (see rule 802.16): a Vulnerable unit needs only half, and damage already dealt to it by the same effect counts.
Envoy of Lightning makes "your spell effects with a single target" Electric. A spell effect has a single target if it was cast with exactly one target.
examples: Twin Flame cast with one target under Envoy of Lightning is Electric.

rules.text: A spell effect cast with two targets does not have a single target, even if one of its targets has become illegal by the time it resolves.
examples: Twin Flame is cast with two targets and one is removed. It is not Electric under Envoy of Lightning.

rules.title: Poisonous
rules.text: Poisonous is an attribute. Its reminder text reads "Poisonous sources damage units in the form of -1/-1 counters."
Damage a Poisonous source deals to a unit is put on that unit as that many -1/-1 counters instead of being marked on it.
examples: Noxious Sporefiend deals 2 combat damage to a unit; the unit gets two -1/-1 counters and no marked damage.

rules.text: Poisonous damage is damage dealt. Abilities that trigger when a unit is dealt damage trigger on it (see rule 112.10).
For damage assignment and for Piercing, a unit's lethal damage is the same whether the source is Poisonous or not.
examples: A Poisonous and Piercing effect deals 5 to a 1/1. One counter is lethal, and the other 4 may pierce.

rules.text: A source with both Deadly and Poisonous destroys the unit it damages and also puts the -1/-1 counters on it.
examples: Deadly and Poisonous damage kills the unit, and the -1/-1 counter lands on it before it dies.

rules.text: Powerful doubles a Poisonous source's damage, and so doubles the -1/-1 counters it puts on a unit.
examples: A Powerful Poisonous effect hit of 2 becomes 4 counters and kills a 4/3.

rules.text: If a Poisonous source's damage to a unit is prevented, no damage is dealt and no -1/-1 counters are put on it.
examples: Sporebloom Siren (2/2, Poisonous) attacks; the defender casts Phytochemical Protection on Jollyglop and blocks with it. The 2 damage is prevented: Jollyglop gets no -1/-1 counters and makes no 1/1s, and Phytochemical Protection puts two +1/+1 counters on it.

rules.text: Poisonous changes only damage dealt to units. Damage a Poisonous source deals to a player is ordinary damage.
examples: An unblocked Poisonous column with 3 power makes the defending player lose 3 life.

rules.text: Poisonous damage triggers Resonant like any other damage (see rule 802.19).
examples: A Poisonous and Resonant source deals 2 to a unit. The unit gets two -1/-1 counters, and the Resonant trigger deals 2 to its controller.

rules.text: Poisonous does not apply in an interaction involving a Pure card (see rule 802.25).
examples: A Poisonous column is blocked by Just a Unit. Just a Unit is dealt ordinary marked damage, not -1/-1 counters.

rules.title: Resonant
rules.text: Resonant is an attribute. Its reminder text, printed under the type line, reads "Whenever a resonant source deals damage to a unit, it deals that much damage to that unit's controller."
examples: Resonant Form's combat damage to a unit also hits that unit's controller.

rules.text: Resonant is a triggered ability of the Resonant source. When the source deals damage to a unit, the trigger goes on the stack, and when it resolves the source deals that much damage to that unit's controller.
examples: The Resonant trigger from combat damage waits on the stack after combat, as its source's trigger, and can be negated.
A Resonant effect deals 1 to a unit; the trigger then deals 1 to its controller as damage from the source.

rules.text: The damage Resonant deals to the controller is not combat damage, even when the damage that triggered it was (see rule 608.8b).
examples: Oorblak, which takes combat damage that would be dealt to its controller, does not take Resonant's extra damage; the player does.

rules.text: "That much damage" is the damage the unit was dealt: after Vulnerable doubled it and after any prevention. If all of the damage to the unit is prevented, Resonant does not trigger.
examples: A Resonant source deals 2 to a Vulnerable unit, which is dealt 4. The Resonant trigger deals 4 to that unit's controller.

rules.text: Resonant's damage is damage from the Resonant source, so everything that changes that source's damage applies to it: an allied Conduit of Pain adds 1 to it, and Powerful doubles it, even though the damage that triggered it was already doubled.
examples: A Powerful Resonant 2/4 deals 4 combat damage to a unit, and then 8 to that unit's controller.
With Conduit of Pain, a Resonant 2/4 deals 2 combat damage to a unit and then 3 to its controller.

rules.text: When both apply to Resonant's damage, an added amount (Conduit of Pain's 1) is added before Powerful doubles (see rule 112.9).
examples: A Powerful Resonant 2/4 with Conduit of Pain deals 4 combat damage, then (4+1)x2 = 10 to the controller.

rules.text: Resonant triggers for each unit the source deals damage to. An effect that damages several units makes one Resonant trigger for each damaged unit.
examples: A Resonant, Powerful Bellowing Boulder with Conduit of Pain deals 4 to each unit, then 10 to a controller for each damaged unit.

rules.text: Resonant triggers only on damage dealt to a unit. Damage a Resonant source deals to a player does not trigger it.
examples: An unblocked Resonant column deals 3 combat damage to the defending player. Resonant does not trigger.

rules.text: Because Resonant is a triggered ability, an effect that makes triggered abilities cost more to trigger (Crevice Lurker) applies to it, and if that cost is not paid the trigger does not happen. It can be negated while it is on the stack.
A Resonant trigger caused by combat damage is put on the stack and resolved as other triggers caused by combat damage are (see rules 608 and 609).
If the Resonant source has left play by the time its trigger resolves, the trigger still deals its damage, reading the source as it last was in play.
examples: A Powerful Resonant unit deals 1 to a unit, which is dealt 2, and then leaves play with its Resonant trigger waiting. The trigger still deals double damage, 4, because the unit was Powerful when it left play.

rules.text: Resonant does not apply in an interaction involving a Pure card (see rule 802.25).
examples: A Resonant column is blocked by Just a Unit. No Resonant trigger happens for the damage dealt to Just a Unit.

rules.title: Thieving
rules.text: Thieving is an attribute. Its reminder text, printed under the type line, reads "Whenever a thieving source deals combat damage to an opponent, draw a card."
When a column with Thieving deals combat damage to an opponent, the column's controller draws a card.
examples: Slink attacks unblocked and deals combat damage to the defending player. Its controller draws a card.

rules.text: The column is the source of the combat damage, so a Thieving column draws one card each time it deals combat damage to an opponent, however many Thieving units it holds and however much damage it deals.
examples: Two Thieving units in one column deal combat damage to a player. Their controller draws one card.

rules.text: Piercing excess counts: a blocked Thieving column whose Piercing excess is dealt to the opponent draws a card.
examples: A Thieving and Piercing column is blocked by a 1/1 and deals 3 of excess to the defending player. Its controller draws a card.

rules.text: If combat damage a Thieving column deals to an opponent is replaced (for example, by Blightsea Polyp, which deals it as rot), the damage was still dealt, and the column's controller still draws a card (see rule 608.8a).
examples: Blightsea Polyp turns a Thieving column's combat damage to the defending player into 1 rot. The attacker still draws a card.

rules.text: Thieving applies only to combat damage. Noncombat damage a Thieving source deals to an opponent does not draw a card.
examples: A Thieving unit deals 2 noncombat damage to an opponent. No card is drawn.

rules.title: Reaping
rules.text: Reaping is an attribute. Its reminder text, printed under the type line, reads "When a reaping source kills one or more units, draw a card. It loses reaping until regroup."
When a Reaping source kills one or more units, its controller draws one card, however many units it killed.
examples: Flame of History kills a unit and its controller draws a card.
Seismomancy kills a unit by damage and draws exactly once.

rules.text: A unit counts as killed by a Reaping source however the source killed it: by damage, by -1/-1 counters, by changing its stats, or by destroying it outright.
examples: Invasive Reassignment swaps a 0/4 into a 4/0, which dies. Reaping draws a card.
Noxious Demise kills a 1/1 with a -1/-1 counter. Reaping draws a card.

rules.text: After a Reaping source's kill has drawn a card, the source loses Reaping until regroup.
examples: If a unit had Reaping and killed a blocker in the first battle round, it would draw a card and then have no Reaping in the second round.

rules.title: Blessed
rules.text: Blessed is an attribute. Its reminder text reads "Damage dealt by a blessed source causes its controller to gain that much life."
examples: Godray deals 3 damage to any target, and Blessed gains its controller 3.

rules.text: When a Blessed source deals damage, its controller gains that much life. This applies to combat and noncombat damage, and to damage dealt to units and to players.
The life is gained at the same time as the damage is dealt. It is not a triggered ability and does not use the stack, and it is gained before it is checked whether any player has reached 0 life.
examples: A player at low life is dealt lethal damage by an opponent at the same moment their own Blessed source deals damage. They gain the life first, and survive if it is enough.

rules.text: A Blessed source cannot kill its own controller with its own damage: damage it deals to its own controller is matched by the life that player gains at the same time.
examples: Godray aimed at a player damages them and heals its controller on the same check.

rules.text: Blessed applies only to damage dealt. A kill without damage, and damage that is prevented, gain no life.
examples: Noxious Demise carrying a Blessed Thing virus kills a unit with a -1/-1 counter. No life is gained.

rules.text: A unit in a column with a Blessed unit has Blessed while that column exists, so damage its abilities deal gains its controller life too (see rule 802.1).
examples: Lithoghul attacks in a column with Flzzz (Blessed) and uses an ability to deal 3 damage. Lithoghul has Blessed from its column, so its controller gains 3 life.

rules.text: Blessed does not apply in an interaction involving a Pure card (see rule 802.25).

rules.title: Afflicting
rules.text: Afflicting is an attribute. Its reminder text reads "When an afflicting source kills one or more units, those units' controllers gain a rot."
