When an Afflicting source kills one or more units, each player who controlled one of those units gains one rot.
examples: Umbral Decay kills a unit with its counters. That unit's controller gains a rot.
Umbral Decay's target survives, shrunk. Nobody gains a rot.

rules.text: A player gains one rot for each kill, however many of their units the source killed at once.
examples: An Afflicting source kills two units of one player at once. That player gains one rot.

rules.text: A unit counts as killed by an Afflicting source however the source killed it: by damage, by -1/-1 counters, by changing its stats, or by destroying it outright.
examples: Umbral Decay's counter kill gives a rot and draws nothing.

rules.text: Afflicting applies to kills by combat damage as well. An Afflicting column that kills units in combat gives their controllers rot.
Afflicting does not apply in an interaction involving a Pure card (see rule 802.25).
examples: An Afflicting column kills Just a Unit (Pure) in combat. Its controller gains no rot.

rules.title: Lethal
rules.text: Lethal is an attribute. Its reminder text reads "Any combat damage from a lethal unit will kill a player."
If a column with Lethal deals any combat damage to a player, however little, that player is killed (see rule 104).
examples: Gublin (1/4) attacks unblocked and deals 1 combat damage to the defending player, who is killed.

rules.text: Lethal applies only to combat damage dealt to a player. It does not change noncombat damage, or damage dealt to units.
examples: A Lethal unit blocked by a 2/2 kills it as any unit would; Lethal does nothing to the blocker.

rules.text: If a Lethal column's combat damage to a player is replaced (for example, by Blightsea Polyp, which deals it as rot), the damage was still dealt, so the player is still killed.
examples: Blightsea Polyp turns a Lethal column's combat damage into 1 rot. The player is still killed.

rules.text: [Removed: no source states how Lethal meets prevention of damage to a player, and no card in the pool prevents damage to a player; R98's prevention ruling is about damage to units. See D-U20-22.]

rules.title: Pure
rules.text: Pure is an attribute. Its reminder text reads "Pure cards and cards they are interacting with ignore all other attributes."
A Pure card ignores its own other attributes too.
examples: An Alluring column that is itself Pure ignores its own Alluring and never triggers.
A Pure unit that is also Feeble can block.

rules.text: In combat, an interaction is one attacking half-column and the blocking half-column paired with it. If either contains a Pure card, the attributes of both are ignored for that exchange.

In a combat exchange involving a Pure card, neither side has Piercing, Deadly, Powerful, Poisonous, Resonant, Blessed, Afflicting or Thieving, and a Vulnerable unit in it is not dealt double. Neither side has Swift or Sluggish, so both strike in the normal sub-step (see rule 608.2d).
examples: Just a Unit switches off a Deadly attacker's Deadly.
A printed Swift column blocked by a Pure unit strikes in the normal sub-step.

rules.text: When blocks are declared, a Pure card in either the attacking column or the units blocking it switches off Flying, Evasive and the lone Sneaky attacker's protection for that column, and a Pure unit's own Feeble does not stop it blocking.
examples: Just a Unit can block a Flying column, and only it can among the defender's units.
Just a Unit blocks an Evasive column alone.

rules.text: Pure does not change a unit's printed stats: a Pure 2/3 is destroyed by 3 damage. But Tough, Balanced and Inverted are attributes, so in an interaction involving a Pure card they do not apply (rule 802.1n).
examples: A Tough 0/4 blocks a column containing Just a Unit (Pure). Tough does not apply in that exchange, so the blocker has 4 defense, not 8.

rules.text: Unaware is an attribute, so in combat it does not apply in an exchange involving a Pure card: the units in that exchange are read at their current stats, not their printed ones (rule 802.1n).
examples: Bubb (Unaware) blocks a column containing Just a Unit (Pure) that has a +1/+1 counter. Unaware does not apply in that exchange, so the counter counts.

rules.text: Outside combat, an interaction is one effect and one recipient of its damage. Pure applies to each such pairing separately.
A Pure source deals plain damage to every recipient: its own Powerful, Deadly, Piercing, Electric, Poisonous, Resonant, Blessed and Unaware do not apply, against units or players.
A Pure recipient is dealt plain damage by any source: the source's attributes do not apply to it, and neither do its own Vulnerable and Unaware.
A recipient that is not Pure, damaged by the same effect as a Pure recipient, is dealt damage with all attributes applying.
examples: A Powerful source deals 1 to Just a Unit and 1 to Bubb in one resolution: 1 to the first and 2 to the second.

rules.text: During a battle, a unit in a column with a Pure unit has Pure for noncombat damage too, as a source and as a recipient (see rule 802.1).
examples: A unit stands in a column with Just a Unit. A Powerful spell deals 1 damage to it: it is dealt 1, not 2.

rules.text: Pure does not change what can be targeted.
examples: Arc Lightning, which says "any target", can target Just a Unit like any other unit.

rules.title: Modular
rules.text: Modular is an attribute. Its reminder text reads "You can apply mods to a modular card from your hand and/or bin as it is played. You still pay their costs."
As a Modular card is played, its controller may apply mods to it from their hand and from their bin, paying each mod's cost. The mods go onto the stack with the card (see rule 702.3b).
Any card in the player's hand or bin whose cost they can pay may be applied to a Modular card, including a card that will do nothing as a mod there. No other condition restricts what may be applied.
Applying a mod to a Modular card is not playing that mod (see rule 701.2).
A graft mod applied to a Modular spell adds its graft effect to the spell as an extra part, and the spell and its grafted effects resolve as one.
A mod whose type line grants attributes as an augment gives those attributes to the Modular spell's effect.
examples: A Powerful mod applied to Spellbind carrying Twin Flame turns its 2 damage into 4.

rules.text: An augment mod's text-box ability does nothing on a Modular spell: a spell cannot gain static or triggered abilities that way.

A Modular card with a mod applied is modded, so it is Unstable: when it leaves the stack, whether it resolved, failed to resolve or was negated, it and its mods are erased instead of going to a bin. An unmodded Modular card goes to the bin as usual.
examples: A graft card in the bin is applied to Spellbind, resolves with it, and is erased, so it cannot be applied this way again.

rules.text: Modular is not shared with the other units of a column.

Some keywords are not combat attributes. Burst and Unstable are printed in purple text and are called non-combat attributes: they describe a card, and generally have nothing to do with combat. The other keywords in this section (Haste, Battle, [once], Ambush and Prophecy) are timing marks, limits and ways to play a card.
examples: A modded Chitin Shredder attacks in a column with a vanilla unit: the vanilla unit shares its Powerful, but it does not become Unstable.

rules.text: Non-combat attributes are not shared in formation. A unit with Burst or Unstable does not give it to the other units in its column.
examples: A modded unit is Unstable; a unit in the same column is not, and when it dies it goes to the bin.

rules.text: Haste is a timing keyword. A card with Haste can be played during the haste step as well as during deployment.
examples: Tidal Menace, a {Haste} 7/2, can be played in the haste step.

rules.text: Printed text that names the "mana step" means the haste step.
examples: Dispatch Courier says "play a unit during the mana step as if it had [Haste]": its controller may play a unit in the haste step.

rules.text: An effect can let a card without Haste be played in the haste step "as if it had [Haste]", as Dispatch Courier does. This changes only when the card may be played.
examples: With Dispatch Courier in play, its controller can play a unit without Haste in the haste step, once each turn.

rules.text: Battle is a timing keyword. A card with Battle can be played only while its player is in battle with another player. It cannot be played during deployment.
Gaining Haste does not let a Battle card be played outside battle. A Battle unit or Battle spell unit that an effect lets be played "as if it had [Haste]" still cannot be played in the haste step.
examples: Dispatch Courier's grant does not let a {Battle} unit be played in the haste step.
Nor does Dispatch Courier let a {Battle} spell unit be played in the haste step.

rules.text: A [Battle] icon printed in front of one ability or play mode, rather than as the card's timing, governs that line only. An activated ability marked [Battle] can be activated only during battle; an Ambush marked [Battle] can be played during battle even if the card itself has no Battle timing (803.6b).
examples: Grox's [Battle] ability cannot be activated outside battle.

rules.text: [once] is a keyword that limits an ability: an ability marked [once] can be activated or triggered only once per turn, tracked for each card. Its rules are in 109.9.
examples: Unstable Apparition's [once] trigger fires once in a turn and again the next turn.

rules.text: Burst is a non-combat attribute printed on spell tokens. When a player casts a spell token with Burst, they cast every spell token of the same name that they control in that region at the same time. It is all or nothing.
examples: Casting one Fireball in the battle region casts every Fireball its controller has there.

rules.text: Spell tokens with different names are separate Burst groups. A player with a Poison and a Fireball may cast one, let it resolve, and then cast the other.
examples: Casting a Fireball casts the other Fireballs and leaves a Poison alone.

rules.text: Spell tokens cast together by Burst are still individual spells. They are played at the same time.
examples: Two Fireballs cast together go on the stack as two items, each with its own target.

rules.text: Each spell token in a Burst group chooses its own targets. The tokens do not have to share a target.

A Burst group goes on the stack all at once. Its caster chooses the order one token at a time, in the order the tokens will resolve, and aims each as it is chosen; the token chosen first resolves first. The other players receive priority only when the whole group is on the stack. A lone token is not ordered.
examples: The Fireball picked first ends on top of the stack.

rules.text: Ambush is a keyword that lets a unit card be played during battle with the effect "Recall target ally, put me into their position in play."
examples: Mirage Walker's Ambush recalls an ally and takes its formation slot.

rules.text: An Ambush is paid for with the cost printed beside the keyword, not the card's own cost: that mana is spent and its affinity pips are required.
examples: Lurking Slimebeast's Ambush [3b] costs 3 mana and needs one water pip.
With four fire mana and no water pip, Lurking Slimebeast cannot be played as an Ambush [3b]; with one water and three fire it can, and exactly 3 mana is spent.

rules.text: An Ambush can be played only during battle. The [Battle] icon in front of the keyword lets the card be played as an Ambush during battle even if the card itself has no Battle timing.
examples: Good Whale, a deploy-timing unit, is played as an Ambush in battle into the attacking column.
During deployment, Lurking Slimebeast can be played normally, but not as an Ambush.

rules.text: The target of an Ambush must be an ally of the Ambush's controller in the battle region. An opponent's unit is never a legal target, even through an effect that redirects targets.
examples: An Ambush can target the attacking ally, but not an enemy unit in the battle region, nor an ally that stayed home.
An opposing Enigmatic Warder tries to redirect an Ambush onto itself: the Ambush still recalls its own ally, and the Warder stays in play.

rules.text: An Ambush is a targeted effect on the stack. Players can respond to it before it resolves.
examples: The ally can be removed in response, and then the Ambush fizzles.

rules.text: When an Ambush resolves, the target ally is recalled and the ambushing unit is put directly into the ally's position in play: into its formation slot if it was in formation, attacking or blocking, and otherwise into the battle region outside formation.
examples: Orblish Horroth ambushing a blocker takes the blocker's formation slot.
Mirrorback Ambusher recalls an ally and takes its position.

rules.text: If, as the Ambush resolves, its target is gone or is no longer an ally of the Ambush's controller, the Ambush fizzles: nothing is recalled, and the ambushing card is put into the bin. Its controller loses both units.
examples: An Ambush whose ally changed sides before it resolved recalls nothing.

rules.text: Ambushing a unit that is the target of another effect saves it. The other effect does not change targets to the ambushing unit; it fails to resolve (fizzles).
examples: A Fireball is aimed at a unit, and that unit's controller answers with an Ambush on it. The unit returns to its hand; the Fireball fizzles, and the ambusher takes no damage.

rules.text: An Ambush on the stack counts as a spell effect, so an effect that negates spell effects can negate it. A negated Ambush puts its ambushing card into the bin.
examples: Nothyr, which negates only nonspell effects, cannot target an Ambush on the stack: an Ambush is on the spell side.
Void Mandible negates an Ambush on the stack: the ambusher never takes the slot and its target is not recalled.
Dreadwave Devourer, which negates a target spell effect, can target an Ambush on the stack; negated, the ambusher goes to its bin and its target is not recalled.

rules.text: A card in the cache under a live permission can be played as an Ambush, as it could from the hand. Under a fulfilled prophecy it is free; under a glimpse its controller pays the Ambush mana but ignores the affinity.

An effect that plays a card for free, such as Tides of the Cosmos, may play an Ambush card as an Ambush. The Ambush cost is not paid, and a limit on the card's cost reads its main cost, not its Ambush cost.
examples: Tides of the Cosmos plays Mirrorback Ambusher as an Ambush: the ally leaves play and the ambusher stands in its place.
With 3 of the Tides budget left, Lurking Slimebeast (main cost 4, Ambush 3) cannot be chosen, but Mirage Walker (main cost 3, Ambush 4) can, and playing it as an Ambush spends no mana.

rules.text: Prophecy is a keyword printed on a card's banner as a cost and a condition. A card with a Prophecy banner may be prophesied: its controller pays the banner's cost, and the card moves to the cache with its prophecy attached.
An effect can give a card a prophecy as it caches the card. The prophecy works as a printed one does once the card is in the cache.
examples: Grob caches a unit with 'One Battle Passes' attached, and the prophecy is fulfilled once a battle has passed.

rules.text: A card may be prophesied only during deployment. A card whose prophecy condition ends in a [Haste] icon may also be prophesied during the haste step.

A card is prophesied from its controller's hand. It may be prophesied from the bin only if the card says so, and from the cache only while a glimpse permission on it is live; a card prophesied in the cache stays where it is.
Prophesying costs the banner's cost: its mana is spent and its affinity pips are required.
A prophecy's condition counts forward from the moment the card is prophesied. "Two Turns Pass" means two turns after the card was prophesied, not two turns of the game.
In a 1v1 game, both battles of a turn count toward "One Battle Passes".
examples: A card prophesied with "One Battle Passes" in deployment, after that turn's two battle rounds, is fulfilled once the first battle round of the next turn is over.

rules.text: Once a prophecy's condition has been met, the prophecy stays fulfilled, even if the state that met it goes away.
examples: A card prophesied on "your life is 5 or less" stays playable after its controller gains life back.

rules.text: Once the prophecy is fulfilled, the card may be played from the cache for free, ignoring affinity, as if it were in its controller's hand.
A fulfilled prophecy changes what the card costs, not when it may be played. The card is played at its own printed timing, and a [Haste] icon in the banner does not move the release.
An X spell released by a fulfilled prophecy is cast with X = 0. A variable bracketed cost on it is a cost, not its X, and is still paid.

A card whose prophecy is fulfilled may also be grafted or augmented from the cache, for free and ignoring affinity. Until the prophecy is fulfilled, the card cannot be played, grafted or augmented from the cache at all.

A condition that counts units dying, such as Vengeance's "13 Units Die", counts only the deaths its controller witnessed: deaths in a region where that player was present. A player is present in their own region, and in an enemy region once they have attacked into it, until regroup.
examples: A player attacks into the opponent's region with a unit, so both players are present there. Two of the opponent's units die in that region: each player counts two deaths toward "Units Die".

rules.text: An effect that plays a card for free, such as Tides of the Cosmos, may play a card with a Prophecy banner as a Prophecy: the card is cached with its prophecy attached, and the banner cost is not paid.
Unstable is a non-combat attribute. If an Unstable card would enter a bin from an active zone (play or the stack), it is erased instead.
examples: Aberrant Statweaver, printed {Unstable}, dies into the erased pile, not the bin.

rules.text: Unstable applies only to a card leaving an active zone. The active zones are play and the stack. An Unstable card that goes to a bin from a hand, the deck, a bin or the cache is put into the bin normally, and is trashed.
A card may print Unstable on its type line. Oorblak and Aberrant Statweaver do.
examples: Oorblak, unmodded, is erased when it dies.

rules.text: An effect may give a card Unstable. It is often given to cards played from the bin, so that they cannot be used more than once: Abyssal Evocation and Spell Excavation give the spells they let you play from the bin Unstable until regroup.
examples: A spell played from the bin under Abyssal Evocation is erased after it resolves, never re-binned.
A spell played under Spell Excavation is erased rather than re-binned.

rules.text: Unstable given "until regroup" lasts until regroup, even after the permission that came with it has ended. A spell unit played under such a grant passes it to the unit it puts into play.
examples: A bin-played spell unit body is still Unstable in the second battle round, after the permission to play spells from the bin has ended, and stops being Unstable at regroup.

rules.text: A card is Unstable for as long as it is modded. When a modded card dies or is erased, it and all of its mods are erased.
examples: A modded host exchanged out of play by Hooba-Mon is erased with its mods, which reach the erased pile.

rules.text: A spell is modded, and so Unstable, when a Virus is applied to it on the stack or a mod is applied to it through {Modular}. When it leaves the stack it is erased with its mods.
A copy of a modded unit is not Unstable when it is made, because it has no mods of its own. A mod attached to it afterwards makes it Unstable in the usual way.
examples: A Borrower of Forms that copied a modded unit is not Unstable and dies to the bin.

rules.text: Moving a mod moves its Unstable with it. The unit the mod leaves stops being Unstable when its last mod is gone, unless something else makes it Unstable; the unit it moves to becomes Unstable.
Unstable replaces where the card goes, not its death. An Unstable unit that is destroyed still dies: its death triggers and other abilities that watch for a unit dying see it.
examples: A modded unit is destroyed. A whenever-another-unit-dies ability triggers, then the unit is erased, not binned.

rules.text: Unstable does not stop a unit from being recalled. A recalled Unstable unit goes to the hand as a card; if it was modded, its mods are put into the bin.
An Unstable card that leaves the stack for a bin, because it resolved, fizzled or was negated, is erased instead.
examples: Aberrant Statweaver negated off the stack is erased.
A printed-Unstable virus whose host dies fizzles to the erased pile.

rules.text: An effect that itself says to put a card into a bin overrides Unstable. Pull Under ("Delete target unit. If you do, put it and all of its mods into your bin.") leaves a modded unit and its mods in that bin.
There are four game modes: live draft, constructed, cube draft and team draft.
The 2023 Rulebook calls cube draft "pre-draft": players draft a complete deck of at least 30 cards before the game begins, then play constructed games with it.
A game is played in one of these player setups: 1v1, free-for-all (FFA), teams, or archenemy.
A 1v1 game is played between two players. It is the recommended setup for a first game.
Free-for-all is described in 903. Team games and archenemy are described in 904.
A 1v1 game counts as a team game: each player is their own team. Free-for-all is not a team game.
examples: With The Silent in play, two spells you have played this battle make your next spell cost [4] more, while your opponent still pays the printed cost: in 1v1 your team is you alone.

rules.text: Where the players sit sets which regions neighbour each other.
In 1v1 the players sit across from each other. Each has one neighbouring region.
In a game of more than two players the players sit in a circle, so each player has a player to their left and a player to their right. Each player has two neighbouring regions.
Battle normally resolves one region at a time, in the order of 601. Once players are comfortable with the game, they may resolve at the same time any regions that have no player in common.
examples: With an attack and a counterattack, the battle in the defending region runs to its end before the counterattack battle begins in the other region.

rules.text: The client plays 1v1 live draft and 1v1 constructed only. It has no free-for-all, team, archenemy, cube-draft or team-draft games, and no intent cards. Rules 903, 904 and 905, and the parts of 902 about cube draft and team draft, describe the printed game, which the client does not enforce.
In constructed, each player brings their own deck, built before the game, and plays from it.
A constructed deck has at least 30 cards. No source sets a maximum.
examples: A 29-card deck is not a legal constructed deck.

rules.text: A constructed deck may hold at most 2 copies of any one card.
examples: A third copy of a card makes the deck illegal.

rules.text: Constructed has no shared deck and no packs.
In constructed, the draw step and the draft step are taken together as one draw phase: each player draws 4 cards from their own deck, then puts 2 cards from their hand on the bottom of their deck.
examples: Turn 1 of a constructed game: each player has their 4-card opening hand, draws 4, and must then put 2 back.

rules.text: The player chooses the 2 cards and puts them on the bottom in any order. Because every card put on the bottom of a deck goes into the recycle pile, which is shuffled before it is drawn from again, the order has no effect on play.

For state checks the draw of 4 and the put-back of 2 are one step: a player's units are not checked for death while that player still has 2 cards to put back, so they are judged on the hand that remains.
examples: Dreadspawn Horror with 1 card in hand: drawing 4 does not kill it, and after the put-back it is a 4/2.
With 3 cards in hand, Dreadspawn Horror's controller draws 4 and puts 2 back, keeping 5 cards: the Horror then dies.

rules.text: A player in a constructed game may make a resource of any element, whether or not their deck holds a card of that element.
Card text that refers to a constructed format applies in a constructed game.
examples: Worldbender in constructed: the player skips the draw-4-put-2-back, the hand gains 3 cards, and the player loses 3 life.
Worldbender in a live draft: the hand gains 3 cards and life is untouched.

rules.text: The matches of a cube draft are constructed games, so such text applies in them too.
The client has a testing mode called "shared", which is not a format. Card text that asks whether the game is constructed treats a shared game as constructed.
examples: Worldbender in shared takes the constructed branch: three cards and 3 life.

rules.text: Single Card Duel is a variant of constructed that the client offers. Each player picks a single card before the game, and their deck is 30 copies of that card.
A Single Card Duel deck is the one exception to the limit of 2 copies of a card.
A Single Card Duel has no draw phase. Each turn, each player simply draws 2 cards; nothing is put back. The opening hand is still 4 cards.
examples: Each player starts turn 1 with 6 cards (4 + 2) and nothing to put back, and draws exactly 2 more on turn 2.

rules.text: If neither player's card can make a unit, the game is not played. It is a draw: each player is told the other's card, and both choose again. A card can make a unit if it is a unit or spell-unit card, or if it creates a unit token.
examples: A unit card and Self-Assembly (which creates a Robot unit token) can make a unit; a spell that creates no unit cannot.

rules.text: In live draft, the players share one deck, built from the chosen elements, and draft cards from it during the game.
Live draft is the standard Algomancy format, and 1v1 live draft is the format suggested for learning the game.
A live draft uses 3 elements for 2–3 players and 4 elements for 4–6 players. For 6 or more players, a cube draft with all 5 elements is recommended instead of a live draft.
In casual games, players take turns choosing the elements, or assign them randomly. The printed rules defer the competitive procedure to Algomancy.io.
In live draft each player begins with 16 cards to draft from: a 6-card hand (the 4-card starting hand plus the first turn's 2 draws) and a 10-card pack.
The draft step is described in 503, and the pack, its refresh every N+1 turns and an eliminated player's pack in 409.
examples: Turns 2 and 3 draw 2 and reopen the draft step; the packs refresh on turn 4.

rules.text: The client lets a live draft be created with custom rules. Custom rules change the deal and nothing else: they never change how a card works.
Pack size may be set from 3 to 15 cards (standard 10). Every pack is dealt and refreshed at that size, and the draft step leaves exactly that many cards in the pack.
examples: With packs of 5, each pack is dealt with 5 cards, the draft step leaves 5 in it, and the turn-4 refresh deals 5.

rules.text: The number of elements may be set from 2 to 7 (standard 3). The pool is every deck card whose elements all lie within the chosen set. Two elements default to fire and wood.
The opening hand may be set from 1 to 15 cards (standard 6), the draws per turn after turn 1 from 0 to 5 (standard 2), and the starting life from 1 to 99 (standard 30).
With "simple cards only", the pool holds only cards with the silver (Simple) complexity symbol.
Cards may be banned by name, and an advanced card filter may be set: only cards that match it are in the pool. A banned or filtered-out card is nowhere in the game.
Custom rules do not change the pack refresh: it still comes every N+1 turns.
examples: With packs of 5 the turn-4 refresh still comes, and deals 5.

rules.text: A custom pool must hold at least 2 × hand + 4 × pack + 6 × draws cards (64 for the standard game). Custom rules below that floor are refused before the game is created. When the elements are to be chosen later, every set of that size must pass.
examples: The standard game needs 64 cards, the beginner deal 44.

rules.text: Custom rules are not printed rules. Packs of other than 10 cards are not in the printed rules, and the client's Beginner preset (two elements, simple cards only, packs of 5) is the client's own softening of the Quick Start.
Cube draft is a format for large groups (6 to 10 or more players). The players draft decks before the game, then use them to play constructed matches, often in a 1v1 tournament bracket.
The cube is all of the game cards, hybrids included, shuffled together: 320 cards from one box. For more than 8 players, two complete sets are used (640 cards).

To draft, deal each player a pack of 10 cards. Then repeat these steps 15 times, until each player has a 30-card deck: (1) each player draws 2 cards from the cube; (2) players may combine their hands with their packs; (3) each player chooses 10 cards from their combined hand and pack and passes them, as a new pack, clockwise to their neighbour.
Players then play constructed matches with the 30-card decks they drafted.
A traditional cube draft may be used instead. Each player is dealt three packs of 13 to 15 cards: 15 cards for 6 players, 13 for 8 players.
Each player looks at their pack, takes one card from it and passes the rest to their neighbour, until the pack is empty. This is done three times, once per pack, passing left, then right, then left.
From the cards they drafted, each player builds a 30-card deck for the constructed matches that follow.
In team draft, each team brings a constructed deck of 30 cards for each player on the team, with at most 2 copies of each card. The team live drafts from that deck during the game.
In team draft, a player who has finished drafting passes their pack to the nearest teammate, not clockwise to the nearest player.
In team draft, packs are never refreshed.
All the other rules of live draft apply in team draft.
The 2023 Rulebook sizes the team-draft deck differently: the team builds a deck of 100 cards, with at most 2 copies of each card.
In a free-for-all (FFA) game, every player plays for themselves. All players fight to be the last one standing.
A free-for-all game is for 2 to 9 players, or more if more copies of the game are available.
Free-for-all has no attack and counterattack: there is one battle round, and no counterattacks.
In free-for-all, all players declare their attacks at the same time, using intent cards (see 905).

After the attacks are declared, battle in each attacked region follows these steps in order: (1) the attacker sets their units into formation; (2) a priority window; (3) the defender sets their blocking formation; (4) a priority window; (5) the combat damage step, in which all units in formation deal combat damage at the same time; (6) the after combat step, the last priority window in that region before regroup.
When two players attack the same player, all three players take part in that battle together, in one region.
The defending player defends against both attacking formations.
All three players can interact with each other and with each other's units in that region.

In a region with more than two players, priority passes around the players in a circle, clockwise, instead of back and forth. The initiative player receives priority first if they are present in the region; otherwise the player nearest to the initiative player, clockwise, does.
The stack works the same way with three players in a region as it does in 1v1.

Apart from the battle phase, which is only partly simultaneous, every phase of a free-for-all game may be taken by all players at the same time: players may make resources in the planning phase, and deploy units in the deployment phase, all at once.
Players who are learning, or playing competitively, may instead take their phases one player at a time, in clockwise order from the initiative player.
In a team game, two teams play against each other, 2v2 or 3v3. 3v3 is the standard team structure.

A team game may be played with split teams, where each player has their own region, or with joint players, where a team shares a single region. A joint-player game is in effect a 1v1 game with more players.
In a team game, each player sits between two opponents.
In a team game, a team wins when it has eliminated the entire opposing team.
Teammates act together in every situation and every phase of the game.

The team of the player who holds the initiative token has the initiative: it is the initiative team (IT), and the other team is the non-initiative team (NIT). The initiative team makes all its plays first; the non-initiative team acts after it.
The teams trade the initiative every turn.
In the deployment phase, the initiative team deploys first, its players in any order they wish, and then passes to the non-initiative team, whose players do the same.
Teammates share priority. They take actions in whatever order they choose among themselves, and a team receives and passes priority as one.

A team game's battle has the same attack-and-counterattack structure as 1v1. The difference is that attacks and blocks take place across several regions, with a separate priority window in each region.

In a team game the battle runs in this order (the Manual gives it for 2v2): (1) the initiative team declares all its attacks at once, into several regions; (2) a priority window in each non-initiative region, in order clockwise from the initiative player; (3) the non-initiative team declares all its blocks and counterattacks at once, into several regions; (4) battle is finished in each non-initiative region in turn, in order clockwise from the initiative player; (5) battle is finished in each initiative region in turn, in order clockwise from the initiative player.
Finishing battle in a region means its remaining steps: a priority window, the combat damage step, and the after combat priority window.
Card text that refers to a player's team refers, in 1v1, to that player alone, since in 1v1 each player is their own team.
examples: The Silent in 1v1: once its controller has played 2 spells this battle, their next spell costs [4] more, while the opponent, who has played none, pays the printed cost.

rules.text: Archenemy is a player setup, typically 2v1, in which the single player gets to take 1 or 2 turns before the other two players begin the game.
The 2023 Rulebook describes the 2v1 game differently: the single player has bonus cards and resources, and faces two weaker opponents.
Intent cards are how players declare attacks in free-for-all: all players declare at the same time, each placing intent cards that show what their cards intend to do.

Attacks are declared with intent cards in these steps: (1) each player places an intent card face down in front of each of their units and other cards, such as spell tokens, showing that card's intended action; (2) when all players have finished, all the intent cards are turned face up; (3) the chosen attacks take place at once.
A player may group several of their units behind one intent card.
A player may place several copies of the same intent card in front of different units.

annexD.text: The pacing and concurrency conventions in this annex are not rules changes: none of them changes what is legal.
A warning or a confirmation never removes a legal option. Where a choice looks like a misclick, the client may ask the player; it does not refuse the choice.
The client never makes a choice that belongs to a player. A real choice is always put to the player who makes it.
An option the rules would refuse is not offered. The client shows only legal options; it does not show an option and then refuse it.

The game takes an action for a player only where the battle leaves them nothing to decide: an attacker with no unit able to attack has the empty attack declared for them, and a defender with no unit in the battle region has the empty block declared for them. These forced actions are logged like any other. A player holding full control is not forced: the window is left to them.
In round 2, a counterattack pool that holds exactly one unit, and no spell token that could ride along, declares the one-unit formation by itself. Engine differs, see F-U23-4.
examples: A player who sent one unit to counterattack, and no spell token, is not asked to form it: the one-unit formation is declared for them.

annexD.text: When all of one player's simultaneously queued triggers are identical (the same card, the same ability and the same composed parts), the player is not asked to order them. They go on in the order they fired. Triggers from different cards or abilities, or composites whose parts differ, are still ordered by the player.
examples: Three allies spawn at once beside Flourishing Flora: its three identical triggers go on the stack without the player being asked to order them.

annexD.text: A non-target choice that an ability makes as it goes on the stack (such as the ally a Wraith's start-of-deployment trigger aims at) is recorded without asking when there is only one candidate. With two or more candidates the player is asked.
examples: A lone Wraith aims at its only ally without asking; with a second ally the player is asked.

annexD.text: A target is asked for even when exactly one candidate is legal. A forced target is still a click.
examples: Divine Foresight ("target opponent") cast in battle still asks its caster to choose the target, though the opponent is the only choice.

annexD.text: Where a choice has a usual answer, the client may offer it as the first option, but it never picks it. The elective combat-damage split leads with "default — share front-to-back", and no automatic action answers that question.
The caster always chooses the order of a Burst group, one token at a time; the client offers no automatic order. A lone token is not asked to be ordered.
The client holds no opinion of its own about legality. Wherever the client decides something the engine also decides, the client's answer is derived from the engine's, in one place.
A highlighted card, a clickable unit, a drop target or a one-click shortcut claims that the engine will take the action. The client draws one only where the engine would accept it.
examples: A unit that cannot be sent to counterattack is not highlighted, and clicking it does nothing.

annexD.text: A hidden simultaneous segment is a part of the turn in which both players act at once and neither sees what the other does until both are done. The resource step, the haste step and deployment are hidden simultaneous segments.
The hiding is done by the server's view of the game, the same way hands are hidden. The rules engine itself hides nothing.
A segment ends at a barrier, when every player is done. At the barrier each player is shown what the other did, in the recap.
Battle is not a hidden segment. Nothing that happens in battle is held back from either player.
While a decision is open for a player (a question the game is waiting on them to answer), that player must answer it, or concede, before taking any other action.
In battle, a decision open for one player stops the other player too: nobody may act until it is answered.
Inside a hidden simultaneous segment, a decision open for one player does not stop the other player, who keeps every action they had, except as described in the next sub-rule.
examples: While one player answers their Wraith triggers at the start of deployment, the other player goes on deploying.

annexD.text: Exception: when answering the open decision would rewind the game to before the other player acted (a resolution that stopped halfway), the other player is stopped as in battle. Online, an action they send meanwhile waits and is applied when the decision closes; they are told it is waiting, not that it is illegal.
Only one decision can be open at a time. An action that would change what the other player's open decision reads when it is answered is refused, and the game stays as it was before the action.
Conceding is never blocked by an open decision, whichever player it belongs to.
Each player's screen shows only that player's own open question: the other player's question and its options are never sent to it. The player being asked has only the question.

When a player holds priority, the client offers up to three ways to pass: Pass, Pass through stack and Pass all. Pass through stack and Pass all are standing passes: promises the client keeps on the player's behalf in later windows.
Pass passes priority once. It sets up nothing for later windows.

Pass through stack passes for the player until the stack items that were there when it was clicked have resolved, and then ends. It hands priority back sooner if a stack item outside that set appears, or if the player is offered an option they did not have when they clicked.
examples: A player clicks Pass through stack; the opponent answers with a new spell, so priority comes back to the player.

annexD.text: Pass through stack is offered only while there is a stack to pass through.
Pass all passes for the player until the phase it was clicked in ends. A new stack item or a new option does not hand priority back.
examples: The opponent casting a spell does not stop Pass all.

annexD.text: Both standing passes still stop before the one pass that would end the battle phase while the player holds spell tokens they could cast, so that that pass is the player's own click.
examples: A player clicks Pass all while holding a castable Fireball token: it passes through the battle but hands back the last pass, the one that would end the battle phase.

annexD.text: What counts as new for a standing pass is measured against the moment it was clicked. An option the player already had then is not new when it comes back later.
examples: An activated ability the player could use when they clicked Pass all becomes unusable for a window and then usable again: the pass does not stop for it.

annexD.text: A standing pass is set up only by a click and can be cancelled at any time: one stop control drops whichever is running. The client shows which promise is running and how it ends.
A player may turn on auto-pass. With it on, the client passes priority for the player only in a window where passing is the only thing they could do. Auto-pass never passes through an open decision.
examples: With a castable card in hand the window is put to the player even with auto-pass on.

annexD.text: An answer the client sends without a click (an automatic pass, or the automatic haste-step ready) is sent once for each time it is owed. It is latched by being unanswered, not by counting game updates, so updates that arrive while it is outstanding do not send it again. Engine differs, see F-U23-2.
If the server refuses an action the client sent on its own, the refusal is not shown as the player's error. It goes to the log and to a plain notice that says the client sent it.
When the haste step opens and the only legal action a player has in it is to finish the step, the client finishes it for them at once, unless they have turned on bluff haste.
If the player has any legal play in the haste step, the client never finishes the step for them.
examples: A playable haste card in hand keeps the player in the step, bluff haste on or off.

annexD.text: Bluff haste is a preference, off by default and remembered by the browser. With it on, the client never finishes the haste step for the player; they stay in the step until they finish it themselves, whether or not they hold anything to play.
The server never finishes the haste step for a player. The automatic ready, when there is one, comes from the player's own client.
While the haste step is open, neither player is shown whether the other has finished it. Each player sees their own readiness, and the end of the step is shown to both.

The game's action counter is still sent to both players and rises on every action, in every hidden segment, so a modified client can tell that its opponent acted and when. The shipped client shows nothing from it.

When passing would end the battle phase while the player still holds spell tokens they could cast, the client asks before sending the pass, because moving to regroup erases them. It asks on that pass only, not in the battle's other windows.

When the battle phase ends with no pass to ask on (an attack declined with no window left, or a whole battle declined), the loss is announced instead: as regroup starts, each player who loses unused spell tokens is told which. Nothing is announced when nothing is lost.
examples: A battle both players decline opens no priority window, and the token loss is still announced.

annexD.text: A battle ended by a card while it resolves (Temporal Rift) cannot be warned about before the pass, since that cannot be known when the pass is made. The announcement covers it, as it covers every way a battle ends.
examples: Under Temporal Rift, a pass does not look like it will end the battle, so the client does not ask; when the Rift ends the battle, the lost spell tokens are still announced as regroup starts.

annexD.text: Full control is held, not set. While a player holds the Control key, the client gives them every stop: auto-pass, standing passes, auto-yields and the automatic haste-step ready all stand down. When they let go, everything returns to how it was.
This includes deployment: while a player holds full control, nothing on their deployment stack resolves automatically. Engine differs, see F-U23-1.

The client's own automatic actions stop at once when Control is pressed. The server's automatic actions stop only once the message reaches it, and an automatic action already sent is not recalled, so full control should be held before acting, not after.
Leaving the window (switching away, hiding the page) releases full control, as if the key had been let go.
examples: Alt-tabbing away is letting go.

annexD.text: Pressing another key while Control is down (Ctrl+Z, or a browser shortcut) makes a chord, not full control: it drops the hold until Control is released.
examples: Ctrl+Z is undo, not full control.

annexD.text: Full control is not remembered between sessions. The client shows whether it is being held.

When a spell has one target slot that must be an ally and another that may be any unit, and the player picks an ally for the second slot, the client asks whether they meant to target their own unit. It never refuses: yes resolves exactly as chosen, and no returns to the same target pick with nothing sent.
examples: A player casts Fight and picks two of their own units: the client asks once before the cast goes out.

annexD.text: The cards that ask are found from their target slots, not listed by name. Today they are Fight and Squish. Organic Exchange, which targets two units with no ally slot, does not ask.

This client has no way to keep priority after acting: when a player puts something on the stack in battle, priority goes to the opponent. A player can still respond to their own spell, once priority comes back to them with it still on the stack.
examples: The defender casts a spell, the attacker passes, and the defender casts a second spell on top of the first.

annexD.text: A game may be played with a chess clock, in which each player has a bank of time. The home screen offers three settings: no clock, 45 minutes and 60 minutes.
Unless the player chooses otherwise, the bank is 45 minutes for a constructed game and 60 minutes for a live draft.
A game with no clock shows no clocks.
Choosing a clock setting does not make a game a custom game.
A player's clock is shown as critical when it is down to a tenth of the game's bank or to one minute, whichever is less.
examples: On a ninety-second bank the warning comes at nine seconds; on a ten-hour bank five minutes left is not yet critical, because the threshold stops at one minute.
On the 45- and 60-minute banks the clock turns critical at one minute.

annexD.text: A player's clock runs only while the game is waiting on that player, and only while both players are connected.
In a step both players take at once, both clocks run; a player's clock stops when that player finishes the step.

A player's clock does not run in a priority window that their standing pass is answering, and the other player, who has nothing to do there, is not billed either. A real choice is billed even while a standing pass is set. If the client's pass has not arrived within a short backstop, the server passes for the player, and that pass is logged like any other.
A player watching a recap is off the clock until the playback ends or the server's hold on it lapses. Acting ends the hold.
A player whose clock runs out loses the game, and the log says they ran out of time. This happens even if neither player acts.

A game is closed when nobody has moved in it for an hour, if fewer than five actions have been taken, or for twelve hours otherwise, and nobody (no player and no watcher) has been connected to it for the five-minute reconnect grace. An open tab keeps an idle game open.
A connected player or a watcher keeps an idle game open, and an empty game is given a grace period for a player to reconnect.
A game closed for being idle has no winner, is not rated, and is recorded as unfinished.
Inside a hidden simultaneous segment, a player may undo their own actions, one at a time, back toward the start of the step, within the limits of the rules below.
The opponent acting in the same step does not stop a player's undo.
An undo cannot go back past what the step itself did as it began, such as a payment or an ability that happens at the start of the step.
examples: An undo stops at what the step did as it began: the answer to a start-of-deployment trigger cannot be taken back.

annexD.text: Actions taken in battle are not undone. For that reason an irreversible activated ability asks for confirmation in battle, while in deployment it activates on the click and undo is the safety net.
A cast that has not yet gone on the stack, while its X, costs or targets are still being chosen, may be cancelled. A Burst group is cancelled whole.
An action that showed a player hidden cards cannot be undone, and neither can anything that player did before it.
examples: A Glimpse in deployment cannot be undone.

annexD.text: Actions the player took after that one can still be undone, back to just after it.
examples: A unit played after the glimpse can be undone, back to just after the glimpse, and not past it.

annexD.text: The refusal reads "you've seen those cards — that can't be taken back".
Only the player who saw the cards is locked. The opponent looking at a shared deck does not lock a player's undo, since inside a hidden step it shows that player nothing.
examples: The opponent glimpsing from the shared deck does not lock the player's undo.

annexD.text: An undo is refused if it would change cards the opponent has already been shown.

Whether an action showed a player hidden cards is measured, not listed: an action counts if what it shows the player depends on the order of hidden cards. A glimpse, a draw, a reveal or a look at a hand counts. Playing a card from hand, recycling, or putting a card on the bottom of a deck does not. In a Single Card Duel nothing locks, since every card in the deck is the same.
examples: A unit's spawn trigger that glimpses 1 in the haste step locks undo too.

annexD.text: The lock survives a server restart and an undo.

In Learn to Play, undo works in every phase, under the same lock: a turn's draw, a glimpse or a look at the Bot's hand ends the undo of whatever came before it. Starting a turn again after a loss is a fresh attempt, not an undo.
When the haste step or deployment ends, each player is shown what the other did there as a playback (the recap): one frame per move, in the order the moves were made.
The recap changes nothing in the game. A game played with recap frames is the same game, action for action, as one without them.
A frame of the opponent's move shows that move on their side, their hand still face down, and the player's own side as the player left it.
A move with nothing to show is not given a frame, but its log line is kept.
The end of turn is played as one frame per trigger, in order.
The resource step is not played back: its close arrives whole, in one update.
Undoing a move inside the step removes that move's frame and keeps the others.

A Glimpse made in a hidden step is shown to the opponent in the recap, exactly once, in the frame of the action that made it, with its card notice. The player who glimpsed sees their own reveal at once. A Glimpse in battle reaches the opponent at once.
examples: A player plays Oracle of Foretelling in deployment: the opponent sees its glimpse in the recap frame of that play, and nowhere else.

annexD.text: The deployment recap pauses after the opponent's moves and again after the end of turn; the haste step's recap pauses the same way. Skip jumps to the next pause, never past it. A quiet end of turn does not pause twice.
A recap can be watched again. Watching again pauses at the same places, shows the glimpse notices again, and hands back the board.
The hand-over to the next turn at the end of a recap pauses longer than a frame. Every recap, live, watched again or in Learn to Play, is paced by the same rule.
The client shows play no faster than one step per second. This one tempo paces both the updates the client receives and the steps within a single update.
Items that happen at the same time under the rules arrive on screen together, then leave one at a time, in resolution order, one tempo step apart. The next group waits until this one has finished.

Only an update the player cannot act on is held back to keep the tempo. A decision for the player, the echo of the player's own action and the end of the game are never held, and an update with legal actions is never held unless auto-pass will answer it.
When an update the player can act on arrives, everything held before it is released with it, in order, so the player is never asked a question over an old board.
The player's own input is never delayed by the tempo.
The screen never falls more than a fixed number of tempo steps behind the live game.
Outside a recap playback, while play is being held back, the S key jumps to the live state. Skipping drops pending animations but still delivers the held log lines. No skip control is drawn for this.
While play is held, whether the opponent is connected, and the clocks, stay current; nothing else on the board changes until the held updates are released.
A disconnect is shown at once, not queued behind held updates, and showing it does not release them.
During a recap playback, skipping does not jump to the live state. Skip (the S key, Space, or the Skip button drawn on the play bar) jumps to the next stop, and on a stop it continues the playback.

The resource step, the haste step and deployment are hidden simultaneous steps. Inside one, both players act at the same time, and neither is shown what the other does until the step ends. The end of the step is the reveal: everything the other player did in the step is shown then. At the end of the haste step and of deployment it is played back in the recap.
examples: During deployment, nothing a player does in their region reaches the other player until deployment ends.

annexD.text: Inside a hidden step, the other player's side of the game is shown as it stood when the step opened. The events the other player's actions produce are held and delivered at the end of the step. Whether the other player has finished the step is not frozen: it is shown live, except in the haste step, where the other player's readiness is hidden while the step is open.
examples: In Learn to Play, a unit the Tutorial Bot casts during deployment is not shown to the learner until deployment closes.

annexD.text: In the haste step and in deployment, the shared deck count and the shared recycle count are shown to both players as they were when the step opened. A player's own play that moves cards into or out of those piles shows on the counts only at the reveal.
examples: A player glimpses during deployment. The shared deck count does not drop for either player until deployment ends.

annexD.text: Nothing is held during the battle phase. What happens in battle is shown to every player as it happens.
examples: Premonition is cast in battle. Its Glimpse reveal reaches the opponent at once.

annexD.text: While the haste step is open, a player is not shown whether the other player has finished it. Each player sees their own readiness. The end of the step is shown to both players.
examples: One player finishes the haste step while the other is still choosing. The other player is not told that the first has finished.

annexD.text: A glimpse that happens inside a hidden step is shown to the other player at the reveal, not when it happens. At the end of the haste step or deployment it plays in the recap, at the moment it happened.
examples: Oracle of Foretelling is played during deployment and glimpses 5. The opponent learns the five cards when deployment ends, in the recap.

annexD.text: The player who glimpses sees their own revealed cards when they glimpse.
examples: A player plays Oracle of Foretelling during deployment and sees the revealed cards at once; the opponent sees nothing of them until the step ends.

annexD.text: At the reveal the other player is shown the glimpse exactly once, with its card notice, and the finished game log holds it once.
Holding a glimpse until the reveal only delays it. The revealed cards are public, and every player sees them.
examples: Foretell is played in battle. The card it reveals is shown to the opponent.

annexD.text: The same holds in Learn to Play: a glimpse by the Tutorial Bot inside a hidden step is shown to the learner in the recap.

During the battle phase, when an item has begun to resolve and is waiting on a choice from its controller, every player is shown that the item is resolving and whose it is. The item has left the stack, and no player can respond to it (see 703.6).
Outside the battle phase the other player is shown nothing of an item resolving. Its controller still sees the question.
examples: Oracle of Foretelling, played in deployment, asks its controller which card to cache; the other player is shown nothing of it. The same kind of question from Premonition in battle is shown to them.

annexD.text: While a resolution waits on a player's answer, every player is shown the board as it is partway through the resolution: whatever the effect has already done is on the table, including what its controller played and paid.
examples: Insidious Invitation lets the caster play a unit first, then asks the opponent. When the opponent is asked, the caster's unit and spent mana are already on the table.

annexD.text: On a board partway through a resolution, the only actions any player may take are answering the open question and conceding.

Outside a hidden simultaneous step, that a player owes an answer to a question is public, and so is the card it comes from when that card is already in view. What the question is is not: its prompt, its options, its candidate targets and its kind are shown only to the player who must answer. Inside a hidden simultaneous step, not even the fact that the other player owes an answer is shown.
examples: The attacker's Tempest Wrangler makes them choose an {Alluring} target. The defender's bar reads "Waiting for Rashi (Tempest Wrangler)" and names neither the prompt nor the candidate.

annexD.text: The waiting player may be told which card the question comes from, but only when that card is already visible to them. Inside a hidden step, it is not named.
No message the client receives names a card in a zone hidden from that player. When cards enter another player's hand, the player is told how many entered, not which.
examples: The opponent draws two cards. The player sees the opponent's hand grow by two card backs and is not sent their names.

annexD.text: When an effect lets a player look at a hand, the cards seen are named in the game log to that player only. The other players' log says only that the hand was looked at.
examples: Thought Extraction is aimed at a player's own hand. The opponent is not shown the cards in it.

annexD.text: A card that an effect moves out of a hidden hand into another hidden zone, without the effect saying "reveal", is named only to the player who chose it. The other players are told that a card moved, not which.
examples: Bripp recycles a card from the looked-at hand. The table is told a card was recycled; only Bripp's controller sees its name.

annexD.text: Both players' caches are shown to both players in full: every cached card, and any prophecy attached to it (see 403.2).
A cached card whose prophecy condition counts toward a number shows its progress on the board, on its owner's cache, to every player. The count shown is the one for the cache's owner.
examples: The opponent has prophesied Vengeance ("13 Units Die"). The player can see on the opponent's cache how many of the 13 deaths have been counted.

annexD.text: A prophecy whose condition is a state rather than a count shows no meter. A fulfilled prophecy shows as fulfilled instead of a meter.
examples: A cached card whose prophecy reads "Your life is 5 or less" puts no meter on the board.

annexD.text: Any player may open either player's erased pile, from the menu of the bare table (see 407.1a).
examples: A player right-clicks the empty table and opens the opponent's erased pile.

annexD.text: Either player may open either player's bin. When something on the stack targets a card in a bin, that card is brought to the top of the bin on the board, for both players.
examples: A Hooba-Mon trigger on the stack targets a card six deep in a bin. That card is drawn on top of the bin for both players.

annexD.text: In constructed, the elements a player's deck contains are sent to both players. Whether they should be public at the start of the game is an open question for the owner (see the discrepancy report).
examples: A fire deck plays a water deck in constructed. Each player is sent that one deck is fire and the other water.

annexD.text: Things that happen at the same time in the rules are shown at the same time, and things that happen one after another are shown one after another.
examples: Combat kills several units at once and their death triggers are queued together. All of them appear on the stack strip in one beat.

annexD.text: This pacing only explains what happened. It never delays the game: the board under it is already final.
examples: While the beats of a death sweep are still playing, the units are already gone from the board state.

annexD.text: Cards that make the same move in one update, from the same place to the same place, move together. Moves between different places are shown one after another. A move whose start or end the client cannot name, such as a card being erased, is shown on its own.
examples: Four units die in one update and their four triggers go to the stack together. They all fly to the stack at once.
A card going from hand to the stack, one going from the stack to the field and one going to the bin are three moves, one after another.
Two cards erased from the field, with nowhere named to go, are not grouped.

annexD.text: A unit that has become a copy of another card is drawn with the art of the card it copied, and stays marked as a copy.
examples: Borrower of Forms copies Sporebloom Siren. It is drawn with Sporebloom Siren's art and a copy mark.

annexD.text: A copy is marked even when its numbers match the card it copied. The bin shows the physical card, not the copied face.
examples: Borrower of Forms (2/2) copies a 2/2. It still wears the copy mark.

annexD.text: A card that only borrows abilities from another, without taking its name, keeps its own art.
examples: Ancient One shares the text box of an adjacent ally but keeps its own portrait.

annexD.text: Where a card's printed text uses a bare X, or names a card, and this copy of the card has a value for it, the text box shows that value in its place. Stat notation (X/X, +X/+X, -X/-X), the [x] cost pip and reminder text are never changed, even when X has a value. A board-read X on the stack is not written into the text box; it is shown as a forecast (see rule D6.9c).
examples: A Poison created with X = 5 reads "Put 5 -1/-1 counters on target unit".

annexD.text: A token's text box shows its actual X in place of X. Stat notation such as X/X, +X/+X and -X/-X is never changed, and neither is reminder text.
examples: A Robot reads its X off its counters, so its text changes when they change.

annexD.text: A card that names a card shows the named card in its text box, and so does a host carrying that text as a mod. With no card named, the printed text stands.
examples: The Everywhere has named Triskaidekaphage. Its text box reads "Triskaidekaphage loses all abilities."

annexD.text: When a card on the stack reads its X from the board at resolution, and the card itself declares how to forecast that X, the stack shows what X would be right now, worded as a forecast. A declared mode narrows the forecast to that mode. If X was paid, the paid X is shown and no forecast is. A board-read X with no declared forecast shows none (see rule D6.9e).
examples: Retribution Thing is on the stack. It shows the X it would deal now.
Retribution Thing was cast in the life-lost mode. The stack shows only that mode's forecast.

annexD.text: Spell tokens in play are counted by name, with the X of each, because casting one burst token casts every token of that name (see 803). Each spell token shows its X as a large die face.
examples: A player holds Fireball 1, Fireball 1 and Fireball 3. The strip shows one Fireball row: three of them, two at X = 1 and one at X = 3.
A Fireball with X = 3 shows a die face with three pips.

annexD.text: A card whose X is read from the board at resolution, but which declares no forecast for it, shows no forecast on the stack.

A card whose printed text box is empty, but whose type line carries attributes, shows those attributes and their reminders in its text box instead of "no rules text". A card with no text and no attributes still says it has no rules text.
examples: Whispering Mantid has no ability text and {Sneaky} on its type line. Its text box shows {Sneaky} and its reminder.
Tidal Menace has no text and no attributes, and still says it has no rules text.

annexD.text: A printed bracket that offers two modes is drawn as two boxes, one around each mode, with the "or" outside them. On the stack, the mode that was not chosen is no longer shown.
examples: Void Memory's "[unit or spell]" is drawn as a unit box and a spell box with "or" between them.

annexD.text: When a once-per-turn ability has been used, its note wears the marker printed on that ability: [Switch1] or [once]. A card that spells the limit out in words, with no marker, gets [Once].
examples: A spent bounded graft ability shows [Switch1], as its card prints.

annexD.text: A card that is {Unstable}, whether printed or acquired, shows {Unstable} on its attribute line, with how it became Unstable.
examples: A modded unit shows {Unstable} on its attribute line, marked as coming from a mod.

annexD.text: A card with a prophecy banner shows the banner in its text box, as printed, and carries the Prophecy reminder.
examples: The Foretold, whose whole printed text box is its banner, shows the banner instead of "no rules text".

annexD.text: A card that can transform shows, in its details, what it transforms into, before the transform's cost is paid. A card that has already transformed shows no such row.
examples: Scholar of the Void's details say it transforms into Beyond, Codex Incarnate, before its hand-discard cost is paid.

annexD.text: The reminder shown for a keyword is the game's own words wherever the game has them, in this order of preference: a reminder printed on a card in the pool; the Manual's sentence under a heading that names the term; a dated quote of a designer-posted card; and only then this client's own sentence.
examples: {Piercing} reads "Excess damage from piercing sources is dealt to the recipient's controller." — the sentence Protective Adaptations prints.
The card-library sentence for {Rot} is used only because neither a card nor the Manual states one.

annexD.text: No reminder, label or rules text shown to a player cites this client's ruling numbers.

Where the game's reminder is shorter than the rule this client enforces, the client's fuller statement is kept and shown under the game's reminder in the card browser. Shortening what a player reads never deletes a rule.
examples: {Piercing} shows the printed sentence, and the card browser also keeps the client's fuller rule beneath it.

annexD.text: The card browser explains every keyword a card names, on its type line or in its text box, and never explains less about a card than the in-game inspector does.
examples: Brough grants {Balanced} from its text box. The browser explains {Balanced} on Brough.

annexD.text: Each item on the stack strip is shown in exactly one state: waiting, resolving, answered (negated), fizzled, or resolved. An item that fizzles is shown as fizzled, never as resolved.
examples: A spell resolves with no legal target. The strip labels it fizzled.

annexD.text: A card on the stack carrying mods is drawn the same way as a unit carrying mods: its mods show beneath it.
examples: A {Modular} spell with a mod is drawn on the stack with the mod peeking out beneath it, as it would be on a unit.

annexD.text: While the other player is building an attack or a block, the live view of it is drawn in the same orientation as the declared one. It differs only in being marked as not yet committed.
examples: When the opponent confirms their attack, no unit changes side or column on the watching player's screen.

annexD.text: A card in hand is marked by what can be done with it now. A card that can be cast is drawn plainly; a card that can only be used another way, such as grafted, augmented or recycled, is drawn differently and says how.
examples: During deployment a {Battle} spell can only be grafted. It is not drawn like a castable deployment card.

annexD.text: A cached card that can be played right now is also shown at the right of the hand. It stays in the cache as well; clicking either copy plays the same card.
examples: A card glimpsed this turn is drawn beside the hand and in the cache row.

annexD.text: In constructed, the menu for recycling a card for a resource lists the elements in the player's own deck first, then Prismite. Every other element of the game, and the Shard, are behind an expander. The menu changes nothing about what is legal: a resource of any element of the game may still be made.
examples: A mono-Fire constructed deck still has all seven elements legal for recycling; the menu just lists Fire first.

annexD.text: Right-clicking a card the player can read shows only things about that card. The erased piles, concede and the game log are on the menu of the bare table. Right-clicking a card back opens the bare-table menu.
examples: Right-clicking a unit offers its details and the judge, not concede.
Right-clicking a card in the opponent's hand opens the table menu.

annexD.text: The game log opens from the bare-table menu and shows the whole log.
examples: A log longer than 80 lines is shown in full.

annexD.text: The board shows each player's cache and bin as a small panel. Clicking a panel opens the full cache or bin. A card in the panel that the player can use right now is the exception: one click on it uses the card, as clicking it in the full cache or bin would. Clicking any other card in the panel opens the full cache or bin.
examples: A cached card that can be played now is played by one click on it in the region's cache panel.
A cached {Battle} card during deployment cannot be played now, so clicking it opens the full cache.
A mod in the bin that can be applied now is one click from the bin panel: the click starts applying it.
A bin card that cannot be used now opens the full bin when clicked.

annexD.text: While an open decision stops a player from acting (see rule D2.1), no card in that player's cache panel is used by one click: clicking one opens the full cache. A cached card that is one of the decision's choices is not picked from the panel. A player whom another player's decision does not stop, inside a hidden simultaneous segment (see rule D2.1b), still uses their cached cards from the panel on one click.
examples: In deployment, a Wraith's start-of-deployment choice is open for one player. That player's castable cached card is not one click from the panel; the other player's castable cached card still is, and playing it leaves the decision open.

annexD.text: A scroll hides a card's long-hover tooltip only if the scroll could have moved that card: a scroll of the whole page, or of a panel the card is inside. A scroll of anything else, such as the side rail, leaves the tooltip shown. When no card is hovered, any scroll hides the tooltip.
examples: The side rail scrolls while the pointer rests on a unit on the board. The unit's tooltip stays.
The page scrolls while the pointer rests on a unit. The tooltip is hidden.
A panel holding a different card scrolls. The hovered card's tooltip stays.

annexD.text: An arrow from an effect to its target is aimed at the exact centre of the target. Where the target shows text near its centre (a player's life total, the name on a card drawn without its picture, the label of a stack item with no picture), the arrowhead stops just short of that text, so the text can still be read. On a card whose picture has loaded, the arrowhead is not moved. If the text cannot be cleared without the head stopping more than a head's length outside the target, the head stops where it otherwise would.
examples: An effect targets a player. The arrow points at their life total, and its head stops short of the number.
An arrow to a unit whose picture has loaded ends in the usual place.
A target whose label is too big to clear keeps the usual stopping point.

annexD.text: A warning or a confirmation never makes a legal play illegal. The option stays offered, and going ahead does exactly what the play would have done without the warning.
examples: Fight aimed at two of the player's own units is still offered and, if confirmed, resolves exactly as it would have.

annexD.text: When choosing X = 0 makes an effect certain to do nothing, the option to stop at X = 0 carries a warning saying so. It stays legal (see 107.2b).
examples: Necromantic Rebuke's option to stop at X = 0 is offered with a warning that it negates nothing.

annexD.text: When a spell has one target that must be an ally and another that may be any unit, and the player picks one of their own units for the second, the client asks whether they meant to. Yes sends the pick. No sends nothing and leaves the same pick open.
examples: Fight's first target is the player's ally; the player then picks another of their own units. The client asks whether they meant to target an ally.

annexD.text: A pass that would end the battle phase, and with it erase the player's unused spell tokens at regroup, first asks the player to confirm. It asks on that pass and on no other window of the battle.
examples: A player holding unused spell tokens passes in the last window of the battle. They are asked to confirm before Regroup erases the tokens.

annexD.text: A dial, a stepper or an "All" button only sets an amount. It never sends an answer; only the confirm button does.
examples: Pressing "All" on a counter-removal cost sets the count to the most it can be, and waits for the player to confirm.

annexD.text: A question whose answer is a number, such as predicting a life total, offers a typed box as well as a dial, so any number in range can be entered. The value itself is sent, not a choice from a list.
examples: Prediction Prophet's prediction can be dialled or typed in as any number in range, and that number itself is sent.

annexD.text: A variable cost paid one point at a time, such as paying X life, offers the same typed box and dial. Nothing is paid until the player confirms. The dial cannot go below what has already been paid.
examples: Paying X life for Flesh Tithe, the player dials to 5 and back to 3; confirming pays 3.
With 1 life already paid, the dial does not go below 1.

annexD.text: The button that ends a variable cost ("That's enough") is drawn as a full button that commits, distinct from the buttons that decline.
examples: "That's enough — X = 3" is a filled button; "decline" stays a quiet one.

annexD.text: A cost that removes counters from allies asks the player to click a unit. One click may take several counters from that unit, up to the most that one unit can give.
examples: Four counters are spread over two allies, two each. One pick can take at most two.

annexD.text: When the dealing player splits combat damage, they are asked one victim at a time, with what is left to assign shown. The client never refuses or forces a split the game would accept.
examples: A strike of 4 into a column of two: the player chooses how much the front unit takes, and the back unit gets the rest.

annexD.text: When an effect does nothing, the game says so and says why. A printed clause that promises a per-seat outcome and then resolves over an empty collection of seats or of picks is announced for that clause, even when another clause of the same card is speaking. Saying so never changes what the effect does.
examples: Bloated Manablub's "Each opponent loses 3 life" resolves in a region with no opponent. The game says so, and no life is lost.
Cull resolves where no player has a unit. The game says so and nothing dies.

annexD.text: A spell that resolves with no legal target fizzles, and the log says "<card>: it has no legal target — nothing happens." (see 704).
examples: Luminous Arc reaches resolution with no target. It fizzles and the log says so.

annexD.text: An "each opponent" effect in a region where no opponent is present says that no opponent is present, and does nothing (see 102.2a).
examples: Bloated Manablub's "Each opponent loses 3 life" during its controller's own deployment says so and takes no life.

annexD.text: A clause that promises something for each player, or each of something, and finds none says so for that clause, even when another clause of the same card has done something.
examples: Recall takes its life when nobody here has a unit to recall, and says the recall did not happen.

annexD.text: An effect that would deal damage to each of a group, and finds nobody in the group, says there was nothing to damage.
examples: A "deal 2 damage to each enemy unit" effect with no enemy unit on the board announces that there was nothing to damage.

annexD.text: An announcement the player is expected to act on, or has lost something by, must be shown somewhere other than the game log. The log is the record, not the notice.
examples: Spell tokens erased after a declined attack are not announced only in the log: the player who lost them is shown a notice where the prompts appear.
